## §A. Status layering

**Base layer** — available whenever the bridge answers: repos, branch workspaces, terminals, agent-vs-shell, `lastActivityAt`, and a **coarse** status (`WORKING` / `NEEDS_INPUT` / `NONE`), plus questions and transcripts.

**Enrichment layer** — only while the Superset desktop app is open: snooze/archive/pin, pinned>active>idle tiering, manual order, pane layout, and the rich dot axes. Bridge reports `enrichmentFresh` + `enrichmentAsOf`.

**Coarse renders honestly.** `NEEDS_INPUT` → red, `WORKING` → yellow, `NONE` → neutral grey. Never synthesise green from coarse data — green means "ready for review", which is the review axis, an enrichment concept. Coarse dots draw as a **hollow ring**, rich dots as a **filled disc**, so the user can tell which dots to trust without reading a banner. Red is red in both.

**Stale ≠ never-enriched.** A workspace can exist in base data with no enrichment row at all (created after the last export) — the exact shape of a bug this codebase already hit. No enrichment row → default tier by base activity, no pin/snooze affordances, coarse dot, *not* greyed. Enrichment row present but not fresh → shown, affordances greyed, "as of 14:02" on the tier header. Conflating them files a brand-new red workspace under a stale tier or hides it in a stale archived section.

**Invariant: the notification path never reads the enrichment layer.** Notification decisions come from base status and question events only. A snoozed workspace going red therefore notifies by construction — in every connection state, with no conditional to get wrong.

## §B. Transport + connectivity classifier

`cloudflared` runs on the desktop dialling out; the bridge binds `127.0.0.1` only. The phone makes ordinary HTTPS/WSS requests from any network. No VPN state anywhere in the UI.

**Detection problem:** Cloudflare's 1xxx codes (1033 = "Cloudflare Tunnel error", no healthy `cloudflared`) appear in the **response body, not a status header**. Parsing Cloudflare's error HTML would break the first time they restyle it.

**Fix:** the bridge stamps `X-Superset-Bridge: <ver>` on every response it originates. Cloudflare stamps `cf-ray` on everything. Between those two headers every state is distinguishable.

| Signal | State | Banner | User action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No response; `NetworkCapabilities` lacks `NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED` | `NO_INTERNET` | "No internet on this phone." | check signal / captive portal |
| `cf-ray` present, no `X-Superset-Bridge`, 502/503/530 | `DESKTOP_OFFLINE` | "mk-xps is offline or asleep." | wake the desktop |
| `X-Superset-Bridge`, 200, `enrichmentFresh == false` | `SUPERSET_CLOSED` | "Superset isn't open on mk-xps. Layout from 14:02; agent status is basic." | open Superset |
| 401/403 **with** our JSON error envelope | `AUTH_REJECTED` | "This device is no longer authorised." | re-pair via QR |
| 403/429 with `cf-ray`, **no** envelope (Access denial, WAF 1020, rate-limit 1015) | `EDGE_REJECTED` | "Blocked at the Cloudflare edge." | check/rotate service token |
| `X-Superset-Bridge`, 200, fresh | `ONLINE` | none | — |

`ConnectionClassifier` in `:core:transport` is the only place mapping outcome→state; one `GET /v1/health` resolves it. A WebSocket drop never infers state on its own — it triggers a classifier run, because a socket closing tells you nothing about why.

All non-`ONLINE` states behave identically for data: keep the last-known tree, queue replies, never blank. Only the copy and the suggested action differ — which is the point, since "check your signal", "wake the desktop", "open Superset" and "re-pair" are four different Tuesdays.

**Keepalive is load-bearing.** Cloudflare supports WebSockets on all plans and closes connections idle in both directions "for a period of time", declining to state the interval and telling you to heartbeat. 20 s server ping / 45 s client dead-man sits inside any plausible value. Tell: if the socket dies at a *metronomic* interval, that's the edge idle close — shorten the ping, don't lengthen the backoff. Diagnostics records socket uptime and last close code.

The edge also enforces an origin-response timeout (Cloudflare 524), so every REST response must be bounded and paginated. No unbounded snapshot, no long-poll.

## §C. Question availability — main-agent vs opaque red (NEW)

Teammate/subagent questions fire `AskUserQuestion` but write no transcript to disk; their text lives only in the desktop renderer. So a terminal can be red for two structurally different reasons, and the client must model both as first-class rather than treating one as a degraded version of the other.

**`ANSWERABLE`** — a main-agent question we hold in full: `headerText`, `questionText`, `options[{label, description}]`, `multiSelect`, `allowFreeText`.

**`OPAQUE`** — the terminal reports `NEEDS_INPUT` but no question record exists (subagent/teammate question, or a question shape we don't yet parse).

Design consequences:

- **Opaque reds still notify.** The user's need — "an agent is blocked" — is identical. What differs is what they can do about it.
- **Tapping an opaque red opens a "Needs input on the desktop" panel, not a question sheet.** It shows what we genuinely know: workspace, branch, agent, how long it's been red, and the last ~10 messages for context. Then one honest line: "This question came from a subagent or teammate. Its text only exists in Superset on the desktop." No option buttons. No answer field.
- **The composer is disabled on an opaque red.** This is a safety rule, not tidiness — see §D. Typing free text at a terminal that is waiting on a question feeds that text to the question. On an opaque red we cannot see what the question is, so we cannot know what we'd be answering. Blocked, with the reason stated.
- **The notification has a distinct shape:** title "Needs input on the desktop", no quick actions, no `RemoteInput`. Tapping opens the panel above.
- **The watch buzzes with a different haptic** — a single short pulse rather than the answerable double — and shows "Needs input — only answerable on the desktop". Distinguishable haptics teach the user which buzzes are actionable from the wrist and which mean "walk to the desk". If you'd rather keep opaque reds phone-only, that's a one-line change in `WatchBridge`; my recommendation is to buzz, because a silently-blocked agent is the failure this app exists to prevent.

A question can transition `OPAQUE → ANSWERABLE` if the bridge later learns the text. The panel and the sheet are separate destinations bound to the same terminal id, so that transition swaps the destination rather than mutating a half-built sheet.

## §D. Answer safety — the bare-digit hazard (NEW, and it drives a lot)

Answering is a **single bare digit that both selects and submits, with no confirmation step**, and stale input has been empirically shown to land as a real user message to the agent. So a mistimed answer does not merely fail — it injects a stray `2` into the transcript, which the agent reads as a genuine instruction. Everything below follows from that.

**1. The client never constructs keystrokes.** It sends semantic intent — `{selectedIndices: [Int]}` or `{freeText: String}` — and the desktop owns the byte encoding. The client is structurally incapable of emitting a stray digit.

**2. Every answer carries a question fingerprint.** The request is `{questionId, questionFingerprint, idempotencyKey, selectedIndices | freeText}`, where the fingerprint is the bridge's revision or a hash over question text + options. The desktop injects only if the live question still matches, otherwise it returns `409 ALREADY_ANSWERED` or `410 SUPERSEDED`. The digit reaches the terminal only when the desktop can prove the same question is still on screen.

**3. Never blind-retry an answer.** This is the rule that matters most, and it inverts normal outbox behaviour. A network timeout after the request was written is *ambiguous* — the answer may have landed. Standard exponential-backoff retry of a POST is exactly what produces a duplicate stray digit. So the outbox gains an `INFLIGHT_UNKNOWN` → `VERIFYING` path: on any ambiguous failure, **do not resend**; poll `GET /v1/questions/<id>` until the question's state is known, then resolve to `CONFIRMED` or re-enqueue as a fresh attempt with a fresh fingerprint. The idempotency key keeps the *server* safe; the verify step keeps the *client* honest about what it displays. `SEND_MESSAGE` entries keep ordinary retry; only answers get this treatment.

**4. Three visible states per answer, never collapsed.** `PENDING` (outlined option, spinner) → `CONFIRMED` (filled tick, "answered") or `FAILED` / `SUPERSEDED` (amber, with the reason and either a retry or "open on desktop"). The word "sent" never appears on its own. Optimistic rendering stays, but optimistic and confirmed are visually distinct at a glance.

**5. Confirmation is two-stage**, since the terminal snapshot isn't available to corroborate. `ACCEPTED` from the bridge means "injected into the live question" → show "answered". The subsequent `question.resolved` event is the confirmation → show "confirmed". `ACCEPTED` with no `resolved` inside ~15 s → "sent, not yet confirmed — check the desktop". Honest about the gap rather than papering it.

**6. `multiSelect` changes the interaction.** Single-select: tap = submit, matching the desktop's one-keystroke behaviour, one tap from the watch. Multi-select: options are checkboxes and nothing is sent until an explicit **Submit**. Mixing these would be the worst outcome — a user trained on tap-to-submit checking three boxes and firing three separate answers.

**7. The composer refuses to send into a pending question.** If a terminal has an `ANSWERABLE` question open, free text typed in the chat composer would be consumed as the answer. The client blocks it and offers the question's own free-text field instead (when `allowFreeText`). On an `OPAQUE` red it blocks outright.

**8. Notification actions are safe only because they share the path.** Quick-action option buttons stay, but the `BroadcastReceiver` never touches the network — it enqueues an outbox entry with the fingerprint it was built with, and the same guards apply. **`RemoteInput` free-text on question notifications is dropped in v1**: free text is the highest-corruption payload and the notification is where staleness is worst. Free text lives in the app, where current question state is visible.

**9. Retraction is a correctness requirement.** Cancel on local answer, on `question.resolved` over WS, on FCM state push, and — new — a **full sweep on every app foreground**, reconciling every posted notification against Room. The likeliest stale-notification scenario is the phone missing an event while dozing, and a stale notification is now a corruption vector, not an annoyance.

**10. The watch validates locally before it costs anything.** `/answer` carries the fingerprint the watch saw. The phone checks it against Room *before* enqueuing and acks `SUPERSEDED` immediately if stale — no network, no risk. Watch DataItem lag is the most likely staleness source and this catches it for free.

## §0. Packaging constraint

Google's Data Layer overview: *"The package name must match across devices. The signature of the package must match across devices."* → phone and wear APKs share one `applicationId` (`family.khaira.supersetcompanion`) and one keystore, different `versionCode`. Violate it and the Data Layer delivers nothing, silently, no exception, no log. Diagnostics shows both installs' signing digest.

## §3. Screens + navigation

**Phone:** Home (sidebar mirror + banner) · Chat detail · **Question sheet** (answerable) · **Opaque-red panel** · Settings/pairing · Diagnostics.

Diagnostics carries: connection state *and the exact signal that produced it* (`cf-ray`, presence of `X-Superset-Bridge`, status), WS uptime + last close code, cursor, base epoch, `enrichmentFresh`/`enrichmentAsOf`, outbox depth **with any `VERIFYING` entries called out**, FCM token, both signing digests, notification-permission state, Access service-token id (never the secret), bridging escape hatch, and a **dot-provenance overlay** labelling every rendered dot with its source layer. This fork's dot bugs were solved by `agent-dot-render.log`; the phone needs the same "why is that dot that colour" answer without a rebuild.

**Adaptive layout.** Home + chat are one `NavigableListDetailPaneScaffold` (`adaptive-navigation` 1.2.0); the rest are Nav2 destinations above it. `currentWindowAdaptiveInfo()` + the default `calculatePaneScaffoldDirective` maps expanded width → two panes, compact/medium → one. The Fold's cover display lands in compact, the inner display in expanded. Predictive back is built in since adaptive 1.1.0; default back has been `PopUntilScaffoldValueChange` since 1.1.0-beta02, so cover-screen back goes detail→list with no custom handling.

**Selection across fold/unfold.** Folding is a configuration change and recreates the Activity. Do **not** use `android:configChanges` — it breaks the size-class recomputation the scaffold depends on. Three layers: `selectedTerminalId: StateFlow<String?>` in `HomeViewModel` backed by `SavedStateHandle` (source of truth, survives process death); `rememberListDetailPaneScaffoldNavigator<String>()` driven *from* that state with a plain `String` key so it serializes; per-terminal scroll offsets in a ViewModel map rather than `rememberSaveable` in a detail pane that recomposes across changing ids. `android:resizeableActivity="true"`.

**Question sheet (structured data only).** Header · question text · options · answer state · free-text field when `allowFreeText` · collapsible context strip of the last ~10 messages. Single-select options are large buttons where **tap = submit**; `multiSelect` renders checkboxes plus an explicit **Submit**. Each option carries its full `description` beneath the label, unclamped. A rendered terminal view is a later enhancement and nothing here depends on it.

**Watch:** question screen (`ScreenScaffold` + `TransformingLazyColumn`: header, uncapped question body, `OptionChip` per option with label **and** full description, dictation/free-text where allowed, "answer on phone") · **opaque-red screen** · sending · answered (`ConfirmationDialog` naming the winning answer and its origin) · and four distinct error states — *phone unreachable*, *queued at phone*, *needs phone auth*, *superseded/expired*. Never one generic failure. `SwipeDismissableNavHost`.

## §4. Data model

Room 2.8.4, **base and enrichment in separate tables** joined by a `@DatabaseView`. Separate because enrichment must be replaceable and expirable as a unit without touching the tree, and one upsert path across both layers would eventually blend them.

**Base:** `repos`(id, name, path, lastActivityAt) · `workspaces`(id, repoId, branch, title, lastActivityAt) · `terminals`(id, workspaceId, title, kind AGENT/SHELL, agentKind, `coarseStatus`, `needsInputSince`, lastActivityAt) · `messages` PK `(terminalId, seq)` with role, text, toolName, toolSummary, toolDetailJson, createdAt, final · `pending_questions`(questionId PK, terminalId, workspaceId, **`availability` ∈ {ANSWERABLE, OPAQUE}**, headerText, questionText, **`multiSelect`**, allowFreeText, **`fingerprint`**, createdAt, state ∈ {PENDING, ANSWERING, ANSWERED, SUPERSEDED, EXPIRED, CANCELLED}, answeredBy, answeredAt, answerJson, `confirmed` Boolean, notificationId) · `question_options` PK `(questionId, index)` with label + uncapped description.

An `OPAQUE` row is created from the base `NEEDS_INPUT` signal with no text — it exists so notification, dedup and retraction all run through one table regardless of availability.

**Enrichment** (each carries `asOf`): `repo_enrichment`(pinnedAt, manualOrder, rollupStatus) · `workspace_enrichment`(tier, manualOrder, pinnedAt, snoozeUntil, archivedAt, paneLayoutJson, rollupStatus) · `terminal_enrichment`(permissionAxis, workingAxis, reviewAxis, backgroundAxis, derivedStatus) · `enrichment_state`(fresh, asOf, sourceEpoch) as one row.

Axes are **mirrored, never re-derived** — this codebase established (DOT-AXES) that status comes from independently latched axes; re-deriving on a second client guarantees drift that stays invisible until a dot is wrong at the worst moment.

**Outbox:** `localId` PK, `idempotencyKey` (UUIDv4, unique), `kind` ∈ {ANSWER_QUESTION, SEND_MESSAGE}, `targetId`, `fingerprint`, `payloadJson`, `createdAt`, `attempts`, `nextAttemptAt`, `state` ∈ {QUEUED, INFLIGHT, **INFLIGHT_UNKNOWN**, **VERIFYING**, ACKED, CONFIRMED, SUPERSEDED, REJECTED}, `lastError`. `sync_state`(cursor, baseEpoch, lastSnapshotAt).

**Render view.** `workspace_view` = `workspaces LEFT JOIN workspace_enrichment`, exposing `statusSource` ∈ {RICH, COARSE}; the UI binds it straight to filled-vs-ring, no branching scattered through composables. Rollups compute from whichever layer each contributor has, precedence red > yellow > blue > green regardless of source, marked COARSE if **any** contributor is coarse — pessimistic, because claiming fidelity you don't have is the failure that matters.

**Cache-first, mandatory.** Render whatever is in Room immediately, always. Connection and sync state drive only the banner and the empty-state choice (no rows + syncing = skeleton; no rows + ready = "nothing here"). Never blank, hide or grey existing rows because a fetch is in flight or readiness is false. Writes and seeding are the exception.

**Reconcile.** `questionId` is desktop-generated and the PK, so redelivery is idempotent; a PENDING event for a locally-ANSWERED question is a replay and is ignored. Answer endpoint idempotent on `(questionId, idempotencyKey)`; `409 ALREADY_ANSWERED {answeredBy, answeredAt, answer}`, `410 SUPERSEDED`, distinct `410 EXPIRED`. The desktop is sole arbiter via compare-and-set; no client decides it won.

## §5. Sync engine

> **Base is delta. Enrichment is replace-whole.**

Base is large and append-heavy and needs cursors and epochs. Enrichment is a few hundred rows the renderer rebuilds from scratch on start — deltaing it invents a merge problem that doesn't exist. On every `enrichment.snapshot`, replace the enrichment tables in one transaction.

**Foreground.** One WebSocket to `wss://superset.khaira.family/v1/stream?cursor=<n>`, bearer token plus Access service-token headers. Opened on Activity resume, closed ~20 s after the last resume so a fold or rotate doesn't churn it. `hello{baseEpoch, minSeq, serverSeq, enrichmentFresh, enrichmentAsOf, capabilities}` → on epoch mismatch or `cursor < minSeq`, paginated snapshot-on-gap, replace in one transaction, resume. Ping 20 s, dead-man 45 s, jittered backoff 1 s→30 s. Every drop runs the classifier before touching the banner.

Events: `base.*` (cursored delta), `enrichment.snapshot` / `enrichment.status{fresh, asOf}` (uncursored), `question.resolved` (the retraction and confirmation signal).

**Capabilities, not inference.** `hello` and the snapshot carry `capabilities: {answer, send}`. If answering is unavailable the sheet goes read-only with "answering needs Superset open on the desktop", and any answer queues as deferred with plain copy. The client never guesses.

**Background — what deliberately does not run.** No persistent WebSocket, no foreground service, no periodic polling. Doze would kill a background socket, Cloudflare would idle-close it, Wear OS 7 further hardened FGS use.

**FCM covers the gap.** High-priority data-only on any transition to RED, always with a user-visible notification. Normal-priority data-only, coalesced ~1/30 s, for everything else including `enrichmentFresh` flips. That split is load-bearing: FCM tracks 7 days of per-instance behaviour and **downgrades high-priority messages that don't produce a user-visible notification**, and deprioritizes further when notification permission is revoked. Pushing state churn at high priority would poison the reds.

Payload, well under FCM's documented 4096-byte cap: `{v:1, kind, eventId, questionId?, workspaceId?, cursor}` — opaque ids only. No question text, branch names or repo paths; FCM is not end-to-end encrypted.

`onMessageReceived` gets seconds and must not do network work → enqueue an **expedited** `OneTimeWorkRequest`, which gets a quota exemption when scheduled directly after a high-priority dispatch. `PushFetchWorker` fetches deltas, writes Room, reconciles notifications, pushes to the watch. `onDeletedMessages()` → force a snapshot.

**Outbox drain.** WorkManager unique work `"outbox"`, `NetworkType.CONNECTED`, `APPEND_OR_REPLACE`, exponential backoff — **for `SEND_MESSAGE` only**. `ANSWER_QUESTION` entries in `INFLIGHT_UNKNOWN` route to `AnswerVerifyWorker`, which polls question state and never resends (§D.3). Entries hold rather than retry while the classifier reports `AUTH_REJECTED`.

## §6. Notifications

**Channels:** `questions` — `IMPORTANCE_HIGH`, vibrate + sound, badge. `sync_errors` — `IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT`, and this now carries `AUTH_REJECTED`, because a revoked token silently killing all pushes is exactly the failure nobody notices for a week. `state` — `IMPORTANCE_LOW`, created but unused in v1.

**Two shapes, one per pending question:**

*Answerable* — id = stable hash of `questionId`; title = branch + agent; `BigTextStyle` full question; content intent → `supersetcompanion://question/<id>`; up to 3 option quick-actions when labels are short (single-select only — multi-select has no meaningful one-tap action); **no `RemoteInput`** (§D.8). `setOnlyAlertOnce(true)`, `setAutoCancel(false)` — cancellation is explicit, from one place.

*Opaque* — title "Needs input on the desktop"; body names the workspace and how long it's been blocked; **no actions**; content intent → `supersetcompanion://terminal/<id>/blocked`.

Both group under `GROUP_QUESTIONS` with an explicit `setGroupSummary(true)` inbox-style summary (Android auto-bundles at 4+, but an explicit summary gives a correct count and a single dismiss).

**POST_NOTIFICATIONS (Android 13+)** requested after pairing behind a rationale screen; denial makes the app unable to do its one job → persistent blocker card with a settings deep link. Check `areNotificationsEnabled()` on every foreground and report it to the desktop, since FCM deprioritizes high-priority sends to instances that cannot post.

**Retraction** — `QuestionNotifier.reconcile(questionId)` is the single funnel, reading Room and cancelling when state ≠ PENDING. Called from the WS handler, `PushFetchWorker`, the local optimistic path, and `NotificationSweeper` on every foreground. Cancels the group summary when the last child goes.

### Bridged-notification suppression

Default Wear behaviour bridges phone notifications to every paired watch; with both apps posting the user gets duplicates, and the bridged copy is the clamped one this architecture exists to avoid.

`setLocalOnly(true)` blocks bridging to all wearables unconditionally, and Google's docs caution it's for notifications that must appear only on the originating device, saying dual phone+watch apps should use bridging options instead. `BridgingManager.fromContext(ctx).setConfig(BridgingConfig.Builder(ctx, isBridgingEnabled = false).addExcludedTags(...).build())` from `androidx.wear.phone.interactions.notifications` is set **on the watch**, at runtime, overriding the manifest — the documented dual-app path.

**Three layers:** (1) `:app-wear` calls `BridgingManager` with bridging disabled on first run, `BOOT_COMPLETED`, and every app start. (2) Phone notifications carry `WearableExtender().setBridgeTag("question")` so a re-enable can exclude exactly that tag. (3) A Diagnostics toggle flipping phone notifications to `setLocalOnly(true)`, off by default, as escape hatch. **Rejected:** manifest `notificationBridgeMode = NO_BRIDGING` — the docs warn it takes effect the instant the watch app installs, before pairing, silently swallowing notifications during setup.

**Watch notification:** channel `questions_wear`, `IMPORTANCE_HIGH`, distinct vibration per §C. **No `fullScreenIntent`** — Android 14+ restricts `USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` to calling and alarm apps for new installs.

## §7. Phone ↔ watch protocol (Data Layer)

`DataClient` for the pending set (DataItems persist and sync, so a watch that was off or out of range gets current state on reconnect with no phone-side retry logic) · `MessageClient` for one-shot events (sending wakes the target's `WearableListenerService`) · `CapabilityClient` for reachability (`superset_companion_watch` / `_phone` in `res/values/wear.xml`) · `ChannelClient` unused.

| Path | Direction | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `/questions/pending/<id>` (DataItem) | phone → watch | `{v, revision, questionId, availability, fingerprint, workspaceLabel, branch, agent, headerText, questionText, options:[{index,label,description}], multiSelect, allowFreeText, createdAt}` |
| `/state` (DataItem) | phone → watch | `{v, revision, connection, canAnswer, pendingCount}` |
| `/wake/question` (Message) | phone → watch | `{questionId, availability}` |
| `/answer` (Message) | watch → phone | `{questionId, fingerprint, idempotencyKey, selectedIndices?, freeText?, answeredAt}` |
| `/answer/ack` (Message) | phone → watch | `{questionId, result: ACCEPTED\|QUEUED\|CONFIRMED\|ALREADY_ANSWERED\|SUPERSEDED\|EXPIRED\|NEEDS_PHONE_AUTH}` |
| `/question/resolved` (Message) | phone → watch | `{questionId, answeredBy}` |

`availability` on the DataItem is what routes the watch to the question screen versus the opaque screen. `fingerprint` round-trips so the phone can reject a stale watch answer locally, with no network cost (§D.10). `/answer/ack` distinguishes `ACCEPTED` from `CONFIRMED` so the watch's confirmation is as honest as the phone's.

**`revision` is mandatory.** DataItems are content-deduped — a byte-identical put produces no `onDataChanged` at all. A monotonic `revision` guarantees change detection. Silent, and it rarely reproduces in testing because content usually happens to differ.

**Red-event wake path.** desktop → FCM high-priority → phone `onMessageReceived` → expedited `PushFetchWorker` → HTTPS fetch → Room → `putDataItem` + `sendMessage("/wake/question")` → watch service wakes → vibrate + local notification → tap → `QuestionActivity` reads the already-synced DataItem. Roughly 3–10 s desktop→buzz. If too slow, the v1.1 optimization is a stub DataItem from the FCM metadata, buzz immediately, fill the body after the fetch.

**Phone unreachable from the watch:** write to a DataStore-backed `WatchOutbox` (cap ~5), show "Saved — will send when your phone is back", retry on `onCapabilityChanged` and next app open. Never show success. The send path sits behind an `AnswerTransport` interface so §8's direct-HTTP option is additive.

## §8. Should the watch talk to the bridge directly?

The tunnel is public, so the Pixel Watch 4 could reach it over its own Wi-Fi/LTE. **Recommendation: no for v1 — keep phone-paired Data Layer.** Your expectation holds; the strongest reason isn't the obvious one.

1. **When the phone is present, "direct" isn't direct.** Google's network-access docs state that with a Bluetooth connection to the phone available, watch traffic is *proxied through the phone*. So in the common case a watch-direct design has the same phone dependency plus a second HTTP stack, a second TLS handshake and a second copy of the credential. Zero reliability gain, all the cost.
2. **It doubles the devices holding an internet-usable code-execution credential.** The endpoint is public and the device token is what stands between the internet and terminal-write. Putting a second copy on the device with the weakest local protections and the highest loss rate is the worst trade available here. This decides it.
3. **Radio acquisition isn't free.** High-bandwidth transport needs an explicit `ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork(TRANSPORT_WIFI)` plus `bindProcessToNetwork`; the radio may be off, and `onAvailable()` never fires with no saved in-range network, so you need timeouts and an "add a Wi-Fi network" escape hatch. Bluetooth-proxied bandwidth can be as low as 4 KB/s — fine for our payloads, but it shows where the platform is steering you.
4. **The wake path would need rebuilding** — a second FCM registration, the desktop tracking two tokens, the watch waking its own radio per red event.
5. **Wear defers background work hard** — screen off long enough is a subset of Doze; stationary is regular Doze.
6. **Even working, the experience is poor** — a long question on a 45 mm screen with no phone fallback and no usable keyboard.

The existing `WatchOutbox` already handles "phone died in my bag" honestly. "Phone at home, answer now" stays unsolved in v1 by choice. **If ever built:** the watch gets its own token scoped to `answer:question` **only** — never `send:message` — its own separately-revocable Access service token, and it falls back to Data Layer whenever a phone node is reachable.

## §9. Security

The endpoint is now public and continuously scanned, so the device token is — unless we add something — the only thing between the internet and terminal-write.

**Two independent credentials.** (1) A **Cloudflare Access service token** (`CF-Access-Client-Id` / `CF-Access-Client-Secret`) checked at the edge under a Service Auth policy, so traffic without it never reaches the desktop, including the pairing endpoint; revocable from the Cloudflare dashboard independently of the phone (documented account limit: 50 service tokens). This is a recommendation to the bridge/infra work, but the client should send it from day one — retrofitting a second header later leaves an exposed endpoint in the meantime. (2) The **per-device bearer token** from the bridge, scoped and revocable. An attacker needs both, from different systems, revocable through different consoles.

**Provisioning without secrets in the APK.** The pairing QR carries `{host, serviceTokenId, serviceTokenSecret, pairingCode, expiresAt}`, single-use, ~120 s TTL. The service token arrives from a screen only the user sees, never from the binary, so decompiling a stolen APK yields nothing.

**Token storage.** `androidx.security:security-crypto` is **deprecated** — all APIs deprecated at 1.1.0-alpha07 (Apr 2025), still deprecated in stable 1.1.0 (Jul 2025), "in favour of existing platform APIs and direct use of Android Keystore". So no `EncryptedSharedPreferences`. `KeystoreSecretBox` uses an `AndroidKeyStore` AES-256-GCM key (`setIsStrongBoxBacked(true)` with fallback), IV generated by `Cipher`, never reused, `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` with a ~300 s window — so both tokens are cryptographically unreadable while the phone is locked. Stolen locked phone → nothing usable. Stolen unlocked phone → full read plus code execution, which the rest targets.

**Biometric gate — recommendation: gate free-text sends, not option taps, never reads.** Free text is unbounded blast radius (arbitrary text into a live terminal is arbitrary code execution) and the gate rides the 5-minute Keystore window, so realistic use prompts about once per session. Option taps stay ungated because gating them destroys the one-tap watch flow that is the product — the right place for "yes, delete everything" is the desktop marking that option destructive, and those inherit the gate. Reads stay ungated because friction buys nothing there. Worth stating plainly: the biometric gate defends against a stolen *unlocked* phone, **not** against the internet. The internet is handled by the Access token, the auth-bound Keystore key, and server-side scopes.

**Certificate pinning — recommendation: don't.** Cloudflare Universal SSL certificates have a **90-day validity period** with renewal beginning 30 days out, and Cloudflare **controls the certificate authorities** and can change them. Pinning the leaf breaks the app at least every 90 days; pinning the CA moves the cliff somewhere you get no notice. For a sideloaded app with no update channel, a break means it can't reach the bridge exactly when you need it, and you're plugging in a cable to fix it. It also doesn't defend the realistic threats, which are a stolen token and a stolen phone. Instead: a `network_security_config.xml` with `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` and no shipped debug overrides, standard platform trust, and the Access service token as the real second factor. A `<pin-set>` with an `expiration` attribute exists as a middle option but silently stops pinning after that date — security theatre with maintenance attached.

**Rest:** scoped tokens (`read:tree`, `read:messages`, `answer:question`, `send:message`) each independently revocable · per-device revocation and ~90-day rotation via a challenge signed by the device's Keystore ECDSA key that never leaves the TEE · `android:allowBackup="false"` plus `dataExtractionRules` excluding both tokens and the Room DB · no tokens/question text/transcript in release logcat, stripped with R8 · `FLAG_SECURE` on chat and question screens as a setting, default off.

## §11. Open risks

1. **Stray-digit corruption is the highest-severity failure in this product.** Every guard in §D is one bug away from being bypassed, and the failure is silent — a `2` in a transcript looks like the user typed it. Recommend an integration test that asserts the client *never* emits a second answer for one `questionId`, and desktop-side logging of every injected answer with its fingerprint, so an incident is reconstructable.
2. **Desktop sleep kills the tunnel.** Windows sleeping stops `cloudflared` → 1033 → `DESKTOP_OFFLINE`. Nothing the client can fix; the prerequisite is a power policy that keeps the machine awake. Expect this to be the most common non-`ONLINE` state.
3. **The public endpoint is scanned continuously.** Expect bridge log noise and occasional Cloudflare WAF/rate-limit hits on *our own* traffic (1015, 1020). The classifier must bucket those as `EDGE_REJECTED`, not `DESKTOP_OFFLINE` — otherwise the user goes and pokes a desktop that was fine. Verify with a deliberate rate-limit trip at M4.
4. **WebSocket idle timeout at the edge, value undocumented.** Cloudflare confirms an idle close and declines to state the interval. 20 s/45 s should be safe; a metronomic death interval is the tell.
5. **Origin-response timeout (524)** on any slow endpoint — the paginated snapshot is the candidate to blow it. Test with a deliberately large tree.
6. **`OPAQUE` reds may be more common than expected.** If most of the desktop's questions come from teammates, the phone becomes a notifier rather than an answerer and the product's value drops sharply. Worth measuring the main-agent/subagent split on a real day *before* M8, because it changes whether the watch is worth building at all.
7. **Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4** — still the most likely thing to be wrong. Verify that `BridgingManager(isBridgingEnabled = false)` actually suppresses the phone's bridged copy when both apps share an `applicationId`, that it survives a reboot, and what happens between install and first launch.
8. **Wear alerting behaviour.** Verify what `IMPORTANCE_HIGH` does with the screen off — display wake, vibration duration — and confirm the two haptic patterns are actually distinguishable on-wrist. Theatre mode, bedtime mode, DND and off-wrist all suppress with no supported bypass.
9. **Cold `WearableListenerService` wake.** Binds on demand, but an app unlaunched for a while can land in a restricted standby bucket. Measure on a watch idle overnight — the scenario that matters is the untested one.
10. **DataItem content dedup** — byte-identical puts produce no `onDataChanged`; the `revision` field is the fix.
11. **FCM high-priority deprioritization** — 7 days of per-instance behaviour; high-priority messages that don't yield a visible notification get demoted, revoked permission demotes further. First suspect if reds arrive late.
12. **Sideloading the wear APK** — `adb` over Wi-Fi for every install, and a signature mismatch makes the Data Layer silently deliver nothing. One keystore, backed up, plus the Diagnostics digest line.
13. **Enrichment-absent vs enrichment-stale** — the likeliest logic bug, with precedent here. Test explicitly: create a workspace with Superset closed, drive it red, confirm it appears un-tiered and notifies.
14. **Fold configuration changes** — anything in bare `remember` is lost; verify the navigator restores across the fold *and* process death.
15. **Wear Compose M3 API churn** — 1.6.x/1.7.0-alpha have been renaming aggressively (`SwipeToReveal` moved packages, `hierarchicalFocus` → `hierarchicalFocusGroup`, `ButtonContent` into `ButtonDefaults`). Pin 1.6.2 exactly.
16. **Uncapped question text on a 45 mm screen** — the justification for the whole watch architecture; validate readability early. If it fails, the answer is summary-plus-expand, not a retreat to bridged notifications.
17. **Battery** — each red event costs an FCM wake, an expedited worker, an HTTPS round trip and a Bluetooth sync. Rate-limit on the desktop, not the phone.
18. **Scope creep at the composer** — the free-text field is one line from becoming a general "start something". Enforce server-side: send accepts only existing terminal ids.

**Deleted:** all Tailscale risks, the `ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK` risk, and the terminal-card binding-race risk (feature cut from v1).

## Bridge contract this depends on (tasks #2 / #3)

- `X-Superset-Bridge: <ver>` on **every** response the bridge originates — the whole error taxonomy rests on this one header.
- JSON error envelope on 4xx, so bridge-rejected is distinguishable from edge-rejected.
- `GET /v1/health` — cheap, used solely by the classifier.
- `GET /v1/snapshot` — **paginated**; base tree + questions (with `availability`, `multiSelect`, `fingerprint`) + recent messages + enrichment export + freshness + `capabilities`.
- `WS /v1/stream?cursor=` — `base.*` cursored on `(baseEpoch, seq)`; `enrichment.snapshot`/`enrichment.status` uncursored; `question.resolved` for retraction and confirmation. Server ping ≤20 s.
- `GET /v1/questions/<id>` — the verify endpoint `AnswerVerifyWorker` polls; must be safe to call repeatedly and must report whether an answer was applied and by whom.
- `POST /v1/questions/<id>/answer` — takes `{questionFingerprint, idempotencyKey, selectedIndices | freeText}`; **the bridge owns the keystroke encoding**; idempotent on `(questionId, idempotencyKey)`; `409 ALREADY_ANSWERED`, `410 SUPERSEDED`, `410 EXPIRED` as distinct outcomes; `ACCEPTED` means *injected into the live question*, not *received*.
- `POST /v1/terminals/<id>/send` — existing terminal ids only; must reject when that terminal has a pending question.
- Per-device scoped tokens with revocation; pairing QR carrying the Access service token; bridge bound to `127.0.0.1`; FCM sender with the high/normal priority split.

superset-companion

A personal Android phone and Wear OS app that carries agent status off the desktop — so an agent waiting on you doesn't wait for hours.

Designv1 Repo C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion · Desktop fork-superset-windows-arm64 · 28 July 2026

The problem

Agents run in Superset terminals all day. When one needs input it turns red and stops — sometimes for hours, because you're not at the machine. The desktop already computes exactly the signal that matters; it just has no way to reach you.

The watch does one job: buzz when an agent is blocked, show the whole question, take your answer. The phone does the fuller job: the agent tree, readable chats, and a reply box.

Scope

In v1Not in v1
Agent tree, sorted by statusCreating chats, terminals, or workspaces
Read chat transcripts on the phoneMirroring snooze / archive / pin / drag order
Send a message to an existing agentAnswering subagent questions (impossible — see below)
Answer a question from phone or watchAnswering Codex questions
Push notification on redOffline queueing of anything

What we proved before designing

Six assumptions were tested against the live system rather than reasoned about. Four held, two did not, and the two failures reshaped the design.

ClaimResultConsequence
host.db readable while Superset holds itProvenMust open mode=ro. immutable=1 froze at a stale value for a full 45-second poll — it would have shipped a phone that silently never updates.
/events WebSocket streams live statusProven91 messages in 60s, one global socket covers every workspace. But events arrive 2–3× duplicated and there's no snapshot on connect.
Question text and options live in the transcriptProvenMain-agent questions only. Pending vs answered is derivable exactly.
Answer bytes can drive the pickerProvenEstablished empirically by driving the real CLI in a pty. Contract below.
terminal.snapshot worksDisproven404 on the running app — it shipped in v1.18.0, released 27 July; the machine still runs 1.17.0.
.askq markers mean a question is pendingDisproven17 stale markers, oldest 21 days. Presence proves nothing; absence is still a sound veto.

Architecture

Pixel Watch 4        Pixel 10 Pro Fold        Cloudflare       mk-xps (Windows)
┌────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐      ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│ question   │◄─────►│ phone app       │◄────►│  edge   │◄────►│ companion bridge │
│ screen     │ Data  │ Kotlin/Compose  │ HTTPS│ +Access │tunnel│ (Electron main)  │
└────────────┘ Layer │ Room cache      │  WSS └─────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘
                     └────────▲────────┘                        loopback + PSK
                              │                                         │
                        FCM ──┘  opaque event id only              host-service
  • FCM wakes the phone on red. The only push pipe on stock Android that survives Doze without your app holding a socket, and free. Payload is ~120 bytes of opaque ids — no question text ever reaches Google.
  • Cloudflare Tunnel carries everything interactive. cloudflared dials outbound, so there are no inbound ports and no origin IP to attack. Works anywhere, including the watch on LTE.
  • Data Layer carries phone ↔ watch.

Where the bridge lives

A fork-owned module in the Electron main process, apps/desktop/src/main/companion-bridge/, on a fixed loopback port. It needs main-process APIs (safeStorage, powerSaveBlocker, renderer IPC) and, more importantly, fork-only new files never conflict on your nightly upstream merges — only three existing files get touched, each behind a FEATURES.md marker.

The port is fixed and fails loud if taken. cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing — presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

The known hole: the bridge dies with the app. host-service watches the desktop app's PID and exits with it, while the pty daemon is detached and survives. So if Superset closes or crashes, your agents keep running and keep going red — with the bridge and FCM sender dead. You chose to accept this rather than restructure, mitigated by a phone-side liveness watchdog: if the last sync showed working agents and no heartbeat arrives for several minutes, the phone raises a local notification saying contact was lost. That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.

Status

Only coarse status is readable without the desktop app running. The rich dot state — the latched axes — and all of snooze/archive/pin/tiering live in the renderer's browser storage, unreachable from outside.

You cut the enrichment layer from v1. The phone shows the agent tree sorted by status, red first. No snooze mirroring, no pin, no drag order. That removes a renderer exporter, multi-window election, a debounce protocol, and a freshness contract — the single largest complexity item in the design — for something with no effect on the red path.

DotFromNotifies
Needs inputBase layer, always availableYes
WorkingBase layerNo
NeutralBase layer — idleNo

Green is deliberately absent. "Ready for review" is a review-axis concept that only exists in the renderer, and synthesising it from coarse data would be a lie. Red and yellow are honest without it.

Answering a question

This is the sharpest part of the design, and the reason so much of it looks paranoid.

The proven contract

Established by driving the real Claude Code CLI (2.1.220) in a pty across four scripted runs — not inferred from source:

  • Single select: one bare digit both selects and submits. No Enter. There is no confirmation step.
  • Several questions in one call: N digits, then Enter on the review screen.
  • Multi-select inverts the rules: digits and space toggle; Enter toggles rather than submits; submitting is right-arrow to the Submit tab, then Enter. A naive implementation that appends Enter to "submit" silently flips a selection instead.
  • Free text: digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8, then Enter.
  • Bracketed paste is inert. A wrapped digit produces cursor noise and no state change, so terminal.send cannot drive the picker at all — only raw terminal.writeInput works.
The stale-answer hazard, reproduced three ways. When the picker is gone, stray digits land in the composer and a following Enter submits them as a real message — observed: a stray 23 became a genuine prompt the model burned a turn answering. Mid-turn, typed input is queued to steer the running agent. And with a different picker open, a digit commits instantly against the wrong question. Because digits commit atomically there is no safe retry and nothing to intercept.

The guard stack

The phone never constructs keystrokes. It sends semantic intent — a question id, a fingerprint, and chosen option indices — and the bridge owns the byte encoding, so the client is structurally incapable of emitting a stray digit. Before writing anything, the bridge checks six things:

  1. The question's tool_use_id still has no tool_result in the transcript.
  2. The agent-session binding still matches — a /resume or restart invalidates it.
  3. The terminal session is still active.
  4. The permission axis is still latched.
  5. A snapshot confirms the picker is still on screen showing that question.
  6. The .askq marker still exists — worthless as proof, but its absence is a sound veto.

Any failure writes nothing and reports the question as stale. Multi-select re-verifies the screen between each keystroke, since each one can land on a changed screen. On timeout the bridge reports "unconfirmed" and never retries — a blind retry could answer a different question that has since opened, which with atomic digits is unrecoverable.

Interaction is online-only. Nothing queues — not answers, not messages. An answer is a time-sensitive keystroke whose meaning depends on the live screen, so executing it minutes later against a different screen is the wrong contract regardless of how it's guarded. Offline, the app shows the cached tree and refuses to send. You refetch and tap again.

What can't be answered

Subagent and teammate questions produce no transcript on disk — verified: five teammate agents fired questions on one terminal and none wrote a file. Their text exists only in the live renderer.

So a red terminal has two shapes. Answerable — a main-agent question we hold in full. Opaque — blocked, but we cannot see on what. Opaque reds still notify, because "an agent is blocked" is the thing you need to know either way; they open a panel saying so plainly, with no answer field, and the chat composer is disabled there. Typing free text at a terminal awaiting a question feeds that text to the question, and on an opaque red we cannot know what we'd be answering.

Worth measuring early. If most of your questions come from teammates rather than main loops, the phone becomes a notifier rather than an answerer — which changes whether the watch app is worth building. Check the split on a real working day before committing to the watch milestones.

Security

The bridge is on the public internet and terminal write is arbitrary code execution on your desktop. Every reviewer independently said a bearer token alone is not enough, and the hostname becomes public knowledge the moment the TLS certificate hits Certificate Transparency logs.

Four independent layers:

  • Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.
  • Per-request signatures. Pairing establishes a key over the QR — an optical channel that never transits Cloudflare. Every request carries a timestamp, nonce, and HMAC over method, path and body hash. Nothing replayable ever crosses the wire.
  • Encrypted bodies. AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the same pairing secret. Cloudflare terminates TLS, so without this it would see your transcripts, question text, answers and repo names in the clear. You chose to seal now rather than retrofit — retrofitting means breaking the wire and re-pairing every device.
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.

Beyond the wire: writes are rate-limited far more tightly than reads (10/min versus 120/min), every injected write is appended to an audit log before it executes, the bridge refuses to write to plain shells (only terminals with an agent binding), free-text sends require a biometric confirmation while option taps don't, and there's a desktop panic switch that strips write access without unpairing.

Certificate pinning is deliberately rejected: Cloudflare's certificates last 90 days and Cloudflare controls the issuing authorities, so pinning breaks the app on a schedule — and for a sideloaded app with no update channel, that means it fails exactly when you need it.

Blast radius, stated plainly. Anyone holding the pairing key can type into your agent terminals from anywhere on earth. The layers change how reachable and how detectable that is, not the consequence. Revocation is from the desktop and takes effect on the next request.
One recommendation worth acting on separately. Your (BUILD-REPAIR) loop lets an unattended agent edit any non-frozen file, and your own notes say containment is not semantic review. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals. The pairing, crypto, edge and injection directories should join the frozen-paths list — a genuine bug there should fail loud for you, not get silently "repaired" by an agent reading a build log an attacker may have influenced.

Client

Native Kotlin, one Gradle project, phone and watch sharing an applicationId and keystore — the Data Layer silently delivers nothing if either differs.

Phone: home (agent tree, red first), chat detail, question sheet, opaque-red panel, pairing, diagnostics. Home and chat sit in one adaptive scaffold so the Fold's inner screen shows both panes and the cover screen shows one. Selection survives folding via saved state, not remember.

Chat reads conversationally: your messages and the agent's replies, with tool calls collapsed to a one-line chip you can tap to expand.

Question sheet: header, full question, options as large buttons with their full descriptions unclamped, and the last ten messages scrollable above for context. Single-select taps submit; multi-select uses checkboxes and an explicit Submit, because training you on tap-to-submit and then showing checkboxes would fire three separate answers.

Watch: one question screen, uncapped and scrollable. This is why it's a real app rather than a bridged notification — Android clamps notification strings to 1024 characters and truncates silently, so you'd answer a question whose second half you never saw. Opaque reds get a distinct haptic, so you learn from your wrist which buzzes are actionable and which mean "walk to the desk".

Every answer shows three states — pending, confirmed, or failed — never collapsed into "sent". Notifications retract when a question is answered anywhere, including a full sweep every time the app foregrounds, since the likeliest stale notification comes from a push missed while dozing.

Prerequisites

1. Create a Firebase project. Free Spark plan, no card. Only you can create it; the service-account credential then lives on the desktop only.

2. Install cloudflared. Not currently on the machine. Create a named tunnel and a DNS record on khaira.family, which is already on Cloudflare. Run it as a Windows service.

3. Configure Cloudflare Access with a service-token policy on the bridge hostname.

Installing v1.18.0 is not a prerequisite. The bridge ships inside the desktop app, so whatever release carries the bridge carries terminal.snapshot too. It only matters if you want to test against the running app before then.

Build order

Each step is demonstrable on its own, and the first three carry no write risk at all — which is the right place to stop if the byte contract needs more soak time.

  1. Bridge, tunnel, pairing, crypto, read-only API. No write path exists yet.
  2. Phone UI on fake data — tree, chat, question sheet, opaque panel, every connection state. Needs no bridge, so it runs in parallel.
  3. Real reads. Pairing by QR, live tree, live transcripts, notifications for every red.
  4. Answer injection behind the full guard stack, single-select first.
  5. Multi-select and free text with per-keystroke screen verification.
  6. Watch app — question screen, answer path, bridged-notification suppression.

Open risks

  • The byte contract is a private contract with a TUI. It can change on any Claude Code release, silently. It needs a canary test against recorded screens per upgrade — particularly the multi-select inversion, which is invisible in code review.
  • Desktop sleep kills the tunnel, and the keep-awake power request doesn't exist yet — I described it earlier as if it did, which was wrong. Expect "desktop offline" to be the most common non-online state until it's built.
  • Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4 is the most likely thing to be wrong, and needs live-device verification.
  • The public endpoint will be scanned continuously. The app must distinguish "blocked at Cloudflare" from "desktop offline", or you'll go poke a desktop that was fine.

Installing v1.18.0 is not a prerequisite. The bridge ships inside the desktop app, so whatever release carries the bridge carries terminal.snapshot too. It only matters if you want to test against the running app before then.

Build order

Each step is demonstrable on its own, and the first three carry no write risk at all — which is the right place to stop if the byte contract needs more soak time.

  1. Bridge, tunnel, pairing, crypto, read-only API. No write path exists yet.
  2. Phone UI on fake data — tree, chat, question sheet, opaque panel, every connection state. Needs no bridge, so it runs in parallel.
  3. Real reads. Pairing by QR, live tree, live transcripts, notifications for every red.
  4. Answer injection behind the full guard stack, single-select first.
  5. Multi-select and free text with per-keystroke screen verification.
  6. Watch app — question screen, answer path, bridged-notification suppression.

Open risks

  • The byte contract is a private contract with a TUI. It can change on any Claude Code release, silently. It needs a canary test against recorded screens per upgrade — particularly the multi-select inversion, which is invisible in code review.
  • Desktop sleep kills the tunnel, and the keep-awake power request doesn't exist yet — I described it earlier as if it did, which was wrong. Expect "desktop offline" to be the most common non-online state until it's built.
  • Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4 is the most likely thing to be wrong, and needs live-device verification.
  • The public endpoint will be scanned continuously. The app must distinguish "blocked at Cloudflare" from "desktop offline", or you'll go poke a desktop that was fine.
