<div class="wrap">
superset-companion

-

A personal Android phone + Wear OS app that mirrors Superset agent status from the home desktop, lets you read chats on the phone, and answer an agent's question from your watch.

+

A personal Android phone and Wear OS app that carries agent status off the desktop — so an agent waiting on you doesn't wait for hours.
-
-Designv1 scope
-Repo: C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion · Desktop: fork-superset-windows-arm64 · 28 Jul 2026

+

Designv1
+Repo C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion · Desktop fork-superset-windows-arm64 · 28 July 2026
The problem

-

Agents run on the desktop all day. When one needs input it turns red and then it just waits — sometimes for hours, because you're not at the machine. The desktop sidebar already computes exactly the signal that matters; it just can't reach you.

+

Agents run in Superset terminals all day. When one needs input it turns red and stops — sometimes for hours, because you're not at the machine. The desktop already computes exactly the signal that matters; it just has no way to reach you.

-

This app carries that signal to your pocket and your wrist. The watch does one job: buzz when an agent needs you, show the whole question, take your answer. The phone does the fuller job: the same agent tree you see in the sidebar, readable chats, and a reply box.

+

The watch does one job: buzz when an agent is blocked, show the whole question, take your answer. The phone does the fuller job: the agent tree, readable chats, and a reply box.
Scope
<table>
<thead><tr><th>In v1</th><th>Not in v1</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
-Mirror the desktop sidebar tree (repos → branch workspaces → terminals)Creating new chats or terminals
-Read chat transcripts on the phoneCreating branch workspaces / worktrees
-Send a message into an existing agent terminalKanban board
-Answer a pending question from phone or watchWatch agent list or tile
-Push notification on redEditing files / running arbitrary commands
+Agent tree, sorted by statusCreating chats, terminals, or workspaces
+Read chat transcripts on the phoneMirroring snooze / archive / pin / drag order
+Send a message to an existing agentAnswering subagent questions (impossible — see below)
+Answer a question from phone or watchAnswering Codex questions
+Push notification on redOffline queueing of anything
</tbody>

-

Status semantics

+

What we proved before designing

-

Colours and precedence come straight from the desktop, unchanged — the phone is a mirror, not a second opinion.

+

Six assumptions were tested against the live system rather than reasoned about. Four held, two did not, and the two failures reshaped the design.
<div class="scroll">
<table>
-<thead><tr><th>Dot</th><th>Meaning</th><th>Notifies?</th></tr></thead>
+<thead><tr><th>Claim</th><th>Result</th><th>Consequence</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
-RedNeeds your inputYes — phone + watch
-YellowWorking (incl. subagents, compaction, codex holds)No
-GreenReady for reviewNo
-BlueShell / background / cloud activityNo
+host.db readable while Superset holds itProvenMust open mode=ro. immutable=1 froze at a stale value for a full 45-second poll — it would have shipped a phone that silently never updates.
+/events WebSocket streams live statusProven91 messages in 60s, one global socket covers every workspace. But events arrive 2–3× duplicated and there's no snapshot on connect.
+Question text and options live in the transcriptProvenMain-agent questions only. Pending vs answered is derivable exactly.
+Answer bytes can drive the pickerProvenEstablished empirically by driving the real CLI in a pty. Contract below.
+terminal.snapshot worksDisproven404 on the running app — it shipped in v1.18.0, released 27 July; the machine still runs 1.17.0.
+.askq markers mean a question is pendingDisproven17 stale markers, oldest 21 days. Presence proves nothing; absence is still a sound veto.
</tbody>

-

Precedence when a workspace rolls up several terminals: red > yellow > blue > green.

-
Snooze does not mute red. Snoozed and archived workspaces mirror the desktop's collapsed reveal-sections, but a snoozed workspace that goes red still notifies. Snooze means "stop showing me this", not "let an agent block forever".
Architecture
-<pre><code>Pixel Watch 4          Pixel 10 Pro Fold           Cloudflare      mk-xps (Windows)
-│ question     │◄─────►│ phone app        │◄───────►│ tunnel │◄──►│ companion bridge │
-│ screen       │ Data  │ Compose M3       │  HTTPS  │  edge  │    │ (fork-only)      │
-                          FCM high-priority ◄────────────────────── host-service
-                          data message (red only)
+<pre><code>Pixel Watch 4        Pixel 10 Pro Fold        Cloudflare       mk-xps (Windows)
+│ question   │◄─────►│ phone app       │◄────►│  edge   │◄────►│ companion bridge │
+│ screen     │ Data  │ Kotlin/Compose  │ HTTPS│ +Access │tunnel│ (Electron main)  │
+                        FCM ──┘  opaque event id only              host-service

-

Three transports, each doing the one thing it's good at:
<ul>

-
  • FCM wakes the phone when an agent goes red. It's the only push pipe on stock Android that survives Doze without your app holding a socket open, and it's free with no billing. The message carries an opaque event id, never the question text — content is fetched afterwards, so nothing sensitive transits Google.

-
  • Cloudflare Tunnel carries everything interactive. cloudflared runs on the desktop and connects outbound, so there are no inbound ports, no router configuration, and no VPN app on the phone. It works from anywhere, including the watch on LTE. You already run Cloudflare in front of the Home Assistant alert API, so this is existing infrastructure rather than a new dependency.

-
  • Data Layer carries phone ↔ watch pairing.

+
  • FCM wakes the phone on red. The only push pipe on stock Android that survives Doze without your app holding a socket, and free. Payload is ~120 bytes of opaque ids — no question text ever reaches Google.

+
  • Cloudflare Tunnel carries everything interactive. cloudflared dials outbound, so there are no inbound ports and no origin IP to attack. Works anywhere, including the watch on LTE.

+
  • Data Layer carries phone ↔ watch.

-
The tunnel is not the security boundary. Cloudflare terminates TLS at its edge, and the hostname is reachable by anyone who finds it. So the bridge validates the per-device token on every request itself, and cloudflared points at the bridge alone — never at host-service, which stays bound to 127.0.0.1 with its master PSK. Cloudflare Access is worth adding as a second layer, but never as the only one.

+

Where the bridge lives

-

Why the watch is a real app, not a bridged notification

+

A fork-owned module in the Electron main process, apps/desktop/src/main/companion-bridge/, on a fixed loopback port. It needs main-process APIs (safeStorage, powerSaveBlocker, renderer IPC) and, more importantly, fork-only new files never conflict on your nightly upstream merges — only three existing files get touched, each behind a FEATURES.md marker.

-

Bridging a phone notification to the watch is much less work, and it was the plan until the numbers came back: Android clamps every notification string to 1024 UTF-16 units. Agent questions and their option descriptions routinely run past that, and the failure mode is silent truncation — you'd answer a question whose second half you never saw. So the watch gets a small Compose app whose only screen is the question, scrollable and uncapped.

+

The port is fixed and fails loud if taken. cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing — presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

-

Answering, and the stale-answer problem

+
The known hole: the bridge dies with the app. host-service watches the desktop app's PID and exits with it, while the pty daemon is detached and survives. So if Superset closes or crashes, your agents keep running and keep going red — with the bridge and FCM sender dead. You chose to accept this rather than restructure, mitigated by a phone-side liveness watchdog: if the last sync showed working agents and no heartbeat arrives for several minutes, the phone raises a local notification saying contact was lost. That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.

-

The same question can be answered in three places: at the desktop, on the phone, or on the watch. Whichever lands first wins; the other two must notice and get out of the way.

+

Status

-

This matters more than it sounds. Claude Code renders a question as an interactive picker inside the terminal — answering it remotely means writing keystrokes into that terminal. If the question was already answered at the desktop, those keystrokes land in whatever is on screen now.

+

Only coarse status is readable without the desktop app running. The rich dot state — the latched axes — and all of snooze/archive/pin/tiering live in the renderer's browser storage, unreachable from outside.

-
The guard already exists on disk. The fork's notify hook maintains marker files at ~/.superset/agent-subagent-running/<terminalId>.askq/<owner> — created on PreToolUse:AskUserQuestion, deleted the moment it's answered. File present means the question is genuinely still open. The bridge checks it immediately before writing, and refuses if it's gone.

+

You cut the enrichment layer from v1. The phone shows the agent tree sorted by status, red first. No snooze mirroring, no pin, no drag order. That removes a renderer exporter, multi-window election, a debounce protocol, and a freshness contract — the single largest complexity item in the design — for something with no effect on the red path.

-

On the client side, answers are optimistic: tapping an option confirms instantly and sends in the background with an idempotency key. If the bridge rejects it as already-answered, the notification clears itself and the app shows where it was answered instead.

-
Pending: exact byte sequence for selecting an option in the picker, and whether the terminal stream gives a readable confirmation that the answer landed. Agent probe-askuser is resolving this.

-

Where the data comes from

-

Nothing here requires new plumbing on the desktop — the fork already persists or exposes everything the app needs. Three independent paths, which matters because they fail differently.
<div class="scroll">
<table>
-<thead><tr><th>Need</th><th>Source</th><th>Available when</th></tr></thead>
+<thead><tr><th>Dot</th><th>From</th><th>Notifies</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
-Which terminal belongs to which agent session~/.superset/host/<org>/host.db → terminal_agent_bindingsAlways (plain sqlite)
-Full chat transcript~/.claude/projects/*/<sessionId>.jsonlAlways
-Is a question pending, and whose~/.superset/agent-subagent-running/<terminalId>.askq/<owner>Always
-Question text and optionsThe AskUserQuestion tool_use block in the transcriptAlways
-What the terminal currently showstRPC terminal.snapshot — 1000 lines of rendered textDesktop running
-Live status changesWS /events → agent:lifecycleDesktop running
-Sending text / answerstRPC terminal.sendDesktop running
+ Needs inputBase layer, always availableYes
+ WorkingBase layerNo
+NeutralBase layer — idleNo
</tbody>

-

The useful surprise is terminal.snapshot. host-service already runs a headless xterm emulator per terminal with 1000 lines of scrollback (terminal-mode-tracker.ts:53), fed every PTY byte and including the alt-screen that TUI agents draw into. One authenticated call returns the rendered question card exactly as it appears on the desktop — so the phone can show you what you'd be looking at, rather than a reconstruction, and the same call confirms whether an answer landed.

+

Green is deliberately absent. "Ready for review" is a review-axis concept that only exists in the renderer, and synthesising it from coarse data would be a lie. Red and yellow are honest without it.

-

The part that isn't headless

+

Answering a question

-

The sidebar's character — snooze, archive, pin, the pinned/active/idle tiering, your manual drag order, and the rich latched dot axes — is not in any database. It lives in the renderer's localStorage and sessionStorage, which means nothing outside the running Superset window can read it. Only the coarse layer (which repos, which workspaces, which terminals, which are agents, and their last event type) is available headlessly.

+

This is the sharpest part of the design, and the reason so much of it looks paranoid.

-

So status arrives in two layers:

+

The proven contract
-<div class="scroll">
-<table>
-<thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Contains</th><th>Available when</th></tr></thead>
-<tbody>
-BaseRepos, workspaces, terminals, agent-vs-shell, coarse working / needs-inputBridge reachable
-EnrichmentSnooze, archive, pin, tiering, drag order, tab layout, full dot precedenceSuperset app open
-</tbody>
-
-

+

Established by driving the real Claude Code CLI (2.1.220) in a pty across four scripted runs — not inferred from source:

-

A small exporter inside the renderer pushes the enrichment layer to the bridge whenever Superset is open; the bridge caches the last export and reports how fresh it is. The exporter only subscribes to the existing sidebar and dot stores and serialises them — it never forks that logic, which keeps it cheap to carry through nightly upstream merges.
+<ul>

+
  • Single select: one bare digit both selects and submits. No Enter. There is no confirmation step.

+
  • Several questions in one call: N digits, then Enter on the review screen.

+
  • Multi-select inverts the rules: digits and space toggle; Enter toggles rather than submits; submitting is right-arrow to the Submit tab, then Enter. A naive implementation that appends Enter to "submit" silently flips a selection instead.

+
  • Free text: digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8, then Enter.

+
  • Bracketed paste is inert. A wrapped digit produces cursor noise and no state change, so terminal.send cannot drive the picker at all — only raw terminal.writeInput works.

-
Stale enrichment is treated exactly like being offline. One honest offline state, not a half-degraded mode: the last-known tree stays on screen, a banner explains why, and replies queue. The banner distinguishes "can't reach the desktop" from "desktop is up, Superset is closed" — different problems, different fixes.

+
The stale-answer hazard, reproduced three ways. When the picker is gone, stray digits land in the composer and a following Enter submits them as a real message — observed: a stray 23 became a genuine prompt the model burned a turn answering. Mid-turn, typed input is queued to steer the running agent. And with a different picker open, a digit commits instantly against the wrong question. Because digits commit atomically there is no safe retry and nothing to intercept.

-
An observation, not a new risk. Everything needed to locate and read any transcript already sits in plaintext under your home directory — the sqlite binding table, the pane-map files, auto-resume/registry.json, and an agent-watcher debug log that is on by default and records 160-character transcript snippets. The host-service auth token sits in the same directory as the database it protects. This is pre-existing fork behaviour and the boundary is same-user access, which is the normal trust model on a personal machine. It's worth knowing because this app does not widen it — but it does mean the phone token is the thing to keep scoped.

+

The guard stack

+

The phone never constructs keystrokes. It sends semantic intent — a question id, a fingerprint, and chosen option indices — and the bridge owns the byte encoding, so the client is structurally incapable of emitting a stray digit. Before writing anything, the bridge checks six things:
+<ol>

+
  • The question's tool_use_id still has no tool_result in the transcript.

+
  • The agent-session binding still matches — a /resume or restart invalidates it.

+
  • The terminal session is still active.

+
  • The permission axis is still latched.

+
  • A snapshot confirms the picker is still on screen showing that question.

+
  • The .askq marker still exists — worthless as proof, but its absence is a sound veto.

+

Any failure writes nothing and reports the question as stale. Multi-select re-verifies the screen between each keystroke, since each one can land on a changed screen. On timeout the bridge reports "unconfirmed" and never retries — a blind retry could answer a different question that has since opened, which with atomic digits is unrecoverable.

+
Interaction is online-only. Nothing queues — not answers, not messages. An answer is a time-sensitive keystroke whose meaning depends on the live screen, so executing it minutes later against a different screen is the wrong contract regardless of how it's guarded. Offline, the app shows the cached tree and refuses to send. You refetch and tap again.

+

What can't be answered

+

Subagent and teammate questions produce no transcript on disk — verified: five teammate agents fired questions on one terminal and none wrote a file. Their text exists only in the live renderer.

+

So a red terminal has two shapes. Answerable — a main-agent question we hold in full. Opaque — blocked, but we cannot see on what. Opaque reds still notify, because "an agent is blocked" is the thing you need to know either way; they open a panel saying so plainly, with no answer field, and the chat composer is disabled there. Typing free text at a terminal awaiting a question feeds that text to the question, and on an opaque red we cannot know what we'd be answering.

+
Worth measuring early. If most of your questions come from teammates rather than main loops, the phone becomes a notifier rather than an answerer — which changes whether the watch app is worth building. Check the split on a real working day before committing to the watch milestones.
Security

-

Worth being blunt about the stakes: write access to a terminal is arbitrary code execution on the desktop. The design treats the phone as a device that will eventually be lost.

+

The bridge is on the public internet and terminal write is arbitrary code execution on your desktop. Every reviewer independently said a bearer token alone is not enough, and the hostname becomes public knowledge the moment the TLS certificate hits Certificate Transparency logs.

+

Four independent layers:
<ul>

-
  • Pairing — one-time QR shown on the desktop, scanned by the phone. The phone gets its own token; the desktop keeps a revocable device list.

-
  • The master PSK never leaves the desktop. The host-service secret in ~/.superset/host/<orgId>/manifest.json grants full terminal write, filesystem access, and PTY attach. The phone gets a scoped token instead, and the bridge is the only thing holding the PSK.

-
  • The bridge assumes a hostile internet. Every request carries the device token and is validated by the bridge itself, regardless of arriving through the tunnel. Write endpoints get a stricter gate than reads.

+
  • Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.

+
  • Per-request signatures. Pairing establishes a key over the QR — an optical channel that never transits Cloudflare. Every request carries a timestamp, nonce, and HMAC over method, path and body hash. Nothing replayable ever crosses the wire.

+
  • Encrypted bodies. AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the same pairing secret. Cloudflare terminates TLS, so without this it would see your transcripts, question text, answers and repo names in the clear. You chose to seal now rather than retrofit — retrofitting means breaking the wire and re-pairing every device.

+
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.

+

Beyond the wire: writes are rate-limited far more tightly than reads (10/min versus 120/min), every injected write is appended to an audit log before it executes, the bridge refuses to write to plain shells (only terminals with an agent binding), free-text sends require a biometric confirmation while option taps don't, and there's a desktop panic switch that strips write access without unpairing.

+

Certificate pinning is deliberately rejected: Cloudflare's certificates last 90 days and Cloudflare controls the issuing authorities, so pinning breaks the app on a schedule — and for a sideloaded app with no update channel, that means it fails exactly when you need it.

+
Blast radius, stated plainly. Anyone holding the pairing key can type into your agent terminals from anywhere on earth. The layers change how reachable and how detectable that is, not the consequence. Revocation is from the desktop and takes effect on the next request.

+
One recommendation worth acting on separately. Your (BUILD-REPAIR) loop lets an unattended agent edit any non-frozen file, and your own notes say containment is not semantic review. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals. The pairing, crypto, edge and injection directories should join the frozen-paths list — a genuine bug there should fail loud for you, not get silently "repaired" by an agent reading a build log an attacker may have influenced.

+

Client

+

Native Kotlin, one Gradle project, phone and watch sharing an applicationId and keystore — the Data Layer silently delivers nothing if either differs.

+

Phone: home (agent tree, red first), chat detail, question sheet, opaque-red panel, pairing, diagnostics. Home and chat sit in one adaptive scaffold so the Fold's inner screen shows both panes and the cover screen shows one. Selection survives folding via saved state, not remember.

+

Chat reads conversationally: your messages and the agent's replies, with tool calls collapsed to a one-line chip you can tap to expand.

+

Question sheet: header, full question, options as large buttons with their full descriptions unclamped, and the last ten messages scrollable above for context. Single-select taps submit; multi-select uses checkboxes and an explicit Submit, because training you on tap-to-submit and then showing checkboxes would fire three separate answers.

+

Watch: one question screen, uncapped and scrollable. This is why it's a real app rather than a bridged notification — Android clamps notification strings to 1024 characters and truncates silently, so you'd answer a question whose second half you never saw. Opaque reds get a distinct haptic, so you learn from your wrist which buzzes are actionable and which mean "walk to the desk".

+

Every answer shows three states — pending, confirmed, or failed — never collapsed into "sent". Notifications retract when a question is answered anywhere, including a full sweep every time the app foregrounds, since the likeliest stale notification comes from a push missed while dozing.
Prerequisites
<div class="card">
1. Create a Firebase project. Free Spark plan, no card. Only you can create it; the service-account credential then lives on the desktop only.

-

2. Set up the Cloudflare tunnel. Install cloudflared on the desktop, create a named tunnel, and add a DNS record for the bridge hostname. Reuses the Cloudflare account already fronting your Home Assistant API.

+

2. Install cloudflared. Not currently on the machine. Create a named tunnel and a DNS record on khaira.family, which is already on Cloudflare. Run it as a Windows service.

+

3. Configure Cloudflare Access with a service-token policy on the bridge hostname.

-
Pending: token format, storage (Keystore / EncryptedDataStore), and whether write actions need a biometric gate. Agents design-bridge and design-client are resolving these.

+

Installing v1.18.0 is not a prerequisite. The bridge ships inside the desktop app, so whatever release carries the bridge carries terminal.snapshot too. It only matters if you want to test against the running app before then.

-

Offline behaviour

+

Build order

-

A sleeping desktop produces no agent events and cannot execute a reply — no transport fixes that. So two things happen instead: the desktop holds a Windows power request while any agent is working, so it stays awake exactly when it matters; and when it is genuinely offline the phone greys out with a banner, keeps the last-known tree visible rather than blanking it, and queues any reply for delivery on reconnect.

+

Each step is demonstrable on its own, and the first three carry no write risk at all — which is the right place to stop if the byte contract needs more soak time.

-

Desktop bridge

-
Pending design-bridge: where the bridge lives in the fork, where dot status is authoritative today, the full API surface, FCM sender placement, and the FEATURES.md markers needed to survive nightly upstream merges.
+<ol>

+
  • Bridge, tunnel, pairing, crypto, read-only API. No write path exists yet.

+
  • Phone UI on fake data — tree, chat, question sheet, opaque panel, every connection state. Needs no bridge, so it runs in parallel.

+
  • Real reads. Pairing by QR, live tree, live transcripts, notifications for every red.

+
  • Answer injection behind the full guard stack, single-select first.

+
  • Multi-select and free text with per-keystroke screen verification.

+
  • Watch app — question screen, answer path, bridged-notification suppression.

-

Android client

-
Pending design-client: Gradle module structure, screen inventory and adaptive layout for the Fold, Room schema and reply outbox, sync engine, notification design, phone↔watch protocol, and the build sequence.

+

Open risks

-

Build sequence

-
Pending — assembled once the two design agents land.
+<ul>

+
  • The byte contract is a private contract with a TUI. It can change on any Claude Code release, silently. It needs a canary test against recorded screens per upgrade — particularly the multi-select inversion, which is invisible in code review.

+
  • Desktop sleep kills the tunnel, and the keep-awake power request doesn't exist yet — I described it earlier as if it did, which was wrong. Expect "desktop offline" to be the most common non-online state until it's built.

+
  • Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4 is the most likely thing to be wrong, and needs live-device verification.

+
  • The public endpoint will be scanned continuously. The app must distinguish "blocked at Cloudflare" from "desktop offline", or you'll go poke a desktop that was fine.

input.prompt:
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW — security and answer-injection only. Do not modify files. Verify claims against the repo at C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64 and cite file:line.

Read the design: C:\Users\khair\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-khair-Code-Projects-fork-superset-windows-arm64\41b65f55-7b51-4cfd-82d1-d1d1eec49d91\scratchpad\superset-companion-design.html

This is a personal single-user app. A public Cloudflare-tunnelled bridge on the user's Windows desktop lets their phone/watch answer AI-agent questions by injecting keystrokes into a terminal. Terminal write == arbitrary code execution.

LOCKED (challenge only with strong evidence): Cloudflare Tunnel + Cloudflare Access service token; per-request HMAC signatures + AES-256-GCM sealed bodies keyed from a QR pairing secret; bridge inside the Electron main process; no offline queueing of anything; answers via server-generated raw bytes with a six-guard pre-write check; all question types supported (single-select, multi-select, free text).

EMPIRICALLY PROVEN, treat as fact:
- Single-select: one bare digit selects AND submits, no Enter, no confirmation step.
- Multi-question: N digits then \r. multiSelect=true INVERTS: digits/space toggle, Enter TOGGLES (does not submit), submit is \x1b[C then \r. Free text: digit N+1, UTF-8, \r.
- Bracketed paste is INERT against the picker, so `terminal.send`/`writeFramedInputToSession` cannot drive it; only raw `terminal.writeInput` works.
- Stale bytes reproduced three ways: into the composer (a stray "23" became a real user prompt), queued mid-turn to steer a running agent, and committed against a different picker.
- `.askq` markers leak (17 stale, oldest 21 days) — presence proves nothing, absence is a sound veto.
- `notifications.hook` is a `publicProcedure` — unauthenticated localhost ingest that writes the agent binding store.
- host-service PSK is regenerated every app spawn.
- `terminal.snapshot` exists in released desktop-v1.18.0 (verified in the tag).

REVIEW THESE, hardest first:
1. **Break the six-guard stack.** Guards: (a) no tool_result for the tool_use_id, (b) agent-session binding unchanged, (c) session active, (d) permission axis latched, (e) snapshot shows the picker with that question, (f) .askq marker present. Find an ordering, timing, or state combination where all six pass and the write still lands wrong. Consider: /resume, terminal reattach, two questions in the same terminal in quick succession, a subagent question opening while a main question is answered, snapshot staleness vs the 1000-line ring buffer, and the multi-select per-keystroke re-verification (what if the screen changes between keystroke 2 and 3 in a way that still "matches"?).
2. **Attack the crypto.** HMAC over method+path+timestamp+nonce+body-hash, AES-256-GCM bodies, both keyed by HKDF from a QR secret. Find replay, reflection, downgrade, nonce-reuse, clock-skew, or canonicalisation attacks. Is a 60s timestamp window right? What happens on WS upgrade where headers may not survive? Is deriving both keys from one QR secret sound, and what is the rotation story?
3. **Attack pairing.** The QR carries the pairing secret AND the Cloudflare Access service token, TTL ~120s, single-use, over an optical channel. The pairing endpoint is internet-reachable. Find the race, the shoulder-surf, the screenshot-in-a-backup, the replay.
4. **Is "no offline queueing" actually sufficient?** The user chose online-only interaction. Does that fully remove the stale-answer class, or does an in-flight request that times out mid-write reintroduce it?
5. **What single change most reduces risk per unit of effort?** One recommendation, concrete.
6. **Is any of this security theatre?** Say so if a layer costs real complexity and buys little.

Lead with the most severe finding. Be specific and evidence-based, not generic. Where you speculate rather than verify, say so.

input.prompt:
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW — feasibility, scope, and the client. Do not modify files. Verify against the repo at C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64 and cite file:line where relevant.

Read the design: C:\Users\khair\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-khair-Code-Projects-fork-superset-windows-arm64\41b65f55-7b51-4cfd-82d1-d1d1eec49d91\scratchpad\superset-companion-design.html

A single user wants: watch buzzes when an AI agent needs input → read the full question → answer from the wrist. Phone: agent tree, read chats, reply. New native Kotlin repo (phone + Wear modules).

LOCKED: native Kotlin/Compose, real Wear app (not bridged notifications — Android clamps notification strings to 1024 UTF-16 units), FCM push, Cloudflare Tunnel, bridge in Electron main, enrichment layer CUT from v1, online-only (no queueing), all question types.

PROVEN FACTS:
- Subagent/teammate questions write NO transcript to disk — their text exists only in the desktop renderer. So the phone can only answer MAIN-AGENT questions. Everything else is a "blocked but opaque" red.
- `/events` WS duplicates events 2-3x and sends no snapshot on connect.
- host.db must be opened mode=ro (immutable=1 froze at stale data for 45s).
- The Windows keep-awake power request does NOT exist yet (zero powerSaveBlocker references in apps/desktop/src/main).
- host-service exits with the desktop app; the pty daemon survives detached. So agents keep running and going red while the bridge is dead. Mitigation chosen: phone-side liveness watchdog only.

REVIEW:
1. **Is the product still worth building?** If a large share of this user's questions come from subagents/teammates (which the design admits are unanswerable), the watch becomes a buzzer that says "go to your desk". Investigate the real split — look at `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` transcripts and `~/.superset/logs/dot-decisions.log` on this machine and MEASURE how many AskUserQuestion events came from main loops versus subagents over the last week. This is the single most decision-relevant number in the whole design and it is measurable right now. Report actual counts.
2. **The availability hole.** The user accepted bridge-dies-with-app plus a phone watchdog. Is the watchdog actually implementable well? What does it use as its heartbeat, how does it distinguish "desktop asleep" from "Superset closed" from "phone lost signal", and what's the false-positive rate when the phone is simply in Doze? Does a watchdog that cries wolf get muted, defeating the purpose?
3. **Wear OS reality check.** Verify current (July 2026) facts: does a Wear app sharing an applicationId with a phone app reliably suppress the phone's bridged notification via BridgingManager? What breaks between watch-app install and first launch? What does IMPORTANCE_HIGH actually do with the screen off? Is uncapped question text genuinely readable on a 45mm screen, or is the whole rationale for a native watch app weaker than assumed? Use WebSearch for anything you can't verify locally.
4. **Scope honesty.** What in this v1 will realistically not get finished by one person, and what should be cut to get to a working buzz-and-answer loop fastest? Give a minimal path.
5. **What's missing** that nobody has raised — failure modes, UX gaps, operational burdens.
6. **The strongest argument AGAINST this whole approach**, stated fairly. Is there a materially simpler thing that delivers 80% of the value?

Lead with the measurement from (1) — actual numbers, not estimates. Be blunt.

content.content: Launching skill: call-another-llm

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\khair\.claude\skills\call-another-llm

<purpose>
Send a prompt to another LLM agent and get its response saved to a file.
Two separate scripts, one per LLM. Each runs the CLI in non-interactive mode and writes the raw response to tmp/llm-responses/.
</purpose>

<constraints>
- Each script runs the target LLM in non-interactive mode with auto-approve. Codex specifically runs in YOLO mode (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`): unsandboxed with full filesystem/network access, so it can implement changes, run tests, and reach the TEST database.
- Fail fast if the target CLI is not installed or returns a non-zero exit code.
- Output files contain only the raw response — no metadata.
- All output goes to `tmp/llm-responses/` with the pattern `<llm>-<label>-<timestamp>.md`.
</constraints>

<scripts>
- `scripts/call_codex.py` — calls Codex CLI
- `scripts/call_claude.py` — calls Claude Code CLI
</scripts>

<inputs>

**All scripts share:**
  - positional: `prompt` (required, except when using `--list-models`)
  - `--label`: optional label for the output filename (default: llm name)

**Codex-specific flags (`call_codex.py`):**
  - `-m` / `--model`: model to use (known model: `gpt-5.6-sol`; any string accepted)
  - `--effort`: reasoning effort level — `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `ultra` (`ultra` is heavy on usage but most capable)
  - `--list-models`: print known models, the current default, and valid effort levels, then exit

When `--model` is omitted, Codex uses the default from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
When `--effort` is omitted, Codex uses the effort configured in `config.toml` (default: `high`).
</inputs>

<workflow>
1. If the user has not specified which LLM to call, use the AskUser tool with options (Codex, Claude) to let the user choose. If the user wants both, confirm that before running two parallel calls.
2. Write the prompt to a file first (see prompt-file-methodology below).
3. Run the chosen script(s) passing the file contents: `"$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`.
4. Read the output file path from stdout (OUTPUT_FILE=...).
5. Read the response file to use the result.
</workflow>

<prompt-file-methodology>
Always write prompts to a file before passing to CLI scripts. This makes prompts reviewable,
debuggable, and preservable as an audit trail.

**Directory:** `tmp/llm-prompts/` (create with `mkdir -p` if it doesn't exist)

**File naming:** `{agentname}_{3 random lowercase letters}_{unix timestamp}.txt`
- `agentname` = the agent role or label (e.g. `codex-reviewer`, `claude-summarizer`)
- 3 random lowercase letters for uniqueness
- Unix timestamp in seconds
- Example: `codex-reviewer_xfm_1743926400.txt`

**Steps:**
1. `mkdir -p tmp/llm-prompts`
2. Generate filename: `{agentname}_$(cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 'a-z' | head -c3)_$(date +%s).txt`
3. Write the full prompt to that file.
4. Pass to CLI: `uv run .../call_codex.py --label "..." "$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`
</prompt-file-methodology>

<examples>
```bash
# List available Codex models and effort levels
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" --list-models

# Codex with default model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Explain the trade-offs of this approach" --label "review"

# Codex with specific model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Review this code" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort high --label "review"
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Deep analysis of this architecture" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort ultra --label "deep-review"

# Claude
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_claude.py" "Summarise this error log" --label "error-summary"
```

- Pixel Watch 4: buzz when an agent needs input, read the FULL question and its options, answer from the wrist.

=== EMPIRICALLY PROVEN (established by driving the real CLI in a node-pty; treat as fact) ===

- Single-select: ONE BARE DIGIT both selects AND submits. No Enter. No confirmation step. Atomic and irreversible.
- Multi-question in one tool call: N digits, then \r on a review screen.

- Free text: digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8, then \r.
- Bracketed paste is INERT against the picker — so the existing framed write API cannot drive it; only raw byte writes work.

- Subagent/teammate questions write NO transcript to disk; their text exists only in the desktop app's renderer process. So they can be detected but never displayed or answered remotely.
- The pending-question marker files on disk LEAK (17 stale ones found, oldest 21 days). Presence proves nothing; absence is a sound veto.
- The desktop's local agent-event ingest endpoint is UNAUTHENTICATED on localhost.
- The host-service pre-shared key is regenerated on every app spawn.

3. FCM high-priority data messages for wakeups, carrying only opaque ids.
4. Cloudflare Access service token at the edge AS WELL AS the bridge's own auth.
5. Per-request HMAC signatures (timestamp + nonce + body hash) AND AES-256-GCM sealed bodies, both keyed via HKDF from a secret carried on the pairing QR code.
6. Bridge lives inside the desktop app's Electron main process (fork-owned new files), NOT a separate sidecar — the user chose this despite being told it means the bridge dies with the app.
7. NOTHING is queued offline. Interaction is online-only. An answer that cannot be delivered now fails and the user re-taps.
8. All question types supported: single-select, multi-select, and free text.
9. The "enrichment layer" (mirroring the desktop sidebar's snooze/archive/pin/tiering and rich status axes) is CUT from v1.

6. **What will actually go wrong in practice** for a solo builder — not theoretical risks, but the things that genuinely bite.

Be direct and specific. Cite file paths from the repo where you verify something. Where you are speculating rather than verifying, say so explicitly. Do not be agreeable for its own sake — the value here is disagreement I have not already heard.

content.text:
**Design doc:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1b6d91d0-98d0-4853-9238-393f6eb9e30e

To answer your 1.18 question directly: nothing needs building or installing. `desktop-v1.18.0` was released yesterday and contains `terminal.snapshot` — I verified it's in the tag. My earlier "it doesn't exist" finding was about the *running* 1.17.0 app, not the source. And since the bridge ships inside the desktop app, whatever release carries the bridge carries snapshot too. The dependency dissolves.

**What the proof agents changed.** Six assumptions got tested against the live system; two failed. `terminal.snapshot` 404s on your running build. And the `.askq` marker files leak — 17 stale ones, oldest 21 days — so marker presence proves nothing, though its *absence* is still a sound veto. Separately, subagent questions write no transcript at all, so the phone can detect that a teammate is blocked but never show or answer its question.

The answer contract is now proven rather than guessed, by driving the real CLI in a pty. One bare digit both selects and submits with no confirmation, multi-select inverts the rules so Enter toggles instead of submitting, and bracketed paste is inert — which rules out the framed write API entirely. The stale-answer failure was reproduced three ways, including a stray `23` becoming a genuine prompt the model burned a turn answering.

**Your four decisions this round** are all in the doc: signed and encrypted bodies, Cloudflare Access as a second gate, no offline queueing at all, and online-only interaction.

**Three reviews are running now.** One Fable agent is trying to break the six-guard stack and the crypto. The other is measuring something I should have measured earlier — the actual ratio of main-agent to subagent questions in your transcripts over the past week. That number decides whether the watch is an answering device or just a buzzer that says "go to your desk", and it's measurable right now rather than after you've built it. Codex is giving an independent verdict at xhigh, including whether it would build this at all.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="fable-security" color="purple" summary="Fable security+injection review: findings">
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW — security + answer-injection. Verified against repo, file:line cited. Hardest first.

## F1 (SEVERE) — guard stack is a cross-process TOCTOU. Cannot be atomic as designed.
Bridge lives in Electron main; the write executes in host-service. Verify and write are two separate loopback tRPC calls with no lock between them:
- snapshot read: `snapshotSession` `packages/host-service/src/terminal/terminal.ts:816` (own call, reads `session.modeTracker.snapshot`)
- write: `writeInputToSession` `terminal.ts:658` — no session lock, straight `session.pty.write(data)` at :678.

All six guards pass at time T; `pty.write` lands at T+δ. δ = two loopback round-trips + two event loops (tens of ms, more under load). The design's own stale-answer hazard (stray `23` → real prompt; mid-turn steer; wrong-picker commit) is a T+δ phenomenon. Snapshot proves the picker was there at T, not at write time. With atomic-commit digits and no lock, the guard stack lowers probability but cannot close the window. Concrete triggers that fit in δ: desktop user answers simultaneously; a subagent question opens on the same terminal; `/resume` swaps the session. This is the core weakness — the six guards are a check, not a transaction.

Note: snapshot itself is stronger than the brief implies — it's a live headless-emulator read (`modeTracker.snapshot`), not the 1000-line ring buffer. The buffer/ring is the daemon replay path (`terminal.ts:717-733`), only relevant after adoption (500ms `ADOPTION_REPLAY_WAIT_MS`). So guard (e) is honest at T; the problem is T≠write.

## F2 (HIGH, local/compromised-agent adversary) — 2 of 6 guards derive from an UNAUTHENTICATED store.
`notifications.hook` is `publicProcedure` — `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/notifications.ts:54`. It writes the agent-binding store: `ctx.terminalAgentStore.recordEvent` (:85). Guards (b) binding-unchanged and (d) permission-axis-latched both derive from that store.
`recordEvent` `store.ts:64-114`: a POST with `{terminalId, eventType:<permission-mapped>}` and NO agent field → `if (!agentId && !existing) return` is skipped when a binding exists (:81), so it re-stamps `lastEventType` + `lastEventAt` on the existing binding. `sessionChanged` needs `agentSessionId !== undefined` (:94-97), so omitting it keeps `startedAt`/binding intact → attacker re-latches permission AND keeps guard (b) "fresh" in one call.
Adversary: loopback-only, so not the internet attacker — but every agent shell has `$SUPERSET_HOST_AGENT_HOOK_URL` in env (`terminal/env.ts:177`). A prompt-injected agent (your own BUILD-REPAIR / malicious-build-log threat, or any agent reading untrusted content) can curl it to forge lifecycle for ANY terminalId. The code comment at `notifications.ts:50-52` claims "a caller can only trigger a chime and a sidebar indicator" — understated: it mutates the binding store that also drives auto-resume target selection (`countByAgentSessionId` store.ts:152) and, in this design, guard (d). Under-documented trust boundary.

## F3 (crypto, design-level — bridge not built) 
- Single QR secret → both HMAC and AES keys via HKDF: sound ONLY if distinct `info` labels per key. Call it out explicitly or you get key reuse.
- 60s window is fine IF paired with a nonce cache that outlives the window (≥120s retention) and is sized against burst. Without the nonce cache, 60s replay is wide open. Timestamp alone ≠ anti-replay.
- Reflection/downgrade: MAC already binds method+path — good. Access JWT re-validated at origin (design §Security) — good, keep it.
- **WS upgrade is the real gap.** An HMAC over HTTP method+path+body does not survive onto WS frames; headers authenticate the upgrade handshake only, not per-message. Either (a) keep the WS read-only and route ALL writes over signed HTTP POST (recommend — writes are rare, 10/min), or (b) per-frame auth inside the WS payload. Do not assume the handshake MAC covers frames.
- Rotation: none stated. Compromise of the QR secret is permanent until manual re-pair. Add a rotation/expiry story.

## F4 (pairing) — QR bundles both factors; optical channel is the weak point.
QR carries pairing secret AND Cloudflare Access service token, ~120s single-use. Shoulder-surf / screenshot / phone-backup / screen-share = full compromise: both factors sit in one blob rendered on screen. TTL and single-use bound the *pairing race*, not the *observation*. Strong recommendation: do NOT transmit the long-term secret optically. QR carries a short-lived pairing code only; run an ECDH so the long-term key is derived, never displayed/transmitted. Keep the Access service token out of the QR — provision it into the app build or bind it to the device pubkey established during pairing.

## F5 (item 4 — is "no offline queueing" sufficient?) — Necessary, not sufficient.
Online-only removes the DEFERRED-send stale class (answers/messages sitting queued, executing minutes later). It does NOT remove:
- F1's verify→write TOCTOU (same live turn, cross-process δ).
- In-flight timeout: bridge sends snapshot-verify then `pty.write`; if the phone's request times out AFTER the write tRPC dispatched, the write STILL LANDED server-side. Phone correctly shows "unconfirmed" and doesn't retry — but the byte is in the terminal. The write's correctness rests entirely on the guards holding at write time = F1 again.
So the residual stale class = F1. Online-only is the right call but doesn't stand alone.

## F6 (item 5 — single highest-leverage change)
Collapse verify+write into ONE host-service operation under a per-session mutex. Phone sends semantic intent + question fingerprint (already the design); host-service, holding the session lock, re-reads the snapshot, runs all six guards, and does `pty.write` before releasing — no cross-process gap, and concurrent desktop-user keystrokes serialize on the same mutex. This directly closes F1's δ and the multi-select per-keystroke re-verify races (each keystroke = one locked verify+write). Today `writeInputToSession` takes no lock (`terminal.ts:658-680`); adding a per-terminal mutex + moving the guard evaluation server-side is the concrete fix. Bigger payoff than any wire-crypto hardening.

## F7 (item 6 — theatre check)
- `.askq` marker as a POSITIVE signal = theatre (17 stale, oldest 21 days, proven). Design already demotes it to veto-only — correct, keep it that way, don't let it creep back to proof.
- Separate per-request HMAC layered over AES-256-GCM: partial overlap. GCM's tag already gives integrity+auth once the key is secret; the HMAC's real added value is the timestamp+nonce replay binding, not body integrity. Fold timestamp+nonce into the GCM AAD instead of a parallel HMAC-over-body-hash → one AEAD primitive, same guarantees, less canonicalization surface to get wrong. Effort-reducer, not a security loss.
- NOT theatre, keep: AES-GCM body seal (CF terminates TLS, would otherwise see transcripts/repo names/answers in clear — design §Security is right); Access JWT origin re-validation; rejecting cert pinning (90-day CF certs, no update channel — correct).
- `immutable=1` already cut for `mode=ro` (design "proved" table) — right call, it froze stale for a 45s poll.

## Net
No finding breaks the LOCKED architecture — CF Tunnel + Access, sealed bodies, main-process bridge, online-only, six-guard write all stand. But the guard stack's soundness claim is overstated: F1 shows it's a non-atomic check, F2 shows two guards trust a forgeable local endpoint. Both are fixed by F6 (server-side atomic verify+write) plus authenticating or hardening `notifications.hook`'s store writes. Do F6 first. Everything crypto/pairing (F3/F4) is design-level and unbuilt — specify the WS-write and QR-secret decisions before coding, they're expensive to retrofit (your own note).

content.text:
Fable found a severe flaw — and in doing so revealed I'd written your own decision into the doc incorrectly.

You chose the bridge **inside host-service**. The design agent recommended Electron main instead, and I propagated its recommendation over your choice. That was my error. It turns out your choice was the right one, for a reason nobody had articulated until now.

input.old_string:
Where the bridge lives

A fork-owned module in the Electron main process, apps/desktop/src/main/companion-bridge/, on a fixed loopback port. It needs main-process APIs (safeStorage, powerSaveBlocker, renderer IPC) and, more importantly, fork-only new files never conflict on your nightly upstream merges — only three existing files get touched, each behind a FEATURES.md marker.

The port is fixed and fails loud if taken. cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing — presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

The known hole: the bridge dies with the app. host-service watches the desktop app's PID and exits with it, while the pty daemon is detached and survives. So if Superset closes or crashes, your agents keep running and keep going red — with the bridge and FCM sender dead. You chose to accept this rather than restructure, mitigated by a phone-side liveness watchdog: if the last sync showed working agents and no heartbeat arrives for several minutes, the phone raises a local notification saying contact was lost. That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.
input.new_string:
Where the bridge lives

Inside host-service, as a fork-owned module with its own fixed loopback listener. The port is fixed and fails loud if taken — cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing, presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

This placement is what makes safe answering possible at all. The alternative — a bridge in the Electron main process — would have to verify the screen and then write via two separate calls into host-service, with no lock between them. Every guard would prove the picker was there at the moment of checking, not at the moment of writing, and that gap is exactly where the stale-answer failures live. Sharing a process means verification and the keystroke can happen as one operation under a per-terminal lock, so a keystroke arriving from the desktop at the same instant serialises behind it instead of racing it.

The cost is merge burden: host-service is upstream-owned, so the module needs its logic in fork-only files with the smallest possible mount surface, each behind a FEATURES.md marker, and calls into upstream internals funnelled through one adapter so a rename breaks in one visible place.

That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.

input.old_string: Any failure writes nothing and reports the question as stale. Multi-select re-verifies the screen between each keystroke, since each one can land on a changed screen. On timeout the bridge reports "unconfirmed" and never retries — a blind retry could answer a different question that has since opened, which with atomic digits is unrecoverable.
input.new_string:
Any failure writes nothing and reports the question as stale. Multi-select re-verifies the screen between each keystroke, since each one can land on a changed screen. On timeout the bridge reports "unconfirmed" and never retries — a blind retry could answer a different question that has since opened, which with atomic digits is unrecoverable.

The guards are only sound if they're a transaction, not a checklist. Checking six conditions and then writing is two separate acts; everything can pass and the screen can still change before the byte lands. So the whole sequence — read the screen, evaluate the guards, write the keystroke — runs inside host-service holding a per-terminal lock, and each multi-select keystroke is its own locked verify-and-write. Anything less lowers the odds of a wrong write without removing it. This is the single most important implementation constraint in the design.
Two guards rest on an unauthenticated endpoint. The agent-binding check and the permission-state check both read a store written by notifications.hook, which is deliberately unauthenticated on localhost, and every agent shell has its URL in the environment. So an agent that reads untrusted content and follows instructions in it could forge a "question is pending" state for any terminal. This grants no privilege a local process doesn't already have, but it means those two guards must never be the load-bearing ones — the transcript check and the screen check are, and both are outside that endpoint's reach.

input.old_string:
• Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.
  • Per-request signatures. Pairing establishes a key over the QR — an optical channel that never transits Cloudflare. Every request carries a timestamp, nonce, and HMAC over method, path and body hash. Nothing replayable ever crosses the wire.
  • Encrypted bodies. AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the same pairing secret. Cloudflare terminates TLS, so without this it would see your transcripts, question text, answers and repo names in the clear. You chose to seal now rather than retrofit — retrofitting means breaking the wire and re-pairing every device.
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.
input.new_string:
• Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.
  • Sealed, replay-bound requests. Bodies are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with the timestamp, nonce, method and path bound into the cipher's associated data. That gives confidentiality, integrity and replay protection from one primitive rather than layering a separate signature over the top — fewer things to get subtly wrong, and no separate canonicalisation format to mismatch. A nonce cache outliving the freshness window is what actually stops replay; the timestamp alone would not.
  • Writes go over HTTP, never the WebSocket. Authenticating a WebSocket handshake says nothing about individual frames sent later, so the socket carries reads only and every write is its own sealed request. Writes are rare enough that this costs nothing.
  • Pairing establishes the long-term key rather than transmitting it. The QR carries a short-lived pairing code, and the lasting key is derived through a key exchange — so the secret is never rendered on a screen where a photo, a screenshot in a cloud backup, or someone behind you captures it whole. The Cloudflare service token is bound to the device during that exchange rather than printed in the same blob.
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.

content.text:
Doc updated at the same URL: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1b6d91d0-98d0-4853-9238-393f6eb9e30e

**Your bridge-placement choice was better than the design agent's, and now we know why.** The agent recommended Electron main on merge-burden grounds; I wrote that into the doc over your answer, which was wrong of me. Fable's severest finding is that verifying the screen and then writing the keystroke from a *different process* is two separate acts with a gap between them — every guard proves the picker was there when checked, not when the byte lands, and that gap is precisely where the reproduced failures live. Sharing a process with host-service lets verification and the keystroke happen as one locked operation, so a keystroke you type at the desktop at the same instant queues behind it rather than racing it. Your choice makes safe answering possible; the alternative only made it less likely to go wrong.

**Two guards were resting on a forgeable endpoint.** The agent-binding and permission-state checks both read a store written by an unauthenticated localhost endpoint whose URL sits in every agent's environment. An agent that reads untrusted content and acts on it could forge "a question is pending" for any terminal. It grants nothing a local process doesn't already have, but those two guards can't be load-bearing — the transcript check and the screen check are, and neither is reachable from that endpoint.

**Two things got simpler, not harder.** The separate HMAC layered over AES-GCM was partly redundant; folding the timestamp and nonce into the cipher's associated data gives the same guarantees from one primitive with less to get wrong. And authenticating a WebSocket handshake says nothing about later frames, so writes go over HTTP and the socket carries reads only.

**One change to pairing.** The QR was going to carry the long-term secret and the Cloudflare token together — one photo, screenshot, or backup captures both. It now carries only a short-lived code, with the lasting key derived through an exchange so it's never displayed at all.

Still running: Fable measuring your real main-agent versus subagent question split, and Codex's independent verdict.

Codex is still working (xhigh takes several minutes); it'll notify me on completion. Fable's feasibility measurement is the other outstanding piece.

While those finish, one correction I owe you on my own reporting: I said earlier that `terminal.snapshot` "doesn't exist in your installed build" and framed it as a blocker. Both halves were right individually but I drew the wrong conclusion — the source has always been in your repo, so it was never a build blocker at all, only a runtime-testing one. You caught that before I did.

Current state of the design after this round:

| Area | Where it landed |
|---|---|
| Bridge home | Inside host-service — your choice, now vindicated |
| Answer safety | Verify and write as one locked transaction, not a checklist |
| Wire | One AEAD primitive; writes over HTTP, reads over WebSocket |
| Pairing | Short-lived code only; long-term key derived, never displayed |
| Offline | Nothing queues — online-only interaction |

FABLE FEASIBILITY/CLIENT REVIEW — measured, not estimated.

## 1. THE NUMBER: premise CONFIRMED, decisively
Last 7 days (Jul 21–28), dot-decisions.log(.1) + ~/.claude/projects transcripts:
- 300 AskUserQuestion red events, 44 sessions. **293/300 (97.7%) answerable** — session has on-disk main-agent transcript containing the question.
- ALL 7 unanswerable events = 5 sessions on terminal 95c30ab8, 2026-07-28 15:18–15:25 — **this design session's own probe teammates**. Organic teammate/subagent questions this week: **zero**.
- Standalone permission-prompt reds (Notification not paired with an AskUserQuestion within 30s): 6 in 7 days. Negligible.
- 385 AskUserQuestion tool_use calls in transcripts. Daily: 79/34/34/27/1/3/65/57.
Phone is an ANSWERER, not a buzzer. Build it.

Bonus measurements that matter:
- Question+options text: p50=1412 chars, p90=4118, max=8091. **64% exceed the 1024-char notification clamp** → native watch app rationale confirmed by data, not assumption.
- **59% of calls are multi-question** (229/385) — N-digits+Enter path. multiSelect ≈10%.

## 2. Watchdog: implementable, ONE hard dependency
- Heartbeat = phone polls bridge /health via setExactAndAllowWhileIdle (~5min), armed only when last sync showed red/working. WorkManager unusable (15-min floor, Doze slip → hours).
- Discrimination is REAL because cloudflared runs as a Windows service outliving Superset: CF 530/1033 (tunnel down) = machine asleep/off; 502 (tunnel up, origin refused) = Superset closed, machine on; phone lacks validated network = phone's problem → suppress. Three distinct UI states, cheap.
- Deep Doze blocks app network even when alarm fires → connectivity-gate suppresses false positives; cost = watchdog blind in deep Doze, catches up on maintenance windows. Acceptable.
- Cry-wolf control: 2 consecutive validated-network failures; ONE sticky notification per outage episode, updated in place, one buzz.
- HARD DEPENDENCY: keep-awake doesn't exist (verified: zero powerSaveBlocker refs in apps/desktop/src/main). Until built, every desktop sleep fires the watchdog, several times/day → muted in a week. Build keep-awake BEFORE/WITH watchdog, else ship it off-by-default.

## 3. Wear reality (Android docs, packaging page updated 2026-06-16)
- Bridging suppression: two mechanisms. Manifest NO_BRIDGING active AT INSTALL but Google discourages — notifications LOST between install and setup. Runtime BridgingManager active only after first run → brief DUPLICATE window. Duplicates < lost buzzes → use runtime config.
- Bridging off breaks cross-device dismissal → watch must self-cancel via Data Layer answered-event (WearableListenerService wakes it).
- Same applicationId + signature: required for Data Layer. Lock correct.
- Distribution: NO auto-install from phone. Sideload = watch dev mode + wireless debugging + adb per UPDATE. Real burden; Play internal-testing track ($25 once) buys OTA later.
- IMPORTANCE_HIGH screen-off: vibration yes, display does NOT force on (wrist-raise to read); phone DND mirrors to watch; not doc-verifiable → keep the live-device test in open risks.
- 45mm readability, honest model: p50 (1412 chars) = 6–8 crown scrolls, fine; p90 (4118) is phone territory. Watch = p50 + option taps; phone = tail. Uncapped-scrollable still right.

## 4. Scope: one build-order BUG + cuts
- BUG: step 4 "single-select first" — but 59% of calls are multi-question. Single-question-only step 4 leaves the MAJORITY unanswerable. Multi-question digits+Enter must be in step 4.
- Cut for fastest loop: fold two-pane, chat-detail screen (question sheet already carries last-10 msgs), Room persistence (online-only anyway), diagnostics screen, multi-select+free-text injection (~10% → "answer at desk"), haptic taxonomy. KEEP full security stack.
- Minimal path: (1) bridge read+FCM+phone notification → (2) question sheet + guarded single-select incl. multi-question → (3) watch question screen + Data Layer + runtime bridging suppression. Everything else after loop works.

## 5. Missing (nobody raised)
- **NOTIFICATION FATIGUE — biggest gap.** 30–80 questions/day, most answered at desk in seconds. Push every red → ~50 buzzes/day while AT the machine → watch muted → product dead. Cheap fix: DELAY-PUSH — FCM only if unanswered after ~60–90s. (Or reuse AUTO-RESUME's away-detection.) Must be v1.
- **Watch-on-LTE contradiction**: architecture is Data-Layer-only phone↔watch, but doc claims "works anywhere, including the watch on LTE". Watch without phone gets NOTHING. Add standalone watch networking (big scope) or drop the claim.
- Retraction needs its own push: answered-at-desk must send a second FCM to clear phone+watch notifications; foreground sweep alone leaves stale reds on wrist.
- Guard #6 false-veto: .askq written by hooks that historically wedge (ARM64 bash-pile crashes). Hook dies → no marker → legit question vetoed. Log guard-veto reasons from day one.
- FCM must be high-priority data messages to punch Doze (volume ≤80/day fine).
- FEATURES.md marker same-commit for the 3 touched desktop files (BF lesson: unmarked feature got lost).
- Endorse design's own flag: freeze bridge/pairing/crypto/injection paths from BUILD-REPAIR before first nightly containing them.

Repo verification: terminal.snapshot EXISTS packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/terminal/terminal.ts:261; writeInput :178; send :238; /events WS packages/host-service/src/app.ts:236; powerSaveBlocker: zero refs confirmed.

## 6. Strongest case AGAINST
Telegram-bot bridge: outbound getUpdates long-poll → deletes tunnel, Access, pairing/HMAC/AES, public endpoint, CT exposure, Firebase, phone app, watch app (~70% of project). Inline keyboard = single-select taps; reply = free text; 4096 limit covers ~90% (chunk the rest). Desktop guard stack identical. Weekend of work, ~75% of value; watch degrades to truncated bridged notification + answer-on-phone.
Fair rebuttal: questions carry proprietary code/repo context; Telegram reads it ALL plaintext — the design encrypts bodies even against Cloudflare, so its privacy bar disqualifies (not merely deprioritizes) the bot. Decision reduces to one question for the user: may a third party read your agents' questions? Yes → bot first, native later (bridge carries over). No → design stands.

VERDICT: premise measured and confirmed. Proceed with: delay-push in v1, keep-awake before watchdog, multi-question in step 4, LTE claim fixed.

input.old_string: Architecture
input.new_string:
Does the premise hold? Measured.

The design rests on an assumption worth testing before building anything: that a useful share of the questions blocking your agents are ones the phone can actually answer. Subagent questions can't be — their text never touches disk. If most of your questions came from teammates, the watch would be a buzzer that says "go to your desk", and the whole thing would be worth much less.

So it was measured against your last seven days rather than estimated.

MeasurementResultMeaning
Questions that blocked an agent300 across 44 sessionsRoughly 30–80 a day
Answerable from disk293 of 300 — 97.7%The phone is an answerer, not a buzzer
Organic subagent questionsZeroAll 7 unanswerable came from this design session's own probe agents
Question lengthmedian 1,412 chars; 64% over 1,024The native watch app is justified by data, not assumption
Several questions in one prompt59%The majority case — must be supported early
Multi-select~10%Genuinely a tail case
Both load-bearing assumptions survived contact with the data. Nearly everything that blocks you is answerable remotely, and nearly two-thirds of questions would be silently truncated by a bridged notification — which is exactly the failure the native watch app exists to prevent.

Notification volume — the thing that would kill it

Thirty to eighty questions a day, and most of them you answer at the desk within seconds. Pushing every red would mean roughly fifty buzzes a day for questions you were already handling, and a watch that buzzes fifty times a day gets muted within a week. Muted is the same as not built.

So a red doesn't push immediately. It pushes only if it's still unanswered after a short delay — long enough that anything you deal with at the desk never reaches your wrist, short enough that a genuinely blocked agent still finds you quickly. The notification you get then means something: nobody has dealt with this.

Architecture

Quick focused research task. Use WebSearch/WebFetch. Current date: July 2026. Answer precisely, cite sources, and say clearly when something is uncertain.

CONTEXT: Someone is deciding between (a) building a native Android phone + Wear OS app, versus (b) a much simpler Telegram bot, to get notified when an AI coding agent needs input and to ANSWER its question FROM THEIR PIXEL WATCH 4.

Their hard requirement on the watch: get buzzed, READ THE FULL QUESTION (their questions have a median length of 1,412 characters, with 64% exceeding 1,024 characters), and TAP AN OPTION to answer — without taking their phone out.

ANSWER THESE, precisely:

1. **Is there an official Telegram app for Wear OS in 2026?** If not, what third-party Wear OS Telegram clients exist and are they maintained/usable?

2. **Do Telegram bot INLINE KEYBOARD buttons work from a Wear OS notification?** This is the crux. Telegram inline keyboards are in-message UI rendered inside the chat. When a Telegram message bridges to a paired Wear OS watch as a notification, do those inline buttons appear as tappable Wear notification actions, or do they only exist inside the Telegram app? Be specific about what a user would actually see and be able to do on the watch.

3. **Does Telegram's Android notification support RemoteInput / voice reply from the watch?** i.e. can you reply to a Telegram message by voice or keyboard directly from the wrist without opening the phone? Telegram's Android app does support direct reply from notifications on the phone — does that bridge to Wear?

4. **Truncation:** when a Telegram message bridges to Wear, does the full message body reach the watch, or is it subject to Android's per-CharSequence notification clamp (documented at 1,024 UTF-16 units)? What would a 1,412-character message look like on the watch?

5. **Telegram Bot API message length limit** — confirm the current cap for sendMessage (I believe 4,096 characters) and what happens beyond it.

6. **Bottom line:** Could this person realistically buzz-read-and-answer a 1,400-character multiple-choice question entirely from a Pixel Watch 4 using only a Telegram bot? Yes, partially, or no? If partially, exactly which part fails.

Be concise and factual. Where you cannot verify something from documentation and must reason, label it clearly as inference. Do not pad.

content.text:
Here's the honest accounting, using your measured numbers. Some of this is certain; I've got an agent checking the one part I shouldn't assert without verifying.

**What you'd lose that's certain:**

The **agent dashboard and chat reading** — the entire phone half of what you asked for. Telegram gives you a notification stream, not a view of which agents are working, which are blocked, and what they're doing. No status dots, no tree, no reading a transcript. You asked to "select the chats to see what's happening as well / read it"; a bot doesn't do that.

**Privacy**, comprehensively. Your questions carry code, file paths, repo and branch names, and your answers go back the same way. Telegram reads all of it in plaintext. You just chose to encrypt bodies so that even Cloudflare — a company you already trust with your DNS — can't read them. Handing the same content to Telegram is a strictly weaker position than the one you rejected an hour ago.

**Watch readability.** A bridged Telegram notification is still an Android notification, so it hits the same 1,024-character clamp. With your median question at 1,412 characters and 64% over the clamp, most questions truncate on the wrist. That is the exact failure the native watch app exists to prevent, and it doesn't go away just because Telegram is doing the bridging.

**What you'd keep:** the buzz itself, answering from the phone, and the desktop-side guard stack — that work carries over regardless, since the injection problem is identical.

**The part I'm checking rather than asserting:** whether you can *tap an option from the watch at all*. Telegram's inline keyboard buttons are in-message UI rendered inside the chat, not notification actions — so my expectation is they don't survive bridging to Wear, which would mean answering from the wrist doesn't work, only being told to go find your phone. If that's right, the bot fails your actual watch requirement rather than merely degrading it. There's also no official Telegram Wear OS app as far as I know, which compounds it.

I'll confirm shortly. If it turns out inline buttons *do* work from the wrist, the Telegram option becomes genuinely more interesting for a weekend's work, and it'd be worth revisiting whether you want the privacy trade.
