input.content:
Crash-consistency review of a small durable-file bookkeeping mechanism in a personal desktop
utility. I wrote this and I want a second opinion on whether it is correct before I depend on it.
There is nothing adversarial in scope here — no attacker, no untrusted network party. The only
thing that can go wrong is a power loss or a hard reset at an unlucky moment, and a filesystem
that does not persist things in the order the code assumes.

## Repo and commit

`C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64`, commit `d28f53506`.
`git show d28f53506` — 536 insertions, mostly in
`packages/host-service/src/companion/answer.ts`, plus `index.ts` and `types.ts`.
Please read the surrounding code too, not only the diff.

## What the code is for

A desktop app runs coding assistants in terminal panes. When one of them stops and asks the user a
multiple-choice question, the user can answer it from their phone, and a small local helper process
types the chosen keystrokes into that pane.

Afterwards the phone asks the helper "did my answer actually get typed?". The helper keeps a
24-hour record of attempts in a JSON file, rewritten with the usual temp-file, fsync, rename dance
on every change. Two possible replies:

- a record for that request exists -> report it and its recorded state
- no record exists -> report "no record", which the phone is allowed to treat as "your answer
  never got through", but ONLY if the request is recent enough to fall inside a coverage window
  the helper publishes alongside the reply

The coverage window is the important part. If the helper says "no record" about a request that IS
inside the window, the phone tells the user the answer never went through, and the user answers the
question a second time. Answering twice is bad: the second answer lands on whatever the assistant
asked next. So the window must never claim to cover a period the file cannot actually vouch for.

## The problem being solved

On Windows, the code cannot force a directory entry to disk — the helper's `writeFileDurable`
calls a `syncDirectory` that is a no-op on that platform. So a hard reset can lose the record
file's most recent rename and leave an older version of the file in place. That older version
still carries the same "recording started at" timestamp as the version that was lost, so it cannot
declare its own gap: the records that vanished would sit inside a window still claiming to cover
them.

Previously the code sidestepped this by always starting the window at the current process start,
which threw away the usefulness of everything written before the last restart.

## What the commit adds

A second small file next to the first, holding an install identifier plus a counter of how many
times the record file has been durably rewritten. The counter is bumped and written BEFORE each
record-file write, in the same directory. On startup the two files are compared:

- counter matches the record file, or is lower -> the record file is the newest version that was
  ever durable, so its own timestamp can be published
- counter is HIGHER than the record file -> the record file lost its last rename, so records are
  missing; narrow the window to this process start
- second file missing, unreadable, malformed, from a different install, or the record file carries
  no counter at all -> nothing can be verified; narrow the window to this process start

A narrowed startup also advances the record file's own timestamp before rewriting it, so the gap
is written down once and the next healthy startup does not re-publish it.

One firm rule: a problem with the second file must never stop the helper from starting. A sibling
module, `keys.ts`, has a similar counter where a rollback genuinely must stop startup, and I do not
want that behaviour copied here — here the only loss is bookkeeping, and refusing to start would
take away the phone's only way to talk to the desktop for no benefit.

## What I would like checked

1. The write-ordering assumption itself. The code relies on the record file's own fsync making the
   second file's earlier rename durable, because both renames are directory metadata in the same
   directory. Is that actually guaranteed on NTFS, or is it an incidental behaviour? If it is not
   guaranteed, both files could roll back together to matching counters, which would look healthy
   and publish a window it should not. I would rather know this is shaky than believe a comment.
   `writeFileDurable` is in `packages/host-service/src/companion/crypto.ts`, around line 1040.
2. Any sequence of events — two writes overlapping, a reset between the two file writes, the
   pruning of old records, a removal, quarantine of a malformed file, the retention floor — where
   the counters agree but records are actually missing.
3. Any place where a problem with the second file causes an exception to escape instead of just
   narrowing the window. Disk full, permission denied, a lock held by a backup or indexer, a
   directory where a file is expected, a read that succeeds and returns nonsense, a failed
   deletion. Startup is the case I care most about.
4. Whether the counter can ever go backwards, be reset, or be reused. Look at the raise helper,
   the promise chain that serialises writes, and the `Math.max` on load. Also whether any code path
   writes the second file WITHOUT a following record-file write, since the durability argument
   depends on that pairing.
5. Whether advancing the record file's timestamp during a narrowed startup loses information a
   later startup needs.
6. Whether a record file with no counter — one written by the previous version of this code — is
   handled safely. It is deliberately NOT trusted. Please confirm that is what the code does, that
   a brand new install with no file at all stays quiet instead of logging a problem that did not
   happen, and that an upgrading install still serves the records it loaded.
7. Whether the long explanatory comments match the code. I treat them as documentation. One of
   them was wrong until recently — it claimed this second file is what lets a completed answer
   still report as completed after a restart, which was never true; the record file always did
   that on its own, and the second file only affects the "no record" reply. I believe several
   copies of that wrong sentence still survive in `answer.ts`. Please point out every one you find,
   and any other sentence that does not match the code.

## Running it

Bun is installed. From the repo root in a bash shell — use `bun ./tmp/x.ts`, not
`bun run tmp/x.ts`, since the latter picks up package scripts instead:

    bun ./tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts        # 28 checks covering the startup decision table
    bun ./tmp/attempt-store-proof.ts
    bun ./tmp/attempt-store-proof2.ts
    bun ./tmp/verify-attempt-store-fixes.ts
    bun ./tmp/witness-wiring-probe.ts
    bun ./tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts    # a clock-regression case another reviewer found
    bun ./tmp/boot-bridge.ts                  # starts the real helper against a scratch directory

    node scripts/check-feature-markers.mjs        # expect: All 92 feature markers present
    node scripts/check-dangerous-diagnostics.mjs  # about two minutes

Please do not report these, they are known and accepted:

- `bunx tsc --noEmit` in `packages/host-service` reports 8 diagnostics, all pre-existing and all
  outside `src/companion/`. Zero inside that directory is what matters.
- The formatter reports line-ending complaints on every file in that directory, including files
  this commit never touched.
- `boot-bridge.ts` shows empty results for anything database-backed; a local stand-in replaces a
  compiled SQLite binding that only the release build produces.

Two shell traps: piping through `tail` or `grep` hides the real exit status, and `grep -c` exits
non-zero when it counts zero.

Feel free to add throwaway scripts under `tmp/`. Please leave `packages/`, `apps/`, `scripts/` and
`FEATURES.md` alone, and do not commit anything.

For each problem, give me the file and line, one sentence on what is wrong, and a concrete
sequence of events leading to the wrong result. Tell me which ones you actually ran versus worked
out by reading. Rank by how much they matter. If a section is fine, say so plainly — a short clean
answer is more useful to me than a long list of maybes.

Two things other reviewers already found, so please do not spend time re-deriving them, though do
check my reasoning if you touch them: a record file with no counter used to be trusted and now is
not; and the raise helper is not wrapped in a try/catch, so a write problem with the second file
currently escapes and stops startup, which breaks the firm rule above.

content.subject: Fix five client honest-state findings (F1-F5)
content.description:
From opus-rev-client on f25e438, all verified independently, all PRE-EXISTING rather than regressions. Apply only after every reviewer has reported, to avoid editing files they are reading.

F1 (severe) BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406 — read-back FetchResult.Failure maps to terminal AnswerOutcome.Failed, violating §11.6. Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.

content.subject: Fix witness-write throw (B1) and unwitnessed-advance belief (C2)
content.description:
Found by opus-rev-server's probes (tmp/review-witness-holes.ts), both reproduced by me. Apply after all reviewers report.

B1 (SEVERE — breaks the stated invariant) answer.ts persist(): `await raiseWitness(next)` is unguarded, so any witness write failure (EPERM/EIO/ENOSPC on the witness rename, e.g. AV lock or ACL on that one file) rejects the whole persist. createAttemptStore does a proving write at startup, so the bridge REFUSES TO START over a witness-only fault — exactly what the design forbids, since a witness fault may only narrow coverage. Reproduced: "HOLE (throws instead of degrading) B1 ... EPERM ... rename answer-attempts-witness.json.tmp".
Fix: try/catch around raiseWitness -> degradeCoverage(reason) -> continue to the attempts write. Ordering already supports it: `file` is built AFTER raiseWitness, so a degrade inside the catch is reflected in the stamp that gets written. Safe because the advanced stamp means the resulting witness-behind-file state (which the next mount believes) claims nothing before this mount.

C2 (over-claim, low severity — production-unreachable precondition) after a generation-null mount whose unlink fails, the file advances unwitnessed (seq 4) while a stale witness says 2; the next mount reads "witness behind file" as the harmless direction and believes the stamp (degrades=0). Bounded: the advanced stamp excludes everything before that mount, so the only invisible rollback is one occurring DURING the unwitnessed mount's own lifetime. Requires generation-null, which openStateAnchor makes impossible in production. Decide deliberately: fix, or document as a bounded residual.

NOT actionable, checked: seq at 2^53 makes the file fail the zod int bound on the next mount -> quarantine -> records lost, but it degrades rather than throws and needs ~9 quadrillion rewrites. A3 in the probe reads alarming but is safe — coverage had narrowed to the mount, so the pre-mount request reports unconfirmed, not "not sent".

content.subject: Fix doc rot (D1-D4), generation optionality (D5), prune/clock invariant (D6)
content.description:
From fable-rev-architecture and fable-rev-durability, verified by me. Apply after all reviewers report.

D1 (I claimed this was fixed and it was not) answer.ts:2910 STILL carries the false claim "That is what keeps a pre-restart answer `confirmed` instead of decaying it to `unconfirmed`". I corrected PROTOCOL.md and types.ts and reported the premise fixed while a third copy survived. Also answer.ts:2889-2893 still states the OLD unconditional semantics ("known: false after a full round trip means the write never reached the bridge"), contradicting the paragraph immediately below it. This copy of the degrade list also omits "no rewrite mark" and "no generation supplied".

D2 The same coverage semantics are re-explained in FOUR places: PROTOCOL.md §11.5, types.ts field docs, index.ts wiring comment, answer.ts handleAnswerStatus header. It desynced inside the very commit that corrected it (D1 is the proof). Make types.ts canonical; reduce the others to pointers.

D3 crypto.ts:1063-1072 says "DO NOT REMOVE IT... keys.ts depends on it" — naming only keys.ts as the write-ordering dependent. Stale as of this commit: answer.ts/(ATTEMPT-WITNESS) now depends on the same guarantee. Whoever edits writeFileDurable reasons from that warning.

D4 keys.ts has zero back-reference to ATTEMPT-WITNESS; the link is one-way. One sentence in the SEND-WITNESS header.

D5 `generation?: string` in createAttemptStore compiles when omitted, then silently costs every mount its pre-restart coverage, guarded only by a warn. Change to `generation: string | null` — required, explicit null. Compile-time fail-fast, runtime never-refuse unchanged. Note the precedent: this commit already throws TypeError for the analogous `log` omission.

D6 (CONFIRMED, probe tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts 4/4, re-run by me) Wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, clock steps back 2h, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) = t0 again covers it while get() returns null. Second variant via the hydration filter under a forward-skewed mount clock. Bounded end-to-end because the client's mandated age comparison refuses "not sent" for a >24h-old submit, so it needs the client to ALSO break contract. Fix if wanted: floor by a high-water mark of prune-time clocks.

D7 Client decodes AnswerStatusResponse.bridgeStartedMs but never reads it — proof 2 does a second heartbeat round trip instead. Either consume it (deletes a round trip and the "no fresh heartbeat -> Unconfirmed" case for new bridges) or annotate as deliberately unread.

OUT OF SCOPE, surface to user, do not fix here: same-mount PAIR revert of state-anchor + devices.json (both renames in one unflushed NTFS window) can reverse a just-made device REVOCATION invisibly — epoch matches per-mount and (seq,digest) stay mutually consistent. keys.ts:37-38 claims index-alone rollback fails closed; the crash-pair case is neither "alone" nor the documented whole-tree limit. Exposure: seconds after a revoke plus a hard reset. It is the one durable-state site with no written answer to "does rollback matter here".

ARCHITECTURAL RECOMMENDATIONS (defer to /simplify): extract attempt-store.ts (~870 lines, self-contained behind the AttemptStore interface; must move the FEATURES.md (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) marker path in the SAME commit or the gate fails). Do NOT build a shared witness primitive with keys.ts — the divergence is policy-deep and a fatal/non-fatal constructor flag is the footgun. Add a rollback-disposition table so every future durable file must answer "what does a rollback here mean".

content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
From fable-rev-honesty, PLAUSIBLE but the consequence is the unrecoverable one. Distinct from D6 (which is about pruned records and is bounded by the client contract); this one produces the actual user-visible lie.

H3: the "ages not wall clocks" design only cancels PHONE-vs-DESKTOP skew. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine (both from Date.now() on the desktop), so a FORWARD step of the desktop clock between coverage start and the query inflates the claimed window by the step size.

Scenario: hard reset rolls the attempts file back and records are lost -> witness degrades, coverage = mount instant (wall clock). Desktop clock then corrects forward 1h (NTP fixing a slow clock, or a user time change). The user's answer landed 40 min ago, pre-crash, and its record was lost. Client computes submitAgeMs 40min < coverageAgeMs ~1h -> provesNeverSent -> user is told "the desktop never saw this request — it was not sent" for an answer that landed -> re-answers the picker -> §11.4 unrecoverable.

Exposure is confined to the coverage=mount (degraded) cases, because a witness-verified window implies no record loss and those windows are retention-floored. That is what makes it clampable.

Fix options: (a) server-side, when degraded, publish recordsSinceMs such that coverageAgeMs <= monotonic elapsed since mount (anchor on process.hrtime rather than Date.now()); or (b) client-side, cap proof 1 with proof 2's lifetime bracket. (a) is better — it fixes the claim at the source rather than making every client compensate.

Backward steps are already safe: recordsSinceMs > serverTimeMs -> coverageAgeMs null -> Unconfirmed, and that is already tested.

Note the shared root with D6: both are Date.now() being treated as monotonic. A single fix — anchoring published instants to a monotonic source — may close both. Consider that before fixing them separately.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
From sol-contract (ultra). Items not already tracked in #18-#21.

S1 (CONFIRMED, upgrades H3/D6 from plausible to reproduced) Sol reproduced the clock defect end-to-end with the real store and handler, and its scenario is better than the one I recorded: a landed record is 23 REAL hours old; the desktop clock jumps forward 2h; prune sees 25h and deletes it; the server advertises a 24h coverage age while the phone measures ~23h; 24h > 23h -> "never sent". Measured: record absent, degradation events none, coverageAgeMs 86,400,000, monotonic submit age 60,000, client predicate TRUE. This merges D6 (#20) and H3 (#21) into ONE confirmed defect: wall time treated as monotonic. Fix at the source with a monotonic anchor.

S2 (NEW) bridgeStartedMs is only Date.now() (index.ts:323) but the client treats equality as exact lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88). Repeated wall time can alias two different bridge lifetimes, making the fallback proof unsafe. Fix: mint a per-lifetime random/monotonic id, or combine Date.now() with the install generation + a counter.

S3 (NEW, medium) `in_flight` is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository correctly maps it to Pending (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:431), but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the status read lands during the ~15s injection window; the server later records confirmed; the phone stays Pending until the user intervenes and the watch shows Unconfirmed. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec — but they must agree.

S4 (NEW, medium) No cross-field or echoed-id validation at either boundary. The server's untrusted-disk schema validates fields independently (answer.ts:1314) and emits them unchanged (answer.ts:2948), so it will happily serve `confirmed` with `resolvedAtMs: null`. Per NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE 1 the SERVER should reject that shape at its own disk boundary, not just have the client cope (which is F2). Separately the client never checks the echoed requestId (Answer.kt:425, BridgeClient.kt:246), so a future erroneous response for request B could settle A — currently unreachable because response AAD binds the request nonce.

S5 (NEW, low) PROTOCOL §11.5 (PROTOCOL.md:1645) declares the proof fields required and non-null, while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null (Answer.kt:385). Missing fields NEED that exception for old-server compatibility, but the spec does not say so — and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Decide which rule wins and make both sides state it.

S6 The false "witness preserves confirmed after restart" claim also survives in the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70 — so the fix list for D1 is five sites, not four.

S7 The retention constant can drift silently: no shared vector or cross-repo assertion covers it. Consider adding it to the differential vector set, which already crosses the language boundary.

CONFIRMED CLEAN by Sol, agreeing with earlier passes: all nine JSON keys/casing/status spellings/units align; the server always emits all three proof fields on both branches; strict `>` in spec, server docs, client and tests; negative/reversed/absent/half windows conservatively lose proof; a degraded window is correct while the wall clock stays continuous; known:true responses are unaffected by degradation; all three compatibility directions are safe.

From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Found the root of it. `syncDirectory` (crypto.ts:1046):

```ts
if (process.platform === "win32") return;
const handle = await open(dir, "r");
```

The win32 early-return rests on the comment's claim that "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (`fs.open` on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". My probe shows that's wrong on both counts: `fs.open` on a directory **succeeds** under Bun on win32 (`r`, `r+`, `a` all open; only `w` gives `EISDIR`), and the `EPERM` comes from **fsync on a read-only handle** — exactly the `"r"` mode the non-win32 path uses. With `r+`, fsync succeeds.

So the platform gap that both `(ATTEMPT-WITNESS)` and `SEND-WITNESS` exist to compensate for was very likely concluded from trying the wrong open mode.

Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

input.prompt:
Fix five verified defects in the Kotlin client of a personal Android/Wear app. Repo: `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion` only — do NOT touch the sibling fork repo, I am editing that concurrently.

All five were found by review of commit `f25e438` and independently confirmed by multiple reviewers. All are PRE-EXISTING, not regressions from that commit. Read `PROTOCOL.md` §11.4, §11.5 and §11.6 first — they are the authoritative contract.

## Why these matter

The app answers a blocked AI agent's multiple-choice question from a phone/watch; a desktop bridge types the keystrokes. Then the phone asks "did it land?". Telling the user "it was not sent" when it DID land makes them answer the same question twice, which §11.4 records as unrecoverable — the second answer lands on whatever the agent asked next. So `Unconfirmed` ("I cannot tell, check the terminal") is always the correct fallback, and rendering ignorance as the terminal `Failed` is the defect class in all five.

## F1 — severe. A failed status READ becomes a terminal Failed.

`app-phone/src/main/java/family/khaira/supersetcompanion/phone/data/BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406`

```kotlin
is FetchResult.Failure -> AnswerOutcome.Failed(result.error.code, result.error.message)
```

Any transport/rate-limit/auth/decode failure on the status read becomes `Failed`. §11.6: "If it cannot be resolved (bridge unreachable), the UI shows it as unconfirmed verbatim — it does not guess in either direction."

Three-part blast radius, fix all of it:

content.subject: Fix five client honest-state findings (F1-F5)
content.description:
From opus-rev-client on f25e438, all verified independently, all PRE-EXISTING rather than regressions. Apply only after every reviewer has reported, to avoid editing files they are reading.

Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.

content.subject: Fix witness-write throw (B1) and unwitnessed-advance belief (C2)
content.description:
Found by opus-rev-server's probes (tmp/review-witness-holes.ts), both reproduced by me. Apply after all reviewers report.

B1 (SEVERE — breaks the stated invariant) answer.ts persist(): `await raiseWitness(next)` is unguarded, so any witness write failure (EPERM/EIO/ENOSPC on the witness rename, e.g. AV lock or ACL on that one file) rejects the whole persist. createAttemptStore does a proving write at startup, so the bridge REFUSES TO START over a witness-only fault — exactly what the design forbids, since a witness fault may only narrow coverage. Reproduced: "HOLE (throws instead of degrading) B1 ... EPERM ... rename answer-attempts-witness.json.tmp".
Fix: try/catch around raiseWitness -> degradeCoverage(reason) -> continue to the attempts write. Ordering already supports it: `file` is built AFTER raiseWitness, so a degrade inside the catch is reflected in the stamp that gets written. Safe because the advanced stamp means the resulting witness-behind-file state (which the next mount believes) claims nothing before this mount.

C2 (over-claim, low severity — production-unreachable precondition) after a generation-null mount whose unlink fails, the file advances unwitnessed (seq 4) while a stale witness says 2; the next mount reads "witness behind file" as the harmless direction and believes the stamp (degrades=0). Bounded: the advanced stamp excludes everything before that mount, so the only invisible rollback is one occurring DURING the unwitnessed mount's own lifetime. Requires generation-null, which openStateAnchor makes impossible in production. Decide deliberately: fix, or document as a bounded residual.

NOT actionable, checked: seq at 2^53 makes the file fail the zod int bound on the next mount -> quarantine -> records lost, but it degrades rather than throws and needs ~9 quadrillion rewrites. A3 in the probe reads alarming but is safe — coverage had narrowed to the mount, so the pre-mount request reports unconfirmed, not "not sent".

I corrected PROTOCOL.md and types.ts and reported the premise fixed while a third copy survived. Also answer.ts:2889-2893 still states the OLD unconditional semantics ("known: false after a full round trip means the write never reached the bridge"), contradicting the paragraph immediately below it. This copy of the degrade list also omits "no rewrite mark" and "no generation supplied".

D2 The same coverage semantics are re-explained in FOUR places: PROTOCOL.md §11.5, types.ts field docs, index.ts wiring comment, answer.ts handleAnswerStatus header. It desynced inside the very commit that corrected it (D1 is the proof). Make types.ts canonical; reduce the others to pointers.

D3 crypto.ts:1063-1072 says "DO NOT REMOVE IT... keys.ts depends on it" — naming only keys.ts as the write-ordering dependent. Stale as of this commit: answer.ts/(ATTEMPT-WITNESS) now depends on the same guarantee. Whoever edits writeFileDurable reasons from that warning.

D6 (CONFIRMED, probe tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts 4/4, re-run by me) Wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, clock steps back 2h, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) = t0 again covers it while get() returns null. content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
From fable-rev-honesty, PLAUSIBLE but the consequence is the unrecoverable one. Distinct from D6 (which is about pruned records and is bounded by the client contract); this one produces the actual user-visible lie.

H3: the "ages not wall clocks" design only cancels PHONE-vs-DESKTOP skew. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine (both from Date.now() on the desktop), so a FORWARD step of the desktop clock between coverage start and the query inflates the claimed window by the step size.

Scenario: hard reset rolls the attempts file back and records are lost -> witness degrades, coverage = mount instant (wall clock). Desktop clock then corrects forward 1h (NTP fixing a slow clock, or a user time change). The user's answer landed 40 min ago, pre-crash, and its record was lost. Client computes submitAgeMs 40min < coverageAgeMs ~1h -> provesNeverSent -> user is told "the desktop never saw this request — it was not sent" for an answer that landed -> re-answers the picker -> §11.4 unrecoverable.

Exposure is confined to the coverage=mount (degraded) cases, because a witness-verified window implies no record loss and those windows are retention-floored. That is what makes it clampable.

Fix options: (a) server-side, when degraded, publish recordsSinceMs such that coverageAgeMs <= monotonic elapsed since mount (anchor on process.hrtime rather than Date.now()); or (b) client-side, cap proof 1 with proof 2's lifetime bracket. (a) is better — it fixes the claim at the source rather than making every client compensate.

Backward steps are already safe: recordsSinceMs > serverTimeMs -> coverageAgeMs null -> Unconfirmed, and that is already tested.

Note the shared root with D6: both are Date.now() being treated as monotonic. A single fix — anchoring published instants to a monotonic source — may close both. Consider that before fixing them separately.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
From sol-contract (ultra). Items not already tracked in #18-#21.

S1 (CONFIRMED, upgrades H3/D6 from plausible to reproduced) Sol reproduced the clock defect end-to-end with the real store and handler, and its scenario is better than the one I recorded: a landed record is 23 REAL hours old; the desktop clock jumps forward 2h; prune sees 25h and deletes it; the server advertises a 24h coverage age while the phone measures ~23h; 24h > 23h -> "never sent". Measured: record absent, degradation events none, coverageAgeMs 86,400,000, monotonic submit age 60,000, client predicate TRUE. This merges D6 (#20) and H3 (#21) into ONE confirmed defect: wall time treated as monotonic. Fix at the source with a monotonic anchor.

S2 (NEW) bridgeStartedMs is only Date.now() (index.ts:323) but the client treats equality as exact lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88). Repeated wall time can alias two different bridge lifetimes, making the fallback proof unsafe. Fix: mint a per-lifetime random/monotonic id, or combine Date.now() with the install generation + a counter.

S3 (NEW, medium) `in_flight` is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository correctly maps it to Pending (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:431), but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the status read lands during the ~15s injection window; the server later records confirmed; the phone stays Pending until the user intervenes and the watch shows Unconfirmed. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec — but they must agree.

S4 (NEW, medium) No cross-field or echoed-id validation at either boundary. The server's untrusted-disk schema validates fields independently (answer.ts:1314) and emits them unchanged (answer.ts:2948), so it will happily serve `confirmed` with `resolvedAtMs: null`. Per NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE 1 the SERVER should reject that shape at its own disk boundary, not just have the client cope (which is F2). Separately the client never checks the echoed requestId (Answer.kt:425, BridgeClient.kt:246), so a future erroneous response for request B could settle A — currently unreachable because response AAD binds the request nonce.

S5 (NEW, low) PROTOCOL §11.5 (PROTOCOL.md:1645) declares the proof fields required and non-null, while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null (Answer.kt:385). Missing fields NEED that exception for old-server compatibility, but the spec does not say so — and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Decide which rule wins and make both sides state it.

S6 The false "witness preserves confirmed after restart" claim also survives in the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70 — so the fix list for D1 is five sites, not four.

content.subject: CRITICAL: detached prune from a stopped store clobbers the new store and lowers the counter
content.description:
From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Serialization and the witness read/write guard are per-INSTANCE only (answer.ts:1892-1967), so the old instance's persist() has no idea a new instance exists.

SEQUENCE (Sol's probe output): old store at F/W=2 begins prune and reads W=2 -> stop/start creates a new store which reaches F/W=3, then records an answer at F/W=4 -> the old prune resumes and writes its stale empty snapshot as W=3, F=3. Measured: before releasing the old prune F=4/W=4 records [old,new]; after F=3/W=3 records []; on reopen no degradation, the new record absent, old coverage retained. The next restart therefore TRUSTS a matching pair while a recorded answer has been destroyed -> false "it was not sent".

THIS BREAKS THE RISE-ONLY CLAIM. I verified rise-only within one instance and reported it as holding; it does not hold across instances. Math.max and the promise tail cannot see another instance's writes.

BROADER CLASS: the same detached-interval pattern covers nonceCache.compact, audit.prune and deviceStore.purgeExpiredRevocations in the same block. Check whether any of those can also clobber a successor's state. The nonce cache is the one to look at hardest, since its rollback consequence is the fatal one.

FIX DIRECTIONS: (a) make teardown await in-flight maintenance, not just clear timers — track the in-flight promise and await it in the unwind entry; (b) give each store instance an ownership token and have persist() refuse if it is no longer the owner (the anchor already has this shape for the send-nonce lifecycle); (c) both. (b) defends even against a leaked reference that outlives teardown.

Also from the same report, comment errors this invalidates: index.ts:699-704 and 723-724 claim teardown prevents old writers overlapping a new bridge — detached maintenance makes that false. And answer.ts:1457 / 1877-1882 claim witness-ahead PROVES an attempts-file version was durably written and then lost; a failure between the witness raise and the primary write produces the identical state with no such version ever existing.

content.subject: Lead: an r+ directory handle may be fsync-able on Windows, which would retire the ordering assumption
content.description:
Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

Related: #22 (the assumption this could retire), #24 (unaffected by this — the lifecycle race is not a durability problem).

content.subject: Short writes (R1), counter saturation (R2), fifth doc site (R3), comment errors (R4)
content.description:
Remaining items from sol-crash-consistency, all smaller than #24/#25.

R1 writeFileDurable (crypto.ts:1082) ignores the `bytesWritten` Node returns. A short write is synced and renamed as though complete; the next start quarantines the truncated JSON and LOSES the records instead of failing fast. Violates the fail-fast-and-loud rule. Fix: assert bytesWritten equals the buffer length and throw if not.

R2 Both schemas accept Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for the counter (answer.ts:1364 and ~1458) while answer.ts:1942 increments it: load 9007199254740991 -> startup writes ...992 -> the next increment yields the SAME value -> the following startup rejects and quarantines it. Unreachable by human usage, reachable from a schema-valid nonsense file. Bound the schema below MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or treat saturation as a degrade rather than letting it self-corrupt.

R3 The doc-rot list in #20 is FIVE sites, not four. Sol found a fifth nobody else did: answer.ts:1658-1663. Full set: 1333-1335, 1384-1387, 1591-1595, 1658-1663, 2905-2912. Plus the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70.

R4 Further comment errors beyond #20 and #24:
- answer.ts:1609-1611 says the store never refuses startup. Witness write failures do (that is B1, #19) — so this comment is false until B1 is fixed, and must be re-checked after.
- answer.ts:1726-1728 claims a failed quarantine rename proves the later durable write would also fail. An obstruction only at the generated quarantine DESTINATION disproves that.
- The "rise-only" wording is true only within one store instance and below the numeric boundary — not across lifecycle overlap (#24) and not at saturation (R2). Reword to state the scope it actually holds in.

R5 Sol's error-handling audit of the witness path: read, JSON and schema failures ARE caught correctly. NOT caught: ENOSPC, EACCES, sync/close errors, and a failed replacement. That is the precise scope of the B1 fix in #19 — the try/catch must cover all of those, not just rename EPERM.

content.subject: Fix five client honest-state findings (F1-F5)
content.description:
From opus-rev-client on f25e438, all verified independently, all PRE-EXISTING rather than regressions. Apply only after every reviewer has reported, to avoid editing files they are reading.

F1 (severe) BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406 — read-back FetchResult.Failure maps to terminal AnswerOutcome.Failed, violating §11.6. Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.

content.subject: Fix witness-write throw (B1) and unwitnessed-advance belief (C2)
content.description:
Found by opus-rev-server's probes (tmp/review-witness-holes.ts), both reproduced by me. Apply after all reviewers report.

B1 (SEVERE — breaks the stated invariant) answer.ts persist(): `await raiseWitness(next)` is unguarded, so any witness write failure (EPERM/EIO/ENOSPC on the witness rename, e.g. AV lock or ACL on that one file) rejects the whole persist. createAttemptStore does a proving write at startup, so the bridge REFUSES TO START over a witness-only fault — exactly what the design forbids, since a witness fault may only narrow coverage. Reproduced: "HOLE (throws instead of degrading) B1 ... EPERM ... rename answer-attempts-witness.json.tmp".
Fix: try/catch around raiseWitness -> degradeCoverage(reason) -> continue to the attempts write. Ordering already supports it: `file` is built AFTER raiseWitness, so a degrade inside the catch is reflected in the stamp that gets written. Safe because the advanced stamp means the resulting witness-behind-file state (which the next mount believes) claims nothing before this mount.

C2 (over-claim, low severity — production-unreachable precondition) after a generation-null mount whose unlink fails, the file advances unwitnessed (seq 4) while a stale witness says 2; the next mount reads "witness behind file" as the harmless direction and believes the stamp (degrades=0). Bounded: the advanced stamp excludes everything before that mount, so the only invisible rollback is one occurring DURING the unwitnessed mount's own lifetime. Requires generation-null, which openStateAnchor makes impossible in production. Decide deliberately: fix, or document as a bounded residual.

NOT actionable, checked: seq at 2^53 makes the file fail the zod int bound on the next mount -> quarantine -> records lost, but it degrades rather than throws and needs ~9 quadrillion rewrites. A3 in the probe reads alarming but is safe — coverage had narrowed to the mount, so the pre-mount request reports unconfirmed, not "not sent".

content.subject: Fix doc rot (D1-D4), generation optionality (D5), prune/clock invariant (D6)
content.description:
From fable-rev-architecture and fable-rev-durability, verified by me. Apply after all reviewers report.

D1 (I claimed this was fixed and it was not) answer.ts:2910 STILL carries the false claim "That is what keeps a pre-restart answer `confirmed` instead of decaying it to `unconfirmed`". I corrected PROTOCOL.md and types.ts and reported the premise fixed while a third copy survived. Also answer.ts:2889-2893 still states the OLD unconditional semantics ("known: false after a full round trip means the write never reached the bridge"), contradicting the paragraph immediately below it. This copy of the degrade list also omits "no rewrite mark" and "no generation supplied".

D2 The same coverage semantics are re-explained in FOUR places: PROTOCOL.md §11.5, types.ts field docs, index.ts wiring comment, answer.ts handleAnswerStatus header. It desynced inside the very commit that corrected it (D1 is the proof). Make types.ts canonical; reduce the others to pointers.

D3 crypto.ts:1063-1072 says "DO NOT REMOVE IT... keys.ts depends on it" — naming only keys.ts as the write-ordering dependent. Stale as of this commit: answer.ts/(ATTEMPT-WITNESS) now depends on the same guarantee. Whoever edits writeFileDurable reasons from that warning.

D4 keys.ts has zero back-reference to ATTEMPT-WITNESS; the link is one-way. One sentence in the SEND-WITNESS header.

D5 `generation?: string` in createAttemptStore compiles when omitted, then silently costs every mount its pre-restart coverage, guarded only by a warn. Change to `generation: string | null` — required, explicit null. Compile-time fail-fast, runtime never-refuse unchanged. Note the precedent: this commit already throws TypeError for the analogous `log` omission.

D6 (CONFIRMED, probe tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts 4/4, re-run by me) Wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, clock steps back 2h, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) = t0 again covers it while get() returns null. Second variant via the hydration filter under a forward-skewed mount clock. Bounded end-to-end because the client's mandated age comparison refuses "not sent" for a >24h-old submit, so it needs the client to ALSO break contract. Fix if wanted: floor by a high-water mark of prune-time clocks.

D7 Client decodes AnswerStatusResponse.bridgeStartedMs but never reads it — proof 2 does a second heartbeat round trip instead. Either consume it (deletes a round trip and the "no fresh heartbeat -> Unconfirmed" case for new bridges) or annotate as deliberately unread.

OUT OF SCOPE, surface to user, do not fix here: same-mount PAIR revert of state-anchor + devices.json (both renames in one unflushed NTFS window) can reverse a just-made device REVOCATION invisibly — epoch matches per-mount and (seq,digest) stay mutually consistent. keys.ts:37-38 claims index-alone rollback fails closed; the crash-pair case is neither "alone" nor the documented whole-tree limit. Exposure: seconds after a revoke plus a hard reset. It is the one durable-state site with no written answer to "does rollback matter here".

ARCHITECTURAL RECOMMENDATIONS (defer to /simplify): extract attempt-store.ts (~870 lines, self-contained behind the AttemptStore interface; must move the FEATURES.md (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) marker path in the SAME commit or the gate fails). Do NOT build a shared witness primitive with keys.ts — the divergence is policy-deep and a fatal/non-fatal constructor flag is the footgun. Add a rollback-disposition table so every future durable file must answer "what does a rollback here mean".

content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
From fable-rev-honesty, PLAUSIBLE but the consequence is the unrecoverable one. Distinct from D6 (which is about pruned records and is bounded by the client contract); this one produces the actual user-visible lie.

H3: the "ages not wall clocks" design only cancels PHONE-vs-DESKTOP skew. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine (both from Date.now() on the desktop), so a FORWARD step of the desktop clock between coverage start and the query inflates the claimed window by the step size.

Scenario: hard reset rolls the attempts file back and records are lost -> witness degrades, coverage = mount instant (wall clock). Desktop clock then corrects forward 1h (NTP fixing a slow clock, or a user time change). The user's answer landed 40 min ago, pre-crash, and its record was lost. Client computes submitAgeMs 40min < coverageAgeMs ~1h -> provesNeverSent -> user is told "the desktop never saw this request — it was not sent" for an answer that landed -> re-answers the picker -> §11.4 unrecoverable.

Exposure is confined to the coverage=mount (degraded) cases, because a witness-verified window implies no record loss and those windows are retention-floored. That is what makes it clampable.

Fix options: (a) server-side, when degraded, publish recordsSinceMs such that coverageAgeMs <= monotonic elapsed since mount (anchor on process.hrtime rather than Date.now()); or (b) client-side, cap proof 1 with proof 2's lifetime bracket. (a) is better — it fixes the claim at the source rather than making every client compensate.

Backward steps are already safe: recordsSinceMs > serverTimeMs -> coverageAgeMs null -> Unconfirmed, and that is already tested.

Note the shared root with D6: both are Date.now() being treated as monotonic. A single fix — anchoring published instants to a monotonic source — may close both. Consider that before fixing them separately.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
From sol-contract (ultra). Items not already tracked in #18-#21.

S1 (CONFIRMED, upgrades H3/D6 from plausible to reproduced) Sol reproduced the clock defect end-to-end with the real store and handler, and its scenario is better than the one I recorded: a landed record is 23 REAL hours old; the desktop clock jumps forward 2h; prune sees 25h and deletes it; the server advertises a 24h coverage age while the phone measures ~23h; 24h > 23h -> "never sent". Measured: record absent, degradation events none, coverageAgeMs 86,400,000, monotonic submit age 60,000, client predicate TRUE. This merges D6 (#20) and H3 (#21) into ONE confirmed defect: wall time treated as monotonic. Fix at the source with a monotonic anchor.

S2 (NEW) bridgeStartedMs is only Date.now() (index.ts:323) but the client treats equality as exact lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88). Repeated wall time can alias two different bridge lifetimes, making the fallback proof unsafe. Fix: mint a per-lifetime random/monotonic id, or combine Date.now() with the install generation + a counter.

S3 (NEW, medium) `in_flight` is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository correctly maps it to Pending (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:431), but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the status read lands during the ~15s injection window; the server later records confirmed; the phone stays Pending until the user intervenes and the watch shows Unconfirmed. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec — but they must agree.

S4 (NEW, medium) No cross-field or echoed-id validation at either boundary. The server's untrusted-disk schema validates fields independently (answer.ts:1314) and emits them unchanged (answer.ts:2948), so it will happily serve `confirmed` with `resolvedAtMs: null`. Per NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE 1 the SERVER should reject that shape at its own disk boundary, not just have the client cope (which is F2). Separately the client never checks the echoed requestId (Answer.kt:425, BridgeClient.kt:246), so a future erroneous response for request B could settle A — currently unreachable because response AAD binds the request nonce.

S5 (NEW, low) PROTOCOL §11.5 (PROTOCOL.md:1645) declares the proof fields required and non-null, while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null (Answer.kt:385). Missing fields NEED that exception for old-server compatibility, but the spec does not say so — and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Decide which rule wins and make both sides state it.

S6 The false "witness preserves confirmed after restart" claim also survives in the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70 — so the fix list for D1 is five sites, not four.

S7 The retention constant can drift silently: no shared vector or cross-repo assertion covers it. Consider adding it to the differential vector set, which already crosses the language boundary.

CONFIRMED CLEAN by Sol, agreeing with earlier passes: all nine JSON keys/casing/status spellings/units align; the server always emits all three proof fields on both branches; strict `>` in spec, server docs, client and tests; negative/reversed/absent/half windows conservatively lose proof; a degraded window is correct while the wall clock stays continuous; known:true responses are unaffected by degradation; all three compatibility directions are safe.

content.subject: CRITICAL: detached prune from a stopped store clobbers the new store and lowers the counter
content.description:
From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Serialization and the witness read/write guard are per-INSTANCE only (answer.ts:1892-1967), so the old instance's persist() has no idea a new instance exists.

SEQUENCE (Sol's probe output): old store at F/W=2 begins prune and reads W=2 -> stop/start creates a new store which reaches F/W=3, then records an answer at F/W=4 -> the old prune resumes and writes its stale empty snapshot as W=3, F=3. Measured: before releasing the old prune F=4/W=4 records [old,new]; after F=3/W=3 records []; on reopen no degradation, the new record absent, old coverage retained. The next restart therefore TRUSTS a matching pair while a recorded answer has been destroyed -> false "it was not sent".

THIS BREAKS THE RISE-ONLY CLAIM. I verified rise-only within one instance and reported it as holding; it does not hold across instances. Math.max and the promise tail cannot see another instance's writes.

BROADER CLASS: the same detached-interval pattern covers nonceCache.compact, audit.prune and deviceStore.purgeExpiredRevocations in the same block. Check whether any of those can also clobber a successor's state. The nonce cache is the one to look at hardest, since its rollback consequence is the fatal one.

FIX DIRECTIONS: (a) make teardown await in-flight maintenance, not just clear timers — track the in-flight promise and await it in the unwind entry; (b) give each store instance an ownership token and have persist() refuse if it is no longer the owner (the anchor already has this shape for the send-nonce lifecycle); (c) both. (b) defends even against a leaked reference that outlives teardown.

Also from the same report, comment errors this invalidates: index.ts:699-704 and 723-724 claim teardown prevents old writers overlapping a new bridge — detached maintenance makes that false. And answer.ts:1457 / 1877-1882 claim witness-ahead PROVES an attempts-file version was durably written and then lost; a failure between the witness raise and the primary write produces the identical state with no such version ever existing.

content.subject: Lead: an r+ directory handle may be fsync-able on Windows, which would retire the ordering assumption
content.description:
Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

Related: #22 (the assumption this could retire), #24 (unaffected by this — the lifecycle race is not a durability problem).

content.subject: Short writes (R1), counter saturation (R2), fifth doc site (R3), comment errors (R4)
content.description:
Remaining items from sol-crash-consistency, all smaller than #24/#25.

R1 writeFileDurable (crypto.ts:1082) ignores the `bytesWritten` Node returns. A short write is synced and renamed as though complete; the next start quarantines the truncated JSON and LOSES the records instead of failing fast. Violates the fail-fast-and-loud rule. Fix: assert bytesWritten equals the buffer length and throw if not.

R2 Both schemas accept Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for the counter (answer.ts:1364 and ~1458) while answer.ts:1942 increments it: load 9007199254740991 -> startup writes ...992 -> the next increment yields the SAME value -> the following startup rejects and quarantines it. Unreachable by human usage, reachable from a schema-valid nonsense file. Bound the schema below MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or treat saturation as a degrade rather than letting it self-corrupt.

R3 The doc-rot list in #20 is FIVE sites, not four. Sol found a fifth nobody else did: answer.ts:1658-1663. Full set: 1333-1335, 1384-1387, 1591-1595, 1658-1663, 2905-2912. Plus the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70.

R4 Further comment errors beyond #20 and #24:
- answer.ts:1609-1611 says the store never refuses startup. Witness write failures do (that is B1, #19) — so this comment is false until B1 is fixed, and must be re-checked after.
- answer.ts:1726-1728 claims a failed quarantine rename proves the later durable write would also fail. An obstruction only at the generated quarantine DESTINATION disproves that.
- The "rise-only" wording is true only within one store instance and below the numeric boundary — not across lifecycle overlap (#24) and not at saturation (R2). Reword to state the scope it actually holds in.

R5 Sol's error-handling audit of the witness path: read, JSON and schema failures ARE caught correctly. NOT caught: ENOSPC, EACCES, sync/close errors, and a failed replacement. That is the precise scope of the B1 fix in #19 — the try/catch must cover all of those, not just rename EPERM.
