- D1c the handleAnswerStatus degrade list now includes the unwritable and no-rewrite-mark cases.
- D3 crypto.ts's write-ordering warning named only keys.ts as its dependent; it now names both mechanisms AND records that the ordering is an inference from NTFS behaviour rather than a documented platform guarantee.
- D5 `generation?: string` is now `generation: string | null` — required, explicitly nullable. Runtime leniency unchanged (a missing generation still degrades, never throws); the strict type is what stops a silent omission. The degrade-reason branch handles undefined as well as null, so an untyped harness caller reads the same message.

STILL OPEN:
- D6 wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, the clock steps back, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) covers it again while get() returns null. Reproduced by tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4) and independently by Sol with the real store and handler.
- D2 the four-place duplication of the coverage semantics is unaddressed; /simplify is assessing whether the fix is editorial (types.ts canonical, pointers elsewhere) or structural (drift made detectable).
- D4 keys.ts still has no back-reference to ATTEMPT-WITNESS; the link remains one-way.
- D7 the client still decodes AnswerStatusResponse.bridgeStartedMs without reading it; /simplify is judging consume-vs-annotate.

D6 shares its root with #21/S1 — Date.now() treated as monotonic — and all of them should be fixed together with a monotonic anchor, not patched separately.
content.activeForm: Fixing doc rot and taxonomy findings

content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
FIXED, server half (PRUNE-FLOOR), pending commit. Probes: tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4, assertions inverted from demonstrating the bug to pinning the fix) and tmp/verify-prune-floor.ts (5/5, new).

What was wrong: recordsSinceMs returned max(coverageSinceMs, now - retentionMs). The second term is recomputed from the WALL CLOCK on every read, while pruning is irreversible. Drop a record at 25h, let the clock step back 2h, and the term moves BACK behind the record just deleted — so the window claimed coverage over a record get() can no longer return. The hydration retention filter had the identical shape via a forward-skewed mount clock.

Fix: a rise-only `prunedThroughMs` — the highest retention boundary the store has ever crossed — persisted in the attempts file and raised in three places: on prune (whether or not anything was dropped, since the boundary was still crossed), on a hydration drop, and by taking the max with the file's own value at load. recordsSinceMs is now floored by it as well, so once records older than X are gone the window never reaches behind X again, whatever the clock does. The field is optional-defaulting-to-0 so a file written before it loads unchanged and the first prune establishes a floor.

STILL OPEN — the other half, and it needs a design decision rather than a patch:
H3/S1 second half. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine, so a FORWARD desktop clock step inflates the claimed window and the client's monotonic submitAge comparison can then yield a false "not sent". Exposure is confined to the degraded (coverage = mount) cases, since a witness-verified window is retention-floored.

Why it is not patched: the inference it corrupts — a terminal "not sent" from an absent record — is being DISABLED anyway, because sol-architect found it unsound for a deeper reason (the overtaking race: /status can pass an admitted /answer that has not yet written in_flight, so absence cannot prove the answer will not be typed). Patching the arithmetic under a disabled inference is wasted work.

The sound fix, per sol-architect, is to stop doing temporal proofs at all: an opaque random coverageEpochId that the client captures before submitting and echoes back, rotated by the server before any coverage gap, reset, unverified restart or prune. The server then owns the proof and the client does no clock arithmetic. That also retires S2 (bridgeStartedMs is a Date.now() value treated as an identity, so two lifetimes can alias). Do it together with the durable CAS, not before.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
From sol-contract (ultra). Items not already tracked in #18-#21.

S1 (CONFIRMED, upgrades H3/D6 from plausible to reproduced) Sol reproduced the clock defect end-to-end with the real store and handler, and its scenario is better than the one I recorded: a landed record is 23 REAL hours old; the desktop clock jumps forward 2h; prune sees 25h and deletes it; the server advertises a 24h coverage age while the phone measures ~23h; 24h > 23h -> "never sent". Measured: record absent, degradation events none, coverageAgeMs 86,400,000, monotonic submit age 60,000, client predicate TRUE. This merges D6 (#20) and H3 (#21) into ONE confirmed defect: wall time treated as monotonic. Fix at the source with a monotonic anchor.

S2 (NEW) bridgeStartedMs is only Date.now() (index.ts:323) but the client treats equality as exact lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88). Repeated wall time can alias two different bridge lifetimes, making the fallback proof unsafe. Fix: mint a per-lifetime random/monotonic id, or combine Date.now() with the install generation + a counter.

S3 (NEW, medium) `in_flight` is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository correctly maps it to Pending (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:431), but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the status read lands during the ~15s injection window; the server later records confirmed; the phone stays Pending until the user intervenes and the watch shows Unconfirmed. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec — but they must agree.

S4 (NEW, medium) No cross-field or echoed-id validation at either boundary. The server's untrusted-disk schema validates fields independently (answer.ts:1314) and emits them unchanged (answer.ts:2948), so it will happily serve `confirmed` with `resolvedAtMs: null`. Per NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE 1 the SERVER should reject that shape at its own disk boundary, not just have the client cope (which is F2). Separately the client never checks the echoed requestId (Answer.kt:425, BridgeClient.kt:246), so a future erroneous response for request B could settle A — currently unreachable because response AAD binds the request nonce.

S5 (NEW, low) PROTOCOL §11.5 (PROTOCOL.md:1645) declares the proof fields required and non-null, while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null (Answer.kt:385). Missing fields NEED that exception for old-server compatibility, but the spec does not say so — and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Decide which rule wins and make both sides state it.

S6 The false "witness preserves confirmed after restart" claim also survives in the harness itself, tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts:70 — so the fix list for D1 is five sites, not four.

S7 The retention constant can drift silently: no shared vector or cross-repo assertion covers it. Consider adding it to the differential vector set, which already crosses the language boundary.

CONFIRMED CLEAN by Sol, agreeing with earlier passes: all nine JSON keys/casing/status spellings/units align; the server always emits all three proof fields on both branches; strict `>` in spec, server docs, client and tests; negative/reversed/absent/half windows conservatively lose proof; a degraded window is correct while the wall clock stays continuous; known:true responses are unaffected by degradation; all three compatibility directions are safe.

content.subject: CRITICAL: detached prune from a stopped store clobbers the new store and lowers the counter
content.description:
From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Serialization and the witness read/write guard are per-INSTANCE only (answer.ts:1892-1967), so the old instance's persist() has no idea a new instance exists.

SEQUENCE (Sol's probe output): old store at F/W=2 begins prune and reads W=2 -> stop/start creates a new store which reaches F/W=3, then records an answer at F/W=4 -> the old prune resumes and writes its stale empty snapshot as W=3, F=3. Measured: before releasing the old prune F=4/W=4 records [old,new]; after F=3/W=3 records []; on reopen no degradation, the new record absent, old coverage retained. The next restart therefore TRUSTS a matching pair while a recorded answer has been destroyed -> false "it was not sent".

THIS BREAKS THE RISE-ONLY CLAIM. I verified rise-only within one instance and reported it as holding; it does not hold across instances. Math.max and the promise tail cannot see another instance's writes.

BROADER CLASS: the same detached-interval pattern covers nonceCache.compact, audit.prune and deviceStore.purgeExpiredRevocations in the same block. Check whether any of those can also clobber a successor's state. The nonce cache is the one to look at hardest, since its rollback consequence is the fatal one.

FIX DIRECTIONS: (a) make teardown await in-flight maintenance, not just clear timers — track the in-flight promise and await it in the unwind entry; (b) give each store instance an ownership token and have persist() refuse if it is no longer the owner (the anchor already has this shape for the send-nonce lifecycle); (c) both. (b) defends even against a leaked reference that outlives teardown.

Also from the same report, comment errors this invalidates: index.ts:699-704 and 723-724 claim teardown prevents old writers overlapping a new bridge — detached maintenance makes that false. And answer.ts:1457 / 1877-1882 claim witness-ahead PROVES an attempts-file version was durably written and then lost; a failure between the witness raise and the primary write produces the identical state with no such version ever existing.

content.subject: Lead: an r+ directory handle may be fsync-able on Windows, which would retire the ordering assumption
content.description:
Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

Related: #22 (the assumption this could retire), #24 (unaffected by this — the lifecycle race is not a durability problem).

content.subject: Short writes (R1), counter saturation (R2), fifth doc site (R3), comment errors (R4)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE in 563c41b56.

FIXED:
- R1 writeFileDurable now checks the bytesWritten Node returns and throws before the rename, so a short write can no longer be fsync'd and renamed as though complete (which previously lost every record in the file at the next start, via quarantine).
- R3 the doc-rot list was five sites, not four — all five cleared, plus the harness heading.
- R4 partial: crypto.ts's syncDirectory reason (measurably wrong — a directory opens fine under Bun on win32 arm64 and r+ fsync succeeds; only the read-only mode gives EPERM) is corrected with the measured results and the reason the no-op nonetheless stays. index.ts's teardown-ordering claim is corrected and now true by construction thanks to MAINTENANCE-DRAIN.

STILL OPEN:
- R2 both schemas accept Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for the rewrite counter while persist() increments it: load ...991 -> write ...992 -> the next increment yields the SAME value -> the following start rejects and quarantines it. Unreachable by human usage, reachable from a schema-valid nonsense file. Bound the schema below MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or treat saturation as a degrade rather than letting it self-corrupt.
- R4 remainder: answer.ts:1609-1611 says the store never refuses startup — now TRUE after the B1 fix, so re-read it and confirm rather than assume. answer.ts:1726-1728 still claims a failed quarantine rename proves the later durable write would also fail, which an obstruction only at the quarantine destination disproves. The "rise-only" wording still needs scoping: it holds within one store instance and below the numeric boundary, but #24 showed it did not hold across lifecycle overlap (now fixed by the drain) and R2 shows it does not hold at saturation.
- R5 the B1 fix does cover the full error class Sol named (ENOSPC, EACCES, sync/close, failed replacement) because it catches everything raiseWitness can throw rather than matching on codes — worth keeping that way rather than narrowing to specific errno values.

content.subject: Altitude findings: pending-destroy key leak (A1), watch Confirmed downgrade (A2), witness factoring (A3)
content.description:
From simp-altitude, the most valuable review of the session. Two are real bugs outside tonight's commits; the rest are structural.

A1 (REAL BUG, key leak) pending-destroy.json needs rollback protection and has none. Verified order: writePendingDestroy(merged) at device-store.ts:1078 lands BEFORE records are deleted and the index persisted. Lose the journal's rename while the index's survives -> purged devices are gone from the index, nothing names their keyRefs, and K_dev stays on disk PERMANENTLY and UNDETECTABLY. That is the exact failure device-store.ts:531-535 says this journal replaced. Keys are revoked and tombstoned so nothing is authorised; the cost is a revoked device's key surviving indefinitely, able to decrypt captured historical traffic.
Correct depth is NOT a third witness (crypto.ts forbids another ordering dependent). The obligation is RE-DERIVABLE: sweep at start for key files whose keyRef appears in no index record, reconstructing the list from ground truth with no second file and no ordering assumption. Cost: KeyStore (keys.ts:929-952) has no enumeration, needs list() (~10 lines readdir) plus ~20 lines of sweep in drainPendingDestroy.
PRINCIPLE WORTH KEEPING: a witness is only right where the obligation cannot be re-derived. Where it can, re-derivation strictly dominates.

A2 (REAL BUG, live, user-visible) the watch downgrades a Confirmed answer. QuestionStore.kt:404-440 guards requestId/questionId identity only, never outcome rank, and outstandingRequestId() (:455) returns the id for Confirmed too — so an incoming Unconfirmed for the SAME requestId falls through to else -> applied = true and overwrites Confirmed. Reachable: WatchBridge.kt:309-322, after a phone process restart the phone has no record, relays WatchAnswerStatus.UNKNOWN, the watch maps else -> Unconfirmed (QuestionStore.kt:401), and a confirmed answer is downgraded on the wrist. The new recordOutcome lattice cannot help — it orders only outcomes passing through the phone's answersState and this path never enters it.
Fix (~25 lines): put rank/supersedes on core/wear/WatchAnswerStatus (already in core, so the wire enum is shared while the ordering is not) and have QuestionStore.onAnswerResult refuse a non-superseding incoming, mirroring recordOutcome. Do NOT move AnswerOutcome wholesale to core — it drags phone UI copy (AnswerOutcome.kt:78-94 BridgeErrorCode.userText) along.

A3 (structural, do when a third dependent is proposed) keys.ts:735-848 and answer.ts:1372-1546 are the same machine — rise-only integer beside a durable file, raised before it, generation-bound, max-at-start, gap->verdict — differing only in mark type and verdict severity, which are parameters. crypto.ts already says "do not add a THIRD", which concedes a third is plausible. The ordering invariant is restated as prose in three places and enforced by nothing. content.subject: Overtaking race: absence cannot prove not-sent without a durable CAS fence
content.description:
From sol-architect (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, ~3.5h). The deepest finding of the session: none of the other eight reviewers found it, and it invalidates the actionable-negative feature independently of the witness.

THE RACE (verified by me): handleAnswer reads the attempt record at answer.ts:2309 and does not durably record in_flight until answer.ts:2504 — 195 lines and several awaits later, spanning guard evaluation and lock acquisition. So:
  1. /v1/answer is admitted, pauses before writing in_flight
  2. /v1/answer/status overtakes it, finds no record, the coverage proof holds
  3. the phone reports the terminal "it was not sent"
  4. the original /answer resumes, writes in_flight, and TYPES THE ANSWER
The user then answers a picker that was already answered, which §11.4 records as unrecoverable. HTTP cancellation does not help: the server snapshots its freshness time before several awaits (http.ts:1119).

WHY THE WITNESS CANNOT FIX THIS: the witness proves things about the PAST. This is a claim about the FUTURE — that an already-admitted request will not act. No amount of durable-state attestation closes it.

IMMEDIATE MITIGATION (in progress, fix-client-two): proven absence resolves to Unconfirmed instead of a terminal Failed. Positive stored statuses are unaffected. This is a deliberate capability regression, not a bug, and the code says so.

THE REAL FIX — durable per-request compare-and-set with a tombstone:
  existing state | /answer            | authoritative /status
  absent         | CAS to in_flight   | CAS to closed_not_received
  in_flight/done | idempotent replay  | return known status
  closed_...     | REFUSE to type     | return not_received
Whichever wins persists BEFORE either typing or returning a terminal negative. If the status-side CAS cannot be persisted, the result stays unconfirmed. A non-atomic check-then-insert is insufficient.

SOL'S PREFERRED TARGET, and I agree it is the right end state: move the attempt ledger into the host SQLite database the bridge already receives, rather than the hand-rolled two-file protocol.
  - SQLite gives the transaction the CAS needs, and `synchronous=FULL` gives DOCUMENTED per-commit durability instead of an undocumented cross-file rename-ordering inference (which is #22, and which crypto.ts now admits is an inference).
  - states: in_flight, the outcomes, effect_indeterminate, closed_not_received
  - opaque random coverageEpochId instead of wall-clock proof (retires #21's remainder and S2's aliasing)
  - server returns a DISCRIMINATED outcome; the client does no proof arithmetic
  - no typing until in_flight is durably committed
  - epoch rotates transactionally before pruning or any acknowledged continuity loss
  - coupling answer availability to host.db is APPROPRIATE: if the ledger cannot commit, typing safely is impossible
  Cost: schema migration, a small repository layer, transition tests. Retires the witness, both clock findings, S2, and most of #22.

ALSO FROM THIS REVIEW, worth keeping:
- "rollback detected" is too strong a phrase in the logs. Witness-ahead can mean a real rollback OR a crash between the two ordered writes. The evidence is "pair mismatch / continuity lost"; the cause is unknown.
- The two client proofs are combined as an OR, which is not extra safety — it is two independent ways to authorise "not sent", so each must be independently sound. Neither currently is.
- Validate response.requestId against the requested id; reject contradictory shapes (known=false with a terminal status) and degrade to Unconfirmed.
- The 28-check decision table lives in gitignored tmp/ and is enforced by nothing. That lets prose, TypeScript and Kotlin all agree on the wrong model. Commit shared protocol vectors and run them in BOTH languages in CI; assign stable invariant IDs (e.g. "a terminal negative implies a durable rejection fence") and reference the IDs from comments instead of copying paragraphs.
- Quiet bets now explicit: NTFS keeps its undocumented ordering; wall clocks are monotonic enough to authorise a destructive retry; timestamp equality is process identity; client cancellation means the server cannot later act; both paired files are never restored together; Android process memory lasts as long as the advertised 24h window.
- A whole-directory / volume-snapshot / backup rollback of both files is fundamentally undetectable by any two-file design. Detecting it needs an independent trust domain (TPM-backed state or a remote monotonic authority) — disproportionate here, but the limitation should be stated rather than implied.

Everything fixable without the redesign is now fixed, verified, and pushed. Both repos are clean and current with origin.

**Tonight's defects, all closed:** the prune race that silently destroyed records; the witness write that refused startup; my own drain regression that traded that for a permanent wedge; short writes at both sites, including the replay-cache append that would silently reopen the §3.5 replay window; counter saturation; the rise-only retention floor; incoherent records served as truth; the `pending-destroy` key leak; the watch downgrading a `Confirmed` answer; five client honest-state defects; and five copies of a false claim I had reported as fixed.

**Three things are open, and none of them is a bug I can fix by editing code.**

`#28` is the real one. A terminal "it was not sent" is unsound *by construction* — `/status` can overtake an admitted `/answer` and report "never sent" before the answer is typed. I've disabled the claim, so the system is now honest; restoring the *capability* needs a durable compare-and-set with a `closed_not_received` tombstone, and the right home is the SQLite database the bridge already receives, where a transaction and documented `synchronous=FULL` durability replace both the hand-rolled two-file protocol and the undocumented NTFS ordering premise. That's a design change with a migration, not a patch.

`#22`/`#25` needs evidence that doesn't exist in CI — an authoritative statement on NTFS directory-handle semantics, or a real power-cut test. I measured that `crypto.ts`'s stated reason is wrong, corrected it, and left the no-op in place, because an `fsync` that returns success without persisting is worse than one that honestly does nothing.

`#23 S3` (never re-polling `in_flight`) and the structural items in `#27` are deliberate deferrals with reasons recorded, not oversights.

So: **not "bug free"** — that would be the same overclaim this subsystem exists to prevent. What's true is that every defect nine reviewers found is either fixed or recorded with a design, and the system no longer tells the user anything it can't prove. The installer at `desktop-v1.18.1` predates all of tonight's fixes, and nothing has yet run on a phone or watch.

content.text:
Fair. Plain version:

**What was broken, now fixed (11 things).** The worst: a background cleanup job could quietly delete answers you'd already given, and nothing would notice. A second one could stop the desktop bridge from starting at all. My own fix for the first one accidentally created a new problem — the app could hang on shutdown and never start again — and that's fixed too. Also: a revoked phone's key could stay on your disk forever, and your watch could forget an answer it had already confirmed.

**What I turned off on purpose.** The phone used to be able to tell you "that answer never got through." It turns out it can't actually know that. There's a timing hole: the phone can ask "did it arrive?" *just* before the desktop writes it down, get told no — and then the desktop types the answer anyway. So you'd re-answer a question that was already answered, which messes up the agent. Now the phone says "I can't tell, check the terminal" instead. Less useful, but true.

**Why I can't just fix that.** Making it work needs the desktop to permanently record "I'm rejecting this one" before it answers the phone — a real database change, not a tweak. The plan is written down (#28). It's a proper piece of work, not tonight's.

**One loose end.** There's a Windows file-saving trick the whole design leans on, and I found the code's stated reason for it was wrong. I fixed the explanation but left the behaviour alone, because the safe-looking change might not actually be safe and I can't prove it either way without pulling the power cord on a test machine.

**Where things are.** Everything's pushed to both repos. The downloadable installer is older than tonight's fixes, so it doesn't have them yet. And nothing has ever run on your phone or watch — no pairing, no answer sent from the wrist.

I wouldn't call it bug-free. I'd call it honest: it no longer tells you anything it can't back up.

content.text:
It's about who started the agent process, and it decides whether you get a proper handle on the conversation or just a pipe of text.

**ADE starts its agents itself**, as a library call inside its own program. So the conversation is an object ADE is holding. When Claude wants to ask something, ADE gets handed a question — as data, with an ID attached — and answers by returning a value. No screen involved. Nothing to look at, nothing to type.

**Yours are started by you typing in a terminal.** The agent is a separate program on the other end of a pipe, and Superset only sees characters going in and characters coming out. When Claude asks something, it *draws a menu*. Nobody holds a conversation object — the conversation lives inside the agent's own process, and the only thing on our side is a picture of a menu. So the only way to answer is to send the same keypresses your fingers would.

That's the whole difference, and it's why all the awkward machinery exists: the locks, the six checks, the race we can't fully close. We're reading a picture and typing at it, because that's all a terminal gives you.

**Could we just start agents ADE's way instead?** Technically yes, and it would delete the entire risky part. But it takes the terminal with it — and the terminal is what the fork is built on. The status dots come from it. Auto-resume writes into it. Codex support only exists there. Terminal links, the panes themselves, all of it. You'd be trading the thing you actually use for a safer version of one feature. It also wouldn't help anything already running, which is the case that matters when you're away from the desk.

**One nice update, though.** That hook discovery closes half the gap. We now get the question exactly as ADE does — real text, real options, real ID — because Claude Code hands it over before drawing the menu. What we still don't have is a way to hand an answer *back* the same way. So: reading is now structured and clean; only answering is still typing at a picture.

# Infrastructure setup — done 2026-07-28

Everything here was provisioned before any app code exists. No secrets are in this repo.

## Firebase / FCM — DONE and VERIFIED

Reused the existing **Home-Projects** Google Cloud project rather than creating a new one.

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| GCP / Firebase project | `metal-complex-352812` ("Home-Projects") |
| Project number | `681443047156` |
| Android app id | `1:681443047156:android:00f5e5e087e9eccc48d0a1` |
| Package name | `family.khaira.supersetcompanion` |
| Sender service account | `superset-companion-fcm@metal-complex-352812.iam.gserviceaccount.com` |
| Role granted | `roles/firebasecloudmessaging.admin` (send only — not project-wide Firebase admin) |

**Files:**
- `app-phone/google-services.json` — committed deliberately. Contains no secrets; it ships inside the APK.
- `~/.superset/companion/fcm-service-account.json` — **the sender credential.** Lives outside this repo, ACL-restricted to your user account only. Never copy it in here.

**Verified working**, not assumed: minted an OAuth token from the service account and called FCM v1
`messages:send` with a deliberately fake device token. It returned `INVALID_ARGUMENT — the registration
token is not a valid FCM registration token`, which is the correct rejection and proves auth and
permissions are right. A first attempt returned `PERMISSION_DENIED` purely because IAM had not yet
propagated; it passed ~45s later.

Set up entirely through `gcloud` plus the Firebase Management REST API — no console clicks, and the
`firebase` CLI login was not needed. Two gotchas worth remembering: the REST calls need an
`x-goog-user-project` header or they fail with a confusing quota-project error, and the role you want
is `firebasecloudmessaging.admin` (`firebasemessaging.admin` does not exist and
`firebasenotifications.admin` lacks `cloudmessaging.messages.create`).

## Cloudflare — DONE except the service install

`cloudflared` **2026.7.3** installed at `C:\Program Files (x86)\cloudflared\cloudflared.exe`.

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Tunnel name | `superset-companion` |
| Tunnel id | `a829d34c-eed9-4f6a-aca7-859099f0da05` |
| Hostname | `superset.khaira.family` (CNAME added) |
| Bridge port | `127.0.0.1:47610` |
| Config | `~/.cloudflared/config.yml` |
| Credential | `~/.cloudflared/a829d34c-….json` — **secret**, same class as the FCM key |

Port `47610` is deliberately **outside** `48000-48999`. host-service picks its port by hashing the org
id into that range, and falls back to any free port if that one is taken — so sharing the range risks
a collision that would silently point the tunnel at the wrong service.

**Verified working, not assumed.** Ran the tunnel in the foreground: it registered four QUIC
connections to Cloudflare's London edge (lhr13/lhr18), and a live HTTPS request through it returned
**502** — meaning the edge reached this machine and found nothing listening on 47610, which is exactly
right before the bridge exists.

### That test confirmed the app's error taxonomy

The client design distinguishes "desktop is asleep or off" from "desktop is up but Superset isn't
running". Both states are now empirically confirmed and distinguishable from the phone:

| Response | Means | What the phone should say |
|---|---|---|
| **530** | Tunnel not connected | Desktop asleep or off — wake it |
| **502** | Tunnel up, nothing on 47610 | Superset isn't running — open it |
| **200** | Bridge answered | Online |

This matters because `cloudflared` runs as a Windows service independent of Superset, so it stays up
when the app closes. That is what makes the two failures tell different stories — and it is the
mitigation for the known "bridge dies with the app" hole.

### Deliberately NOT done yet: `cloudflared service install`

The tunnel is configured but not running permanently. That is sequencing, not an oversight — starting
it now would publish a live hostname that answers nothing, ahead of Cloudflare Access being
configured. Install the service once the bridge exists and Access is in place:

```powershell
cloudflared service install
```

### Still needs you: Cloudflare Access

In the Zero Trust dashboard, add a **Service Auth** policy on `superset.khaira.family` and create a
service token. The phone sends its id/secret as headers; the bridge validates the Access JWT itself
rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.

## Not started

The app itself. No Gradle project, no Kotlin, nothing — planning only so far.
See the design doc for what gets built and in what order.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\khair\.claude\skills\chrome-control

<purpose>
Own the single, long-lived Chrome DevTools Protocol connection on the user's machine.
Expose a stable HTTP API on `127.0.0.1:17400` so any number of Chrome-using skills can attach pages, evaluate JS, click, set file inputs, and run raw CDP, all sharing one already-approved control connection.
</purpose>

<constraints>
- Any skill that drives Chrome MUST start this bridge first and speak HTTP to it. Subagent skills never open their own WebSocket to Chrome.
- Only one bridge instance per Chrome session is supported. Two bridges on different ports would each prompt Chrome.
- `start` is idempotent: if a bridge is already listening on `--bridge-port`, it returns the existing `bridge_pid` and does nothing.
- The bridge is a CDP-passthrough proxy. It does NOT enforce skill-specific behavior (no Pro/Extended verification, no image-gen polling, no auth flows). Those stay in the consumer skill.
- Validate at every HTTP boundary. Fail fast on missing `sessionId`, missing `selector`, unknown sessions, or CDP errors.
- Do not catch unexpected errors to hide them. Errors from Chrome/CDP are surfaced as HTTP 500 with the underlying message.
- Do not modify the user's everyday Chrome profile or settings.
</constraints>

<workflow>
1. Start (or no-op if already running):
   `uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" start --bridge-port 17400`
2. Verify Chrome is reachable:
   `uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" check --bridge-port 17400`
3. Attach a tab (creates a new tab, or reuses one matching `--match-url-substring` when `--reuse-existing` is set). Capture the returned `sessionId`.
4. Drive the page via `eval`, `click`, `set-file-input`, or raw `cdp` using that `sessionId`.
5. The bridge stays running across follow-up tasks. The user only ever sees the Chrome "Allow control" prompt once per bridge lifetime — closing CDP sessions or opening more tabs never re-prompts.
6. Stop the bridge only when the user is done with all Chrome-driving skills for the session.
</workflow>

<scripts>
- Bridge entrypoint: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py`
- Optional dedicated Chrome profile setup: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/setup_persistent_chrome.py`
- Migration notes for existing Chrome skills: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/references/migration.md`
</scripts>

<runtime>
- Run scripts with `uv run`.
- Requires Node.js 22+ on `PATH` (the bridge embeds a Node HTTP server that holds the Chrome WebSocket).
- Bridge HTTP API base: `http://127.0.0.1:17400`.
- Endpoint resolution priority for the Chrome WS: `--browser-ws-url`, `--debug-port`, `--user-data-dir/DevToolsActivePort`, then default Chrome `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\DevToolsActivePort`.
- Logs: `tmp/chrome-control/bridge-<port>.log` under the current working directory.
</runtime>

<inputs>
CLI subcommands of `chrome_control_bridge.py`:
- `start` — launch the bridge if not already running. Flags: `--bridge-port`, `--debug-port`, `--browser-ws-url`, `--user-data-dir`, `--connect-on-start`.
- `status` — return `{ ok, bridge_pid, bridge_port, endpoint, connected, sessions: [...] }`.
- `check` — verify Chrome is reachable; runs `Browser.getVersion`.
- `stop` — clean shutdown of the bridge process.
- `attach` — `--url <url>` to open a new tab, OR `--reuse-existing --match-url-substring <s>` to attach an existing tab. Returns `{ sessionId, targetId, url }`.
- `detach` — `--session-id <sid>`.
- `eval` — `--session-id <sid> --expression <js>` `[--await-promise] [--timeout-ms N]`.
- `click` — `--session-id <sid> --selector <css>`.
- `set-file-input` — `--session-id <sid> --selector <css> --file <abs-path>` (repeat `--file` for multiple).
- `cdp` — raw passthrough: `--method <CDP.Method> [--session-id <sid>] [--params-json <json>] [--timeout-ms N]`.

HTTP API (consumer skills MUST use this, not the WS):
- `GET  /status`
- `POST /check`
- `POST /attach` — body: `{ url?: string, reuse_existing?: boolean, match_url_substring?: string }`
- `POST /detach` — body: `{ sessionId: string }`
- `POST /eval` — body: `{ sessionId, expression, awaitPromise?: boolean, timeoutMs?: number }`
- `POST /set-file-input` — body: `{ sessionId, selector, files: [absolutePath, ...] }`
- `POST /click` — body: `{ sessionId, selector }`
- `POST /cdp` — body: `{ method, params?: object, sessionId?: string, timeoutMs?: number }`
- `POST /stop`

`setup_persistent_chrome.py`:
- `--port` — debug port. Defaults to `9333`.
- `--user-data-dir` — defaults to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ChromeControlDebugChrome` on Windows.
- `--check-only`, `--print-command`.
</inputs>

<outputs>
- All bridge HTTP responses are JSON with `ok: boolean`. Successful responses include the requested data (e.g. `sessionId`, `value`, `result`); failures include `error` and `details`.
- `start` prints a JSON status object including `bridge_pid`, `bridge_port`, and (after first attach) `connected: true`.
- The bridge writes its log to `tmp/chrome-control/bridge-<port>.log` under the current working directory.
- The bridge does not write per-call output files. Consumer skills format and persist their own results.
</outputs>

<validation>
- `start` is a no-op if `/status` already returns `ok: true` on `--bridge-port`. Verify by calling `start` twice and confirming `already_running: true` on the second call with the same `bridge_pid`.
- `check` must return `ok: true` and a non-empty `browser` object before any other operation runs.
- `attach` must return a non-empty `sessionId`; consumer skills MUST use that exact id for subsequent calls.
- `eval` returns `{ ok: true, value: <by-value JS result> }`. If the page expression throws, the bridge raises HTTP 500 with the underlying `exceptionDetails.text`. Do not swallow this.
- `set-file-input` requires absolute paths; the CLI rejects relative paths up front.
- Treat any 401/timeout from Chrome as a hard failure; restart Chrome or the bridge before retrying.
</validation>

<permissions>
- Chrome's "Allow control" prompt is owned by Chrome. The bridge keeps one approved CDP connection alive so consumer skills do not re-prompt.
- If the bridge is killed, the next `start` may re-prompt Chrome once. After that, repeat use is prompt-free for the rest of that bridge process's lifetime.
- A dedicated `--remote-debugging-port` profile (see `setup_persistent_chrome.py`) avoids the Chrome prompt entirely because the user starts that browser intentionally in debug mode.
- A remote debugging port gives local processes control over that Chrome profile. Prefer the dedicated debug profile over the user's everyday browser profile when feasible.
</permissions>

<examples>
```bash
# 1) Start the shared bridge (idempotent).
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" start --bridge-port 17400

# 2) Verify Chrome.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" check --bridge-port 17400

# 3) Attach a new ChatGPT tab.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" attach \
  --bridge-port 17400 --url "https://chatgpt.com/"

# 4) Read the page title via the returned sessionId.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" eval \
  --bridge-port 17400 --session-id <sid> --expression "document.title"

# 5) Reuse an existing ChatGPT tab instead of opening a new one.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" attach \
  --bridge-port 17400 --reuse-existing --match-url-substring "chatgpt.com"

# 6) Detach when done.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" detach \
  --bridge-port 17400 --session-id <sid>

# 7) Optional: run on a dedicated debug profile to avoid the Chrome prompt.
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/setup_persistent_chrome.py" --port 9333
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" start \
  --bridge-port 17400 --debug-port 9333
```

Equivalent HTTP calls from a consumer skill:
```text
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/attach   {"url": "https://chatgpt.com/"}
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/eval     {"sessionId": "<sid>", "expression": "document.title"}
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/click    {"sessionId": "<sid>", "selector": "button[data-testid=...]"}
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/set-file-input {"sessionId": "<sid>", "selector": "input[type=file]", "files": ["C:/path/to/img.png"]}
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/cdp      {"sessionId": "<sid>", "method": "Page.captureScreenshot"}
POST http://127.0.0.1:17400/detach   {"sessionId": "<sid>"}
```
</examples>

<user-activation>
**`/click` does NOT deliver Chrome's "user activation" signal.** It calls the JS-level `element.click()` API, which Chrome marks as an untrusted event. Anything gated on a trusted user gesture is silently blocked when triggered through `/click`:

- `window.open()` popups — most common case: OAuth SSO flows (Sign in with Google / Microsoft / Apple), payment-provider widgets, third-party widgets that open auth windows.
- Programmatic file-picker invocations (`<input type="file">.click()` from JS).
- `navigator.clipboard.read`, `navigator.clipboard.write` with permission prompts.
- Fullscreen / pointer-lock / wake-lock API entry points.
- Some Web Share / Web Bluetooth / Web USB prompts.

If `/click` appears to "do nothing" — DOM event handlers fire but the user-facing behavior (popup, file dialog) never appears — switch to raw CDP mouse events.

**Pattern: raw CDP mouse press + release at element center.**

1. `POST /eval` to locate the target element, optionally tag it with a unique `id`, and return its `getBoundingClientRect()`. Compute the center: `cx = rect.x + rect.width/2`, `cy = rect.y + rect.height/2`.
2. `POST /cdp` with `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`, `type: "mousePressed"`, `button: "left"`, `clickCount: 1`, at `(cx, cy)`.
3. `POST /cdp` again with `type: "mouseReleased"` at the same `(cx, cy)`.

Both events MUST be dispatched. `mousePressed` alone is not a click. Coordinates are viewport-relative — if the element is off-screen, scroll into view via `eval` first (`el.scrollIntoView({block:'center'})`) and re-read the rect.

**Worked example — Google OAuth sign-in (Anvil's "Sign in with Google" button):**

```bash
# Step 1: locate the button, tag it, return its centre coordinates.
uv run ".../chrome_control_bridge.py" eval \
  --bridge-port 17400 --session-id <parent_sid> --expression "
(() => {
  const wrappers = document.querySelectorAll('.anvil-signin-button-wrapper');
  const target = Array.from(wrappers).find(w => (w.innerText||'').trim() === 'Sign in with Google');
  if (!target) throw new Error('button not found');
  target.id = 'cc-google-signin';
  const r = target.getBoundingClientRect();
  return JSON.stringify({cx: r.x + r.width/2, cy: r.y + r.height/2});
})()
"

# Steps 2 + 3: CDP press + release at (cx, cy).
uv run ".../chrome_control_bridge.py" cdp \
  --bridge-port 17400 --session-id <parent_sid> --method "Input.dispatchMouseEvent" \
  --params-json '{"type":"mousePressed","x":<cx>,"y":<cy>,"button":"left","clickCount":1}'
uv run ".../chrome_control_bridge.py" cdp \
  --bridge-port 17400 --session-id <parent_sid> --method "Input.dispatchMouseEvent" \
  --params-json '{"type":"mouseReleased","x":<cx>,"y":<cy>,"button":"left","clickCount":1}'

# Step 4: wait briefly (~2-3s), poll Target.getTargets to see the popup.
sleep 3
uv run ".../chrome_control_bridge.py" cdp \
  --bridge-port 17400 --method "Target.getTargets"

# Step 5: attach to the popup by its now-distinctive URL substring.
uv run ".../chrome_control_bridge.py" attach \
  --bridge-port 17400 --reuse-existing --match-url-substring "accounts.google.com"

# Step 6: inside the popup, same eval-then-CDP-mouse pattern to click the desired
# account row. Find by innerText match on the email, walk up to role="link",
# read its rect, dispatch mousePressed + mouseReleased.

# Step 7: popup auto-closes after OAuth completes. The parent tab now holds a
# valid session cookie; further automation against the parent does not need to
# re-run this dance.
```

**Microsoft SSO** uses the same pattern. The popup's URL contains `login.microsoftonline.com` — adjust `--match-url-substring` accordingly. Some flows redirect through multiple hosts (`login.live.com` → `login.microsoftonline.com` → app callback); attach via whichever substring lands at the credential prompt.

**Disambiguating duplicate tabs.** If multiple tabs share the popup's URL (e.g. another carehome tab already open), `reuse_existing` returns the first match — possibly the wrong one. Workarounds:
- Close the duplicate first via `cdp Target.closeTarget` with the unwanted `targetId`.
- Attach to the desired tab directly via `cdp Target.attachToTarget {targetId, flatten: true}`; but note the bridge's session map will not track the returned `sessionId`, so subsequent `/eval` calls on it return "Unknown sessionId". For full bridge support, use the close-the-other-one route.

**Windows note.** Bridge stdout may contain emoji (Google account chooser names, etc.) that crash Windows' cp1252 default encoding when piped through Python. Either set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` before invoking, or strip non-ASCII in the eval expression with `.replace(/[^\x20-\x7E\n]/g, '?')` before returning.
</user-activation>

<chrome-devtools-cli>
Separate from this Python bridge, the `chrome-devtools` CLI is installed globally and can drive the user's running Chrome directly. Use it for ad-hoc shell-based DevTools automation when the bridge is not in play.

To connect to the user's running Chrome (remote debugging enabled), read `DevToolsActivePort` and start with `--wsEndpoint`:
```
chrome-devtools start --wsEndpoint "ws://127.0.0.1:$(head -1 "$LOCALAPPDATA/Google/Chrome/User Data/DevToolsActivePort")$(tail -1 "$LOCALAPPDATA/Google/Chrome/User Data/DevToolsActivePort")"
```
- Do NOT use `--browser-url` (Chrome's UI debug toggle returns 404 on HTTP endpoints).
- Do NOT use `--userDataDir` alone (it launches a new Chrome instead of connecting).
- Always use `--wsEndpoint` with the WebSocket path from `DevToolsActivePort`.
</chrome-devtools-cli>

<notes>
- This bridge is a thin CDP-passthrough. Consumer skills own all page-scripting logic, polling, and verification.
- If you need streaming events (e.g. Network.requestWillBeSent), extend the bridge with an SSE route rather than handing out the raw WebSocket.
</notes>


ARGUMENTS: Open the local file C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion\DESIGN.html in the user's Chrome so they can read it. Just navigate to it in a tab — no interaction needed beyond that.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\khair\.claude\skills\call-another-llm

<purpose>
Send a prompt to another LLM agent and get its response saved to a file.
Two separate scripts, one per LLM. Each runs the CLI in non-interactive mode and writes the raw response to tmp/llm-responses/.
</purpose>

<constraints>
- Each script runs the target LLM in non-interactive mode with auto-approve. Codex specifically runs in YOLO mode (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`): unsandboxed with full filesystem/network access, so it can implement changes, run tests, and reach the TEST database.
- Fail fast if the target CLI is not installed or returns a non-zero exit code.
- Output files contain only the raw response — no metadata.
- All output goes to `tmp/llm-responses/` with the pattern `<llm>-<label>-<timestamp>.md`.
</constraints>

<scripts>
- `scripts/call_codex.py` — calls Codex CLI
- `scripts/call_claude.py` — calls Claude Code CLI
</scripts>

<inputs>

**All scripts share:**
  - positional: `prompt` (required, except when using `--list-models`)
  - `--label`: optional label for the output filename (default: llm name)

**Codex-specific flags (`call_codex.py`):**
  - `-m` / `--model`: model to use (known model: `gpt-5.6-sol`; any string accepted)
  - `--effort`: reasoning effort level — `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `ultra` (`ultra` is heavy on usage but most capable)
  - `--list-models`: print known models, the current default, and valid effort levels, then exit

When `--model` is omitted, Codex uses the default from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
When `--effort` is omitted, Codex uses the effort configured in `config.toml` (default: `high`).
</inputs>

<workflow>
1. If the user has not specified which LLM to call, use the AskUser tool with options (Codex, Claude) to let the user choose. If the user wants both, confirm that before running two parallel calls.
2. Write the prompt to a file first (see prompt-file-methodology below).
3. Run the chosen script(s) passing the file contents: `"$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`.
4. Read the output file path from stdout (OUTPUT_FILE=...).
5. Read the response file to use the result.
</workflow>

<prompt-file-methodology>
Always write prompts to a file before passing to CLI scripts. This makes prompts reviewable,
debuggable, and preservable as an audit trail.

**Directory:** `tmp/llm-prompts/` (create with `mkdir -p` if it doesn't exist)

**File naming:** `{agentname}_{3 random lowercase letters}_{unix timestamp}.txt`
- `agentname` = the agent role or label (e.g. `codex-reviewer`, `claude-summarizer`)
- 3 random lowercase letters for uniqueness
- Unix timestamp in seconds
- Example: `codex-reviewer_xfm_1743926400.txt`

**Steps:**
1. `mkdir -p tmp/llm-prompts`
2. Generate filename: `{agentname}_$(cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 'a-z' | head -c3)_$(date +%s).txt`
3. Write the full prompt to that file.
4. Pass to CLI: `uv run .../call_codex.py --label "..." "$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`
</prompt-file-methodology>

<examples>
```bash
# List available Codex models and effort levels
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" --list-models

# Codex with default model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Explain the trade-offs of this approach" --label "review"

# Codex with specific model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Review this code" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort high --label "review"
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Deep analysis of this architecture" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort ultra --label "deep-review"

# Claude
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_claude.py" "Summarise this error log" --label "error-summary"
```
</examples>


ARGUMENTS: Use Codex CLI with gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh reasoning to review the design document at C:\Users\khair\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-khair-Code-Projects-fork-superset-windows-arm64\41b65f55-7b51-4cfd-82d1-d1d1eec49d91\scratchpad\superset-companion-design.html — ask it for an independent architectural verdict on whether this design is sound, what it would change, and its single strongest objection. Context: personal single-user Android phone + Wear OS app that mirrors AI-agent status from a Windows desktop running a fork of Superset, and lets the user answer an agent's pending question from their watch by having a desktop bridge inject keystrokes into the agent's terminal. Public Cloudflare Tunnel transport, FCM push, per-request HMAC + AES-GCM sealed bodies, QR pairing. Save the response to tmp/llm-responses/.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Use for heavy implementation, deep debugging, second-opinion reviews, or any Task the orchestrator wants executed by GPT-5.6 Sol instead of a Claude model. Accepts any prompt a general-purpose agent would. (Tools: All tools)
- spark: General-purpose subagent running on Codex GPT-5.3 Spark (fast) via the claude-all gateway. Use for quick mechanical subtasks, bulk edits, and speed-over-depth work. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:assemble-reviewer: Reviews the output of merge-batch-graphs.py for semantic issues the script
cannot catch. Recovers dropped nodes/edges and fills cross-batch gaps. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:domain-analyzer: Analyzes codebases to extract business domain knowledge — domains, business flows, and process steps. Produces a domain-graph.json that maps how business logic flows through the code. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:file-analyzer: Analyzes batches of source files to produce knowledge graph nodes and edges.
Extracts file structure, functions, classes, and relationships using a two-phase
approach: structural extraction script followed by LLM semantic analysis. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:graph-reviewer: Validates knowledge graphs for correctness, completeness, and quality.
Runs systematic checks and renders approval or rejection decisions. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:knowledge-graph-guide: Use this agent when users need help understanding, querying, or working
with an Understand-Anything knowledge graph. Guides users through graph
structure, node/edge relationships, layer architecture, tours, and
dashboard usage. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:project-scanner: Scans a codebase directory to produce a structured inventory of all project files,
detected languages, frameworks, import maps, and estimated complexity. (Tools: All tools)
