F1 (severe) BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406 — read-back FetchResult.Failure maps to terminal AnswerOutcome.Failed, violating §11.6. Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.

content.subject: Fix witness-write throw (B1) and unwitnessed-advance belief (C2)
content.description:
B1 FIXED and verified (563c41b56): raiseWitness wrapped, degrades on any write fault, proven through the write path specifically by tmp/verify-b1-fix.ts (a directory at the witness path fails on READ first and proves nothing; the probe puts a directory at the .tmp name instead so reads succeed and writes fail). Continuing after the degrade is safe because degradeCoverage advances coverageSinceMs before `file` is built.

C2 STILL OPEN. After a generation-less mount whose witness unlink fails, the file advances unwitnessed while a stale witness stays behind it; a later good mount reads "witness behind file" as the harmless direction and believes the stamp. Reproduced twice independently (opus-rev-server's tmp/review-witness-holes.ts case C2, and Sol with a real Windows deny-delete lock).

Why it is still open rather than fixed: it requires a generation-null mount, and the only production caller (index.ts) passes anchor.generation, which openStateAnchor guarantees is canonical or throws. The D5 fix (generation is now `string | null`, required) makes an accidental omission a compile error, which removes the realistic route in. Residual needs a wiring regression PLUS an unlink failure PLUS a hard reset.

Hardening option if it is ever wanted, from fable-rev-durability: have a generation-null mount freeze the file's seq at 0, or write a tombstone-generation witness, so the next good mount sees witness-ahead or a generation mismatch and degrades instead of trusting. A write survives a Windows sharing violation more often than a delete does, which is the argument for the tombstone over the unlink.

content.subject: Fix doc rot (D1-D4), generation optionality (D5), prune/clock invariant (D6)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE in 563c41b56. Remaining work is D6 only.

FIXED and verified:
- D1 all five copies of the false "witness keeps a landed answer reading confirmed across a restart" claim in answer.ts (1335, 1386, 1600, the createAttemptStore generation doc, and the handleAnswerStatus header), plus the tmp/attempt-witness-proof.ts case-1 heading that repeated it. Multiline grep confirms none remain in source.
- D1b answer.ts:2889-2893 no longer states known:false unconditionally — it now names the coverage range up front instead of contradicting the paragraph below it.
- D1c the handleAnswerStatus degrade list now includes the unwritable and no-rewrite-mark cases.
- D3 crypto.ts's write-ordering warning named only keys.ts as its dependent; it now names both mechanisms AND records that the ordering is an inference from NTFS behaviour rather than a documented platform guarantee.
- D5 `generation?: string` is now `generation: string | null` — required, explicitly nullable. Runtime leniency unchanged (a missing generation still degrades, never throws); the strict type is what stops a silent omission. The degrade-reason branch handles undefined as well as null, so an untyped harness caller reads the same message.

STILL OPEN:
- D6 wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, the clock steps back, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) covers it again while get() returns null. Reproduced by tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4) and independently by Sol with the real store and handler.
- D2 the four-place duplication of the coverage semantics is unaddressed; /simplify is assessing whether the fix is editorial (types.ts canonical, pointers elsewhere) or structural (drift made detectable).
- D4 keys.ts still has no back-reference to ATTEMPT-WITNESS; the link remains one-way.
- D7 the client still decodes AnswerStatusResponse.bridgeStartedMs without reading it; /simplify is judging consume-vs-annotate.

D6 shares its root with #21/S1 — Date.now() treated as monotonic — and all of them should be fixed together with a monotonic anchor, not patched separately.
content.activeForm: Fixing doc rot and taxonomy findings

content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
FIXED, server half (PRUNE-FLOOR), pending commit. Probes: tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4, assertions inverted from demonstrating the bug to pinning the fix) and tmp/verify-prune-floor.ts (5/5, new).

What was wrong: recordsSinceMs returned max(coverageSinceMs, now - retentionMs). The second term is recomputed from the WALL CLOCK on every read, while pruning is irreversible. Drop a record at 25h, let the clock step back 2h, and the term moves BACK behind the record just deleted — so the window claimed coverage over a record get() can no longer return. The hydration retention filter had the identical shape via a forward-skewed mount clock.

Fix: a rise-only `prunedThroughMs` — the highest retention boundary the store has ever crossed — persisted in the attempts file and raised in three places: on prune (whether or not anything was dropped, since the boundary was still crossed), on a hydration drop, and by taking the max with the file's own value at load. recordsSinceMs is now floored by it as well, so once records older than X are gone the window never reaches behind X again, whatever the clock does. The field is optional-defaulting-to-0 so a file written before it loads unchanged and the first prune establishes a floor.

STILL OPEN — the other half, and it needs a design decision rather than a patch:
H3/S1 second half. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine, so a FORWARD desktop clock step inflates the claimed window and the client's monotonic submitAge comparison can then yield a false "not sent". Exposure is confined to the degraded (coverage = mount) cases, since a witness-verified window is retention-floored.

Why it is not patched: the inference it corrupts — a terminal "not sent" from an absent record — is being DISABLED anyway, because sol-architect found it unsound for a deeper reason (the overtaking race: /status can pass an admitted /answer that has not yet written in_flight, so absence cannot prove the answer will not be typed). Patching the arithmetic under a disabled inference is wasted work.

The sound fix, per sol-architect, is to stop doing temporal proofs at all: an opaque random coverageEpochId that the client captures before submitting and echoes back, rotated by the server before any coverage gap, reset, unverified restart or prune. The server then owns the proof and the client does no clock arithmetic. That also retires S2 (bridgeStartedMs is a Date.now() value treated as an identity, so two lifetimes can alias). Do it together with the durable CAS, not before.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE. Two of four fixed and pushed.

S1 clock — FIXED, server half (b272da2dd, PRUNE-FLOOR). A rise-only persisted retention floor means a backward clock step can no longer re-expose pruned records. The forward-step half is deliberately unfixed; see #21 for why (it only corrupts the inference now disabled by c03d7bb, and the sound answer is an opaque coverage epoch, not better arithmetic).

S4 boundary validation — FIXED (0d9944056). Two cross-field refinements refuse `confirmed` with a null resolvedAtMs and `failed` with a null failureCode at the disk boundary. Nothing this bridge writes produces either, so on disk they mean corruption or a hand-edit; the file is now quarantined once and loudly instead of the shape being served as truth for 24 hours. Proof tmp/verify-crossfield.ts also pins that all four real shapes still load — a rule that quarantined genuine records would be a self-inflicted outage.

STILL OPEN:

S2 bridgeStartedMs is Date.now() but the client treats equality as lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88), so two lifetimes can alias and the fallback proof is unsafe. Do NOT patch by widening the timestamp — it is the wrong primitive. It is retired wholesale by #28's opaque coverageEpochId, which replaces both temporal proofs with a server-owned identity. Fix it there.

S3 in_flight is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository maps it to Pending correctly, but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the read lands during the ~15s injection window, the server later records confirmed, and the phone sits on Pending until the user intervenes while the watch shows Unconfirmed.
Not fixed tonight deliberately: this is a behavioural addition (a bounded poll loop with backoff, cancellation on resolve, and a decision about what the watch shows meanwhile), not a correction, and it interacts with #28 — if the status response becomes a discriminated union with a server-owned epoch, the polling contract should be designed against THAT rather than retrofitted twice. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec, but the two must agree.

S5 PROTOCOL §11.5 declares the proof fields required and non-null while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null. Missing NEEDS that exception for old-bridge compatibility, but the spec does not say so, and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Editorial + a decision about which rule wins; fold into #28's protocol work.

S6/S7 done: the fifth doc site was cleared in 83a02d0a8, and the retention constant now lives in CompanionConstants so client and server no longer duplicate it in unrelated files.

content.subject: CRITICAL: detached prune from a stopped store clobbers the new store and lowers the counter
content.description:
From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Serialization and the witness read/write guard are per-INSTANCE only (answer.ts:1892-1967), so the old instance's persist() has no idea a new instance exists.

SEQUENCE (Sol's probe output): old store at F/W=2 begins prune and reads W=2 -> stop/start creates a new store which reaches F/W=3, then records an answer at F/W=4 -> the old prune resumes and writes its stale empty snapshot as W=3, F=3. Measured: before releasing the old prune F=4/W=4 records [old,new]; after F=3/W=3 records []; on reopen no degradation, the new record absent, old coverage retained. The next restart therefore TRUSTS a matching pair while a recorded answer has been destroyed -> false "it was not sent".

THIS BREAKS THE RISE-ONLY CLAIM. I verified rise-only within one instance and reported it as holding; it does not hold across instances. Math.max and the promise tail cannot see another instance's writes.

BROADER CLASS: the same detached-interval pattern covers nonceCache.compact, audit.prune and deviceStore.purgeExpiredRevocations in the same block. Check whether any of those can also clobber a successor's state. The nonce cache is the one to look at hardest, since its rollback consequence is the fatal one.

FIX DIRECTIONS: (a) make teardown await in-flight maintenance, not just clear timers — track the in-flight promise and await it in the unwind entry; (b) give each store instance an ownership token and have persist() refuse if it is no longer the owner (the anchor already has this shape for the send-nonce lifecycle); (c) both. (b) defends even against a leaked reference that outlives teardown.

Also from the same report, comment errors this invalidates: index.ts:699-704 and 723-724 claim teardown prevents old writers overlapping a new bridge — detached maintenance makes that false. And answer.ts:1457 / 1877-1882 claim witness-ahead PROVES an attempts-file version was durably written and then lost; a failure between the witness raise and the primary write produces the identical state with no such version ever existing.

content.subject: Lead: an r+ directory handle may be fsync-able on Windows, which would retire the ordering assumption
content.description:
Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

Related: #22 (the assumption this could retire), #24 (unaffected by this — the lifecycle race is not a durability problem).

content.subject: Short writes (R1), counter saturation (R2), fifth doc site (R3), comment errors (R4)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE in 563c41b56.

FIXED:
- R1 writeFileDurable now checks the bytesWritten Node returns and throws before the rename, so a short write can no longer be fsync'd and renamed as though complete (which previously lost every record in the file at the next start, via quarantine).
- R3 the doc-rot list was five sites, not four — all five cleared, plus the harness heading.
- R4 partial: crypto.ts's syncDirectory reason (measurably wrong — a directory opens fine under Bun on win32 arm64 and r+ fsync succeeds; only the read-only mode gives EPERM) is corrected with the measured results and the reason the no-op nonetheless stays. index.ts's teardown-ordering claim is corrected and now true by construction thanks to MAINTENANCE-DRAIN.

STILL OPEN:
- R2 both schemas accept Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for the rewrite counter while persist() increments it: load ...991 -> write ...992 -> the next increment yields the SAME value -> the following start rejects and quarantines it. Unreachable by human usage, reachable from a schema-valid nonsense file. Bound the schema below MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or treat saturation as a degrade rather than letting it self-corrupt.
- R4 remainder: answer.ts:1609-1611 says the store never refuses startup — now TRUE after the B1 fix, so re-read it and confirm rather than assume. answer.ts:1726-1728 still claims a failed quarantine rename proves the later durable write would also fail, which an obstruction only at the quarantine destination disproves. The "rise-only" wording still needs scoping: it holds within one store instance and below the numeric boundary, but #24 showed it did not hold across lifecycle overlap (now fixed by the drain) and R2 shows it does not hold at saturation.
- R5 the B1 fix does cover the full error class Sol named (ENOSPC, EACCES, sync/close, failed replacement) because it catches everything raiseWitness can throw rather than matching on codes — worth keeping that way rather than narrowing to specific errno values.

content.subject: Altitude findings: pending-destroy key leak (A1), watch Confirmed downgrade (A2), witness factoring (A3)
content.description:
A1 pending-destroy key leak — FIXED and pushed (c1d6dcca5, ORPHAN-SWEEP). Re-derives the wipe obligation from ground truth (key files whose keyRef appears in no index record) instead of adding a third witness, so a lost journal rename costs one start's delay rather than a permanent leak. KeyStore.list() reads names only, never parses, so an orphan is destroyable even when corrupt or bound to a previous install. The sweep runs at CONSTRUCTION only, argued structurally: keys.put() creates the key file before create() records it and put is outside the store's serialiser, so on the purge path a brand-new device's key is legitimately unreferenced and a sweep would brick a phone mid-pairing. `referenced` spans revoked-but-unpurged records too, because §5.1 keeps a revoked device's key on purpose. Proof tmp/a1-orphan-sweep.ts reproduces the leak end to end and shows the referenced key surviving. Written by a subagent that died on an API timeout; I reviewed the diff, both call sites and the set arithmetic before committing.

A2 watch Confirmed downgrade — FIXED and pushed (c03d7bb). rank/supersedes now live on WatchAnswerStatus in core/, which both surfaces already shared for the wire, so there is ONE definition of which status may replace which instead of a phone lattice plus an open-coded watch approximation. QuestionStore refuses a non-superseding incoming. 10 new tests including the UNKNOWN-after-phone-restart relay specifically. AnswerOutcome deliberately stayed in app-phone.

STILL OPEN, all structural rather than defects:

A3 witness factoring. keys.ts and answer.ts hold the same machine (rise-only integer beside a durable file, raised before it, generation-bound, max-at-start, gap->verdict) differing only in mark type and verdict severity. The ordering invariant is prose in three places and enforced by nothing. Do it when a THIRD dependent is proposed, not before — and factor ONLY the ordering and mark read/write/compare, leaving each caller's verdict local. sol-architect's shape is better than a boolean flag: return typed evidence (verified / uninitialized / untrusted+reason) and let the consumer map it to policy, so the fatal-vs-degrade distinction cannot be inverted by an argument. Note that #28 may retire this entirely by moving the ledger to SQLite.

A4 extraction of attempt-store.ts. Better motivated than first thought: the 866-line block takes EXACTLY ONE identifier from the rest of answer.ts (GUARD_CLASSES, used once as a zod enum key source), so the module boundary already exists and the file layout hides it. Cost, all in ONE commit: move GUARD_CLASSES + GuardClass to types.ts or attempt-store.ts -> answer.ts closes an import cycle, then update the FEATURES.md (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) marker path or the gate fails. Deferred tonight so a rename would not bury the behavioural diff.

A5 doc duplication is SEVEN production sites, not four. Canonical home should be PROTOCOL.md §11.5. The marker gate cannot help (grep -rqsF is a presence check; content equality would fail the build on every wording improvement). The one real structural lever: the semantics already have executable copies in AnswerStatusCoverageTest.kt and provesNeverSent — name §11.5 in the test names and treat that file as the second normative copy. Partially addressed in 83a02d0a8 (types.ts made canonical for TS, answer.ts and index.ts reduced to pointers); the Kotlin and FEATURES.md sites remain.

A6 the evidence bar in crypto.ts for retiring the syncDirectory no-op will never be cleared in CI, so record that both witnesses are PERMANENT rather than provisional. If evidence ever arrives, KEEP them as defence-in-depth — their detection surface is strictly larger (single-file AV quarantine-restore, per-file version restore, a copied companion tree, generation-bound anchor replacement; a directory fsync sees none of those) but DROP the raise-before-write coupling, which is the fragile half and the only half a working fsync retires.

content.subject: Overtaking race: absence cannot prove not-sent without a durable CAS fence
content.description:
From sol-architect (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, ~3.5h). The deepest finding of the session: none of the other eight reviewers found it, and it invalidates the actionable-negative feature independently of the witness.

THE RACE (verified by me): handleAnswer reads the attempt record at answer.ts:2309 and does not durably record in_flight until answer.ts:2504 — 195 lines and several awaits later, spanning guard evaluation and lock acquisition. So:
  1. /v1/answer is admitted, pauses before writing in_flight
  2. /v1/answer/status overtakes it, finds no record, the coverage proof holds
  3. the phone reports the terminal "it was not sent"
  4. the original /answer resumes, writes in_flight, and TYPES THE ANSWER
The user then answers a picker that was already answered, which §11.4 records as unrecoverable. HTTP cancellation does not help: the server snapshots its freshness time before several awaits (http.ts:1119).

WHY THE WITNESS CANNOT FIX THIS: the witness proves things about the PAST. This is a claim about the FUTURE — that an already-admitted request will not act. No amount of durable-state attestation closes it.

IMMEDIATE MITIGATION (in progress, fix-client-two): proven absence resolves to Unconfirmed instead of a terminal Failed. Positive stored statuses are unaffected. This is a deliberate capability regression, not a bug, and the code says so.

THE REAL FIX — durable per-request compare-and-set with a tombstone:
  existing state | /answer            | authoritative /status
  absent         | CAS to in_flight   | CAS to closed_not_received
  in_flight/done | idempotent replay  | return known status
  closed_...     | REFUSE to type     | return not_received
Whichever wins persists BEFORE either typing or returning a terminal negative. If the status-side CAS cannot be persisted, the result stays unconfirmed. A non-atomic check-then-insert is insufficient.

SOL'S PREFERRED TARGET, and I agree it is the right end state: move the attempt ledger into the host SQLite database the bridge already receives, rather than the hand-rolled two-file protocol.
  - SQLite gives the transaction the CAS needs, and `synchronous=FULL` gives DOCUMENTED per-commit durability instead of an undocumented cross-file rename-ordering inference (which is #22, and which crypto.ts now admits is an inference).
  - states: in_flight, the outcomes, effect_indeterminate, closed_not_received
  - opaque random coverageEpochId instead of wall-clock proof (retires #21's remainder and S2's aliasing)
  - server returns a DISCRIMINATED outcome; the client does no proof arithmetic
  - no typing until in_flight is durably committed
  - epoch rotates transactionally before pruning or any acknowledged continuity loss
  - coupling answer availability to host.db is APPROPRIATE: if the ledger cannot commit, typing safely is impossible
  Cost: schema migration, a small repository layer, transition tests. Retires the witness, both clock findings, S2, and most of #22.

ALSO FROM THIS REVIEW, worth keeping:
- "rollback detected" is too strong a phrase in the logs. Witness-ahead can mean a real rollback OR a crash between the two ordered writes. The evidence is "pair mismatch / continuity lost"; the cause is unknown.
- The two client proofs are combined as an OR, which is not extra safety — it is two independent ways to authorise "not sent", so each must be independently sound. Neither currently is.
- Validate response.requestId against the requested id; reject contradictory shapes (known=false with a terminal status) and degrade to Unconfirmed.
- The 28-check decision table lives in gitignored tmp/ and is enforced by nothing. That lets prose, TypeScript and Kotlin all agree on the wrong model. Commit shared protocol vectors and run them in BOTH languages in CI; assign stable invariant IDs (e.g. "a terminal negative implies a durable rejection fence") and reference the IDs from comments instead of copying paragraphs.
- Quiet bets now explicit: NTFS keeps its undocumented ordering; wall clocks are monotonic enough to authorise a destructive retry; timestamp equality is process identity; client cancellation means the server cannot later act; both paired files are never restored together; Android process memory lasts as long as the advertised 24h window.
- A whole-directory / volume-snapshot / backup rollback of both files is fundamentally undetectable by any two-file design. Detecting it needs an independent trust domain (TPM-backed state or a remote monotonic authority) — disproportionate here, but the limitation should be stated rather than implied.

content.subject: SQLite answer ledger with transactional CAS and coverage epoch
content.description:
DONE — schema, migration, ledger module, and proof. Not yet wired into the bridge (that is the next step) and not committed.

Schema (src/db/schema.ts, migration 0012 generated via `bun run generate`, never hand-written): `answer_attempts` keyed by requestId with the five statuses plus the new `closed_not_received` TOMBSTONE, and a dedicated single-row `answer_coverage_epoch`. Written by the first agent before it died mid-stream; I reviewed and kept it. Its reasoning was good — `createdAtMs` separate from `startedAtMs` so retention has one unambiguous clock across both row shapes, a dedicated epoch table rather than host_settings (that table is nullable user knobs any settings path can write; this is a notNull safety token the ledger must own), and `effect_indeterminate` deliberately NOT added because it is not distinct from `unconfirmed` here.

Module (src/companion/attempt-ledger.ts, written by me after the agent died): claimForAnswer / resolveStatus / recordOutcome / get / prune / rotateEpoch / currentEpoch. The CAS is `INSERT .. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` inside one transaction, so exactly one caller sees changes===1 — a decision procedure rather than a race. A SELECT-then-INSERT there would be the very bug being replaced.

Key implementation facts worth keeping:
- drizzle's better-sqlite3 transactions are SYNCHRONOUS callbacks, so the whole CAS is sync. Async wrappers would have broken atomicity.
- `tx as HostDb` does not typecheck and should not: a transaction has no $client. Helpers take a structural `Queryable = Pick<HostDb, "select"|"insert"|"update"|"delete">` that both satisfy.
- PRAGMA synchronous is ASSERTED to be FULL and fails loud. createDb does not set it, and in WAL mode NORMAL means a commit survives a process crash but NOT power loss — losing a committed in_flight claim is exactly the rollback the fence prevents. It fails rather than silently setting it because the connection is shared with the rest of the host service.
- recordOutcome updates WHERE status = 'in_flight'. That predicate is a safety property: without it an outcome could overwrite a tombstone and erase the fence, or revive a row a concurrent prune dropped. An orphaned outcome logs loudly and never throws (keystrokes may already have landed).
- Rows are validated individually at the read boundary, so one corrupt row costs ONE requestId its status — the JSON file quarantined all 24h of everyone's records for one bad one.

Proof tmp/verify-answer-ledger.ts, 20/20 against a real database:
- the overtaking race in BOTH orders (status-first plants the fence and the admitted answer is then refused permanently; answer-first claims and status reports in_flight)
- 32 concurrent claims -> exactly 1 winner, 31 idempotent replays
- a tombstone is never written over a real row
- a stale or absent coverage epoch degrades and plants NO fence
- pruning rotates in the same transaction, so a pruned request is never reported never-received
- an outcome cannot erase a tombstone, and the orphan is reported
- an incoherent row is refused and its neighbour is unaffected

UNLOCK that made this testable: better-sqlite3 has no win-arm64 binding here and the old tmp stub answered every query with nothing, so no database path had ever run locally. It is now a real shim over bun:sqlite (tmp/better-sqlite3-shim.js, in both gitignored node_modules). Real migrations, WAL, synchronous=FULL, real `changes` counts. The shim THROWS on anything unimplemented rather than returning a wrong answer.

content.subject: Pre-existing: pairing probe fails to open the step-4 sealed response
content.description:
RESOLVED — the bridge was right, the probe was four revisions stale. tmp/companion-pairing-check.ts now reports ALL PASS.

This mattered because that probe is the only genuine INTEROP test of the pairing key schedule: it implements the phone side from PROTOCOL.md §3.1/§4.4 rather than reusing the bridge's own helpers. It had been failing, and a red harness gets ignored — so "does pairing actually work" was unanswered while nothing had ever paired on hardware.

Four retired contracts it was asserting, each one the probe lagging a hardening:

1. K_dev derived as hkdfExpandLabel(prk, LABEL + pid + deviceId) — the ids as base64url TEXT. crypto.ts's INTEROP NOTE records that §3.1 was ambiguous, that the two sides once declared OPPOSITE conventions so pairing could never succeed, and that it was resolved in favour of RAW BYTES to match the Android client's KeyDerivation. Fixed with hkdfExpandInfo + hkdfInfoWithSuffix over decoded id bytes. This was the cause of the unknown_device failure.
2. The step-4 AAD in RESPONSE form (inventing a twelve-zero-byte nonce and a literal 200). §4.4 step 4 enumerates the REQUEST form — there is no client request nonce on that hop (the LAN messages are cleartext JSON, not envelopes) and no status code the client can bind before reading the body. pairing.ts records that an earlier revision did exactly what the probe was still doing, the AADs differed by 16 bytes, and every pairing failed the GCM tag as pair_bad_mac — indistinguishable from a real MITM.
3. createDeviceStore(dir) — it now requires the state anchor and key store, and (ONE-STORE-PER-ANCHOR) forbids two stores owning one anchor, so a simulated restart must close the previous anchor first.
4. Opaque keyRef strings ("k1", "k2"). keyRef must now be a canonical 22-char base64url id, because a keyRef named after anything guessable let a replayed deviceId overwrite a live device's K_dev before create() could refuse.

Evidence obtained, which is the point: K_dev derives IDENTICALLY on both sides, the step-4 sealed response opens, macDesktop verifies, and every negative path holds — bad MAC burns the window after three, wrong pid gives pair_wrong_peer, v=2 gives pair_version_unsupported, attempts are rate limited, and nothing is stored on any failure.

Diagnostic technique worth keeping: the failure was isolated by moving the "phone-derived K_dev equals the key the bridge stored" assertion BEFORE the first openSealed. That separates a key-schedule disagreement from an AAD or envelope disagreement, which unknown_device deliberately cannot distinguish (§3.6 makes it indistinguishable from "device not known"). It also proved the change was not a regression: reverting keys.ts and crypto.ts to HEAD via a path-limited git stash reproduced the identical failure.

content.subject: Fix five client honest-state findings (F1-F5)
content.description:
From opus-rev-client on f25e438, all verified independently, all PRE-EXISTING rather than regressions. Apply only after every reviewer has reported, to avoid editing files they are reading.

F1 (severe) BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406 — read-back FetchResult.Failure maps to terminal AnswerOutcome.Failed, violating §11.6. Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.

content.subject: Fix witness-write throw (B1) and unwitnessed-advance belief (C2)
content.description:
B1 FIXED and verified (563c41b56): raiseWitness wrapped, degrades on any write fault, proven through the write path specifically by tmp/verify-b1-fix.ts (a directory at the witness path fails on READ first and proves nothing; the probe puts a directory at the .tmp name instead so reads succeed and writes fail). Continuing after the degrade is safe because degradeCoverage advances coverageSinceMs before `file` is built.

C2 STILL OPEN. After a generation-less mount whose witness unlink fails, the file advances unwitnessed while a stale witness stays behind it; a later good mount reads "witness behind file" as the harmless direction and believes the stamp. Reproduced twice independently (opus-rev-server's tmp/review-witness-holes.ts case C2, and Sol with a real Windows deny-delete lock).

Why it is still open rather than fixed: it requires a generation-null mount, and the only production caller (index.ts) passes anchor.generation, which openStateAnchor guarantees is canonical or throws. The D5 fix (generation is now `string | null`, required) makes an accidental omission a compile error, which removes the realistic route in. Residual needs a wiring regression PLUS an unlink failure PLUS a hard reset.

Hardening option if it is ever wanted, from fable-rev-durability: have a generation-null mount freeze the file's seq at 0, or write a tombstone-generation witness, so the next good mount sees witness-ahead or a generation mismatch and degrades instead of trusting. A write survives a Windows sharing violation more often than a delete does, which is the argument for the tombstone over the unlink.

The degrade-reason branch handles undefined as well as null, so an untyped harness caller reads the same message.

- D6 wall-clock regression re-opens the published window over PRUNED records, so recordsSinceMs's stated invariant is false: prune at t0+25h drops a record, the clock steps back, recordsSinceMs = max(t0, now-24h) covers it again while get() returns null. Reproduced by tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4) and independently by Sol with the real store and handler.
- D2 the four-place duplication of the coverage semantics is unaddressed; /simplify is assessing whether the fix is editorial (types.ts canonical, pointers elsewhere) or structural (drift made detectable).
- D4 keys.ts still has no back-reference to ATTEMPT-WITNESS; the link remains one-way.
- D7 the client still decodes AnswerStatusResponse.bridgeStartedMs without reading it; /simplify is judging consume-vs-annotate.

D6 shares its root with #21/S1 — Date.now() treated as monotonic — and all of them should be fixed together with a monotonic anchor, not patched separately.
content.activeForm: Fixing doc rot and taxonomy findings

content.subject: Clamp the coverage window against a forward desktop clock step (H3)
content.description:
FIXED, server half (PRUNE-FLOOR), pending commit. Probes: tmp/attempt-prune-clock-probe.ts (4/4, assertions inverted from demonstrating the bug to pinning the fix) and tmp/verify-prune-floor.ts (5/5, new).

What was wrong: recordsSinceMs returned max(coverageSinceMs, now - retentionMs). The second term is recomputed from the WALL CLOCK on every read, while pruning is irreversible. Drop a record at 25h, let the clock step back 2h, and the term moves BACK behind the record just deleted — so the window claimed coverage over a record get() can no longer return. The hydration retention filter had the identical shape via a forward-skewed mount clock.

Fix: a rise-only `prunedThroughMs` — the highest retention boundary the store has ever crossed — persisted in the attempts file and raised in three places: on prune (whether or not anything was dropped, since the boundary was still crossed), on a hydration drop, and by taking the max with the file's own value at load. recordsSinceMs is now floored by it as well, so once records older than X are gone the window never reaches behind X again, whatever the clock does. The field is optional-defaulting-to-0 so a file written before it loads unchanged and the first prune establishes a floor.

STILL OPEN — the other half, and it needs a design decision rather than a patch:
H3/S1 second half. coverageAgeMs = serverTimeMs - recordsSinceMs is a wall-clock difference taken across time on ONE machine, so a FORWARD desktop clock step inflates the claimed window and the client's monotonic submitAge comparison can then yield a false "not sent". Exposure is confined to the degraded (coverage = mount) cases, since a witness-verified window is retention-floored.

Why it is not patched: the inference it corrupts — a terminal "not sent" from an absent record — is being DISABLED anyway, because sol-architect found it unsound for a deeper reason (the overtaking race: /status can pass an admitted /answer that has not yet written in_flight, so absence cannot prove the answer will not be typed). Patching the arithmetic under a disabled inference is wasted work.

The sound fix, per sol-architect, is to stop doing temporal proofs at all: an opaque random coverageEpochId that the client captures before submitting and echoes back, rotated by the server before any coverage gap, reset, unverified restart or prune. The server then owns the proof and the client does no clock arithmetic. That also retires S2 (bridgeStartedMs is a Date.now() value treated as an identity, so two lifetimes can alias). Do it together with the durable CAS, not before.

content.subject: Witness durability rests on an undocumented rename-ordering assumption
content.description:
From sol-contract (GPT-5.6 Sol, ultra). This questions the premise the whole mechanism rests on, and the same premise underpins keys.ts SEND-WITNESS.

THE CLAIM (crypto.ts:1046, answer.ts:1410, answer.ts:1942): the witness write is made durable by the ATTEMPTS file's subsequent content fsync, because the witness's rename record sits in the same directory metadata log that the fsync flushes.

SOL'S OBJECTION: Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE, and states a volume handle is required to flush all files on a volume. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH exists as a SEPARATE, explicit move-durability guarantee, and Node exposes no equivalent durable-rename option. So "F's fsync publishes W's rename" is an incidental filesystem ordering assumption, not a documented guarantee.

IF IT IS WRONG: witness W and attempts file F can both roll back to a matching version n-1. The next mount then sees EQUAL counters, logs no degradation, has lost the record, and publishes the old coverage — and the client reports a landed answer as "never sent". That is the exact failure the witness was built to prevent, and it would be invisible.

EVIDENCE STATUS, stated honestly by Sol: it restored both pre-write files and reproduced known:false with zero degradation events and a true client age comparison — i.e. the POSTCONDITION is confirmed harmful. Whether a real NTFS hard reset can actually produce that joint rollback is REASONED, not power-cut reproduced.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS COMMIT: keys.ts's SEND-WITNESS relies on the identical assumption for send-nonce anti-rollback, where the consequence is AES-GCM nonce reuse. If the assumption is unsound, that mechanism is weaker than its comments claim too — though it fails closed (refuses to start) rather than lying.

WHAT TO DO — do not silently "fix" this, it needs a decision:
(a) Get authoritative evidence: a documented NTFS/Windows guarantee, or a real crash-consistency test (power-cut / VM reset harness), or
(b) Weaken the comments to state it as a best-effort ordering assumption rather than a proof, and say what is NOT covered, or
(c) Find a construction that does not depend on cross-file rename ordering at all — e.g. put the counter INSIDE the attempts file plus a separate append-only (never renamed) witness log, since append+fsync has no rename to lose. Note the replay cache is already structurally immune for exactly this reason (append+fsync per admit, rename only at compaction where a lost rename reverts to a SUPERSET = conservative).

Option (c) is the only one that removes the doubt rather than documenting it.

content.subject: Sol findings: clock (S1), lifetime aliasing (S2), in_flight polling (S3), boundary validation (S4)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE. Two of four fixed and pushed.

S1 clock — FIXED, server half (b272da2dd, PRUNE-FLOOR). A rise-only persisted retention floor means a backward clock step can no longer re-expose pruned records. The forward-step half is deliberately unfixed; see #21 for why (it only corrupts the inference now disabled by c03d7bb, and the sound answer is an opaque coverage epoch, not better arithmetic).

S4 boundary validation — FIXED (0d9944056). Two cross-field refinements refuse `confirmed` with a null resolvedAtMs and `failed` with a null failureCode at the disk boundary. Nothing this bridge writes produces either, so on disk they mean corruption or a hand-edit; the file is now quarantined once and loudly instead of the shape being served as truth for 24 hours. Proof tmp/verify-crossfield.ts also pins that all four real shapes still load — a rule that quarantined genuine records would be a self-inflicted outage.

STILL OPEN:

S2 bridgeStartedMs is Date.now() but the client treats equality as lifetime IDENTITY (BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:88), so two lifetimes can alias and the fallback proof is unsafe. Do NOT patch by widening the timestamp — it is the wrong primitive. It is retired wholesale by #28's opaque coverageEpochId, which replaces both temporal proofs with a server-owned identity. Fix it there.

S3 in_flight is never re-polled. The server durably records in_flight before typing (answer.ts:2383) and the repository maps it to Pending correctly, but the phone performs exactly one status read, "never in a loop" (ConversationViewModel.kt:383), and the watch converts Pending to unknown (WatchBridge.kt:529). PROTOCOL.md:1721 and :1732 REQUIRE pending display and continued polling. Scenario: the read lands during the ~15s injection window, the server later records confirmed, and the phone sits on Pending until the user intervenes while the watch shows Unconfirmed.
Not fixed tonight deliberately: this is a behavioural addition (a bounded poll loop with backoff, cancellation on resolve, and a decision about what the watch shows meanwhile), not a correction, and it interacts with #28 — if the status response becomes a discriminated union with a server-owned epoch, the polling contract should be designed against THAT rather than retrofitted twice. Either implement bounded polling or change the spec, but the two must agree.

S5 PROTOCOL §11.5 declares the proof fields required and non-null while the Kotlin serializer coerces missing, null, fractional, quoted, object, boolean and overflow values to null. Missing NEEDS that exception for old-bridge compatibility, but the spec does not say so, and coercing MALFORMED values contradicts §0's hard-error rule. Editorial + a decision about which rule wins; fold into #28's protocol work.

S6/S7 done: the fifth doc site was cleared in 83a02d0a8, and the retention constant now lives in CompanionConstants so client and server no longer duplicate it in unrelated files.

content.subject: CRITICAL: detached prune from a stopped store clobbers the new store and lowers the counter
content.description:
From sol-crash-consistency (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, EXECUTED with a probe against the real implementation). This is the most severe finding of the entire review: it needs no filesystem assumption, no clock step, and no wiring fault — just a stop/start while an hourly prune is in flight.

MECHANISM (verified by me): index.ts:654-657 fires `interval(HOUR_MS, async () => { await attempts.prune(Date.now()); ... })`. Teardown (index.ts:685-689) only does `clearInterval(timer)` — it NEVER awaits an in-flight callback. So a prune already executing when the bridge stops keeps a live reference to the OLD AttemptStore closure (its records map, its seq, its paths). Serialization and the witness read/write guard are per-INSTANCE only (answer.ts:1892-1967), so the old instance's persist() has no idea a new instance exists.

SEQUENCE (Sol's probe output): old store at F/W=2 begins prune and reads W=2 -> stop/start creates a new store which reaches F/W=3, then records an answer at F/W=4 -> the old prune resumes and writes its stale empty snapshot as W=3, F=3. Measured: before releasing the old prune F=4/W=4 records [old,new]; after F=3/W=3 records []; on reopen no degradation, the new record absent, old coverage retained. The next restart therefore TRUSTS a matching pair while a recorded answer has been destroyed -> false "it was not sent".

THIS BREAKS THE RISE-ONLY CLAIM. I verified rise-only within one instance and reported it as holding; it does not hold across instances. Math.max and the promise tail cannot see another instance's writes.

BROADER CLASS: the same detached-interval pattern covers nonceCache.compact, audit.prune and deviceStore.purgeExpiredRevocations in the same block. Check whether any of those can also clobber a successor's state. The nonce cache is the one to look at hardest, since its rollback consequence is the fatal one.

FIX DIRECTIONS: (a) make teardown await in-flight maintenance, not just clear timers — track the in-flight promise and await it in the unwind entry; (b) give each store instance an ownership token and have persist() refuse if it is no longer the owner (the anchor already has this shape for the send-nonce lifecycle); (c) both. (b) defends even against a leaked reference that outlives teardown.

Also from the same report, comment errors this invalidates: index.ts:699-704 and 723-724 claim teardown prevents old writers overlapping a new bridge — detached maintenance makes that false. And answer.ts:1457 / 1877-1882 claim witness-ahead PROVES an attempts-file version was durably written and then lost; a failure between the witness raise and the primary write produces the identical state with no such version ever existing.

content.subject: Lead: an r+ directory handle may be fsync-able on Windows, which would retire the ordering assumption
content.description:
Sol flagged the stated reason as wrong; I have now REPRODUCED it on the real runtime. Probe: tmp/dirsync-probe.ts.

MEASURED, Bun 1.3.14, win32 arm64 (the actual host-service runtime):
  open(dir,"r")  -> open OK, fsync EPERM
  open(dir,"r+") -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"a")  -> open OK, fsync OK
  open(dir,"w")  -> open FAILS EISDIR
  fsPromises open(dir,"r+") + handle.sync() -> OK
  r+ immediately after a real tmp->rename in that directory -> fsync OK

THE STATED REASON IS FALSE IN TWO WAYS. crypto.ts:1024-1026 says "Node cannot open a directory handle on win32 (fs.open on a directory fails EISDIR/EPERM)". In fact (a) opening a directory succeeds for r, r+ and a — only `w` gives EISDIR; (b) the EPERM comes from fsync on a READ-ONLY handle, which is precisely the mode the non-win32 path uses (crypto.ts:1048 `open(dir, "r")`). The gap was most likely concluded from trying `r` on Windows, getting EPERM, and generalising.

CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS: syncDirectory need not early-return on win32 (crypto.ts:1047). Renames could be made durable directly, and the cross-file rename-ordering assumption (#22) would stop being load-bearing for BOTH (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) and keys.ts SEND-WITNESS. The witness becomes defence-in-depth rather than the thing correctness rests on. That is a simplification, not more machinery.

WHAT IS STILL NOT PROVEN — do not skip this. A successful fsync call is not evidence that NTFS persisted the directory metadata log. Windows exposes no documented user-space directory-fsync, and Microsoft documents FlushFileBuffers as flushing THE SPECIFIED FILE (a volume handle is required to flush all files); the documented durable-rename primitive is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH), which Node does not surface. So FlushFileBuffers on a directory handle may be a silent no-op that returns success.

REQUIRED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING:
1. Authoritative documentation on what FlushFileBuffers does for a directory handle on NTFS, or
2. A crash-consistency test (VM hard-reset / power-cut harness) showing a rename survives with the directory fsync and can be lost without it.

A syncDirectory that appears to work but does not would be WORSE than an honest no-op, because every mechanism above it would stop compensating. If the evidence cannot be obtained, the correct outcome is to FIX THE COMMENT's stated reason (it is wrong regardless) while keeping the no-op and the witness.

Related: #22 (the assumption this could retire), #24 (unaffected by this — the lifecycle race is not a durability problem).

content.subject: Short writes (R1), counter saturation (R2), fifth doc site (R3), comment errors (R4)
content.description:
PARTIALLY DONE in 563c41b56.

FIXED:
- R1 writeFileDurable now checks the bytesWritten Node returns and throws before the rename, so a short write can no longer be fsync'd and renamed as though complete (which previously lost every record in the file at the next start, via quarantine).
- R3 the doc-rot list was five sites, not four — all five cleared, plus the harness heading.
- R4 partial: crypto.ts's syncDirectory reason (measurably wrong — a directory opens fine under Bun on win32 arm64 and r+ fsync succeeds; only the read-only mode gives EPERM) is corrected with the measured results and the reason the no-op nonetheless stays. index.ts's teardown-ordering claim is corrected and now true by construction thanks to MAINTENANCE-DRAIN.

STILL OPEN:
- R2 both schemas accept Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for the rewrite counter while persist() increments it: load ...991 -> write ...992 -> the next increment yields the SAME value -> the following start rejects and quarantines it. Unreachable by human usage, reachable from a schema-valid nonsense file. Bound the schema below MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or treat saturation as a degrade rather than letting it self-corrupt.
- R4 remainder: answer.ts:1609-1611 says the store never refuses startup — now TRUE after the B1 fix, so re-read it and confirm rather than assume. answer.ts:1726-1728 still claims a failed quarantine rename proves the later durable write would also fail, which an obstruction only at the quarantine destination disproves. The "rise-only" wording still needs scoping: it holds within one store instance and below the numeric boundary, but #24 showed it did not hold across lifecycle overlap (now fixed by the drain) and R2 shows it does not hold at saturation.
- R5 the B1 fix does cover the full error class Sol named (ENOSPC, EACCES, sync/close, failed replacement) because it catches everything raiseWitness can throw rather than matching on codes — worth keeping that way rather than narrowing to specific errno values.

content.subject: Altitude findings: pending-destroy key leak (A1), watch Confirmed downgrade (A2), witness factoring (A3)
content.description:
A1 pending-destroy key leak — FIXED and pushed (c1d6dcca5, ORPHAN-SWEEP). Re-derives the wipe obligation from ground truth (key files whose keyRef appears in no index record) instead of adding a third witness, so a lost journal rename costs one start's delay rather than a permanent leak. KeyStore.list() reads names only, never parses, so an orphan is destroyable even when corrupt or bound to a previous install. The sweep runs at CONSTRUCTION only, argued structurally: keys.put() creates the key file before create() records it and put is outside the store's serialiser, so on the purge path a brand-new device's key is legitimately unreferenced and a sweep would brick a phone mid-pairing. `referenced` spans revoked-but-unpurged records too, because §5.1 keeps a revoked device's key on purpose. Proof tmp/a1-orphan-sweep.ts reproduces the leak end to end and shows the referenced key surviving. Written by a subagent that died on an API timeout; I reviewed the diff, both call sites and the set arithmetic before committing.

A2 watch Confirmed downgrade — FIXED and pushed (c03d7bb). rank/supersedes now live on WatchAnswerStatus in core/, which both surfaces already shared for the wire, so there is ONE definition of which status may replace which instead of a phone lattice plus an open-coded watch approximation. QuestionStore refuses a non-superseding incoming. 10 new tests including the UNKNOWN-after-phone-restart relay specifically. AnswerOutcome deliberately stayed in app-phone.

STILL OPEN, all structural rather than defects:

A3 witness factoring. keys.ts and answer.ts hold the same machine (rise-only integer beside a durable file, raised before it, generation-bound, max-at-start, gap->verdict) differing only in mark type and verdict severity. The ordering invariant is prose in three places and enforced by nothing. Do it when a THIRD dependent is proposed, not before — and factor ONLY the ordering and mark read/write/compare, leaving each caller's verdict local. sol-architect's shape is better than a boolean flag: return typed evidence (verified / uninitialized / untrusted+reason) and let the consumer map it to policy, so the fatal-vs-degrade distinction cannot be inverted by an argument. Note that #28 may retire this entirely by moving the ledger to SQLite.

A4 extraction of attempt-store.ts. Better motivated than first thought: the 866-line block takes EXACTLY ONE identifier from the rest of answer.ts (GUARD_CLASSES, used once as a zod enum key source), so the module boundary already exists and the file layout hides it. Cost, all in ONE commit: move GUARD_CLASSES + GuardClass to types.ts or attempt-store.ts -> answer.ts closes an import cycle, then update the FEATURES.md (ATTEMPT-WITNESS) marker path or the gate fails. Deferred tonight so a rename would not bury the behavioural diff.

A5 doc duplication is SEVEN production sites, not four. Canonical home should be PROTOCOL.md §11.5. The marker gate cannot help (grep -rqsF is a presence check; content equality would fail the build on every wording improvement). The one real structural lever: the semantics already have executable copies in AnswerStatusCoverageTest.kt and provesNeverSent — name §11.5 in the test names and treat that file as the second normative copy. Partially addressed in 83a02d0a8 (types.ts made canonical for TS, answer.ts and index.ts reduced to pointers); the Kotlin and FEATURES.md sites remain.

A6 the evidence bar in crypto.ts for retiring the syncDirectory no-op will never be cleared in CI, so record that both witnesses are PERMANENT rather than provisional. If evidence ever arrives, KEEP them as defence-in-depth — their detection surface is strictly larger (single-file AV quarantine-restore, per-file version restore, a copied companion tree, generation-bound anchor replacement; a directory fsync sees none of those) but DROP the raise-before-write coupling, which is the fragile half and the only half a working fsync retires.

content.subject: Overtaking race: absence cannot prove not-sent without a durable CAS fence
content.description:
From sol-architect (GPT-5.6 Sol ultra, ~3.5h). The deepest finding of the session: none of the other eight reviewers found it, and it invalidates the actionable-negative feature independently of the witness.

THE RACE (verified by me): handleAnswer reads the attempt record at answer.ts:2309 and does not durably record in_flight until answer.ts:2504 — 195 lines and several awaits later, spanning guard evaluation and lock acquisition. So:
  1. /v1/answer is admitted, pauses before writing in_flight
  2. /v1/answer/status overtakes it, finds no record, the coverage proof holds
  3. the phone reports the terminal "it was not sent"
  4. the original /answer resumes, writes in_flight, and TYPES THE ANSWER
The user then answers a picker that was already answered, which §11.4 records as unrecoverable. HTTP cancellation does not help: the server snapshots its freshness time before several awaits (http.ts:1119).

WHY THE WITNESS CANNOT FIX THIS: the witness proves things about the PAST. This is a claim about the FUTURE — that an already-admitted request will not act. No amount of durable-state attestation closes it.

IMMEDIATE MITIGATION (in progress, fix-client-two): proven absence resolves to Unconfirmed instead of a terminal Failed. Positive stored statuses are unaffected. This is a deliberate capability regression, not a bug, and the code says so.

THE REAL FIX — durable per-request compare-and-set with a tombstone:
  existing state | /answer            | authoritative /status
  absent         | CAS to in_flight   | CAS to closed_not_received
  in_flight/done | idempotent replay  | return known status
  closed_...     | REFUSE to type     | return not_received
Whichever wins persists BEFORE either typing or returning a terminal negative. If the status-side CAS cannot be persisted, the result stays unconfirmed. A non-atomic check-then-insert is insufficient.

SOL'S PREFERRED TARGET, and I agree it is the right end state: move the attempt ledger into the host SQLite database the bridge already receives, rather than the hand-rolled two-file protocol.
  - SQLite gives the transaction the CAS needs, and `synchronous=FULL` gives DOCUMENTED per-commit durability instead of an undocumented cross-file rename-ordering inference (which is #22, and which crypto.ts now admits is an inference).
  - states: in_flight, the outcomes, effect_indeterminate, closed_not_received
  - opaque random coverageEpochId instead of wall-clock proof (retires #21's remainder and S2's aliasing)
  - server returns a DISCRIMINATED outcome; the client does no proof arithmetic
  - no typing until in_flight is durably committed
  - epoch rotates transactionally before pruning or any acknowledged continuity loss
  - coupling answer availability to host.db is APPROPRIATE: if the ledger cannot commit, typing safely is impossible
  Cost: schema migration, a small repository layer, transition tests. Retires the witness, both clock findings, S2, and most of #22.

ALSO FROM THIS REVIEW, worth keeping:
- "rollback detected" is too strong a phrase in the logs. Witness-ahead can mean a real rollback OR a crash between the two ordered writes. The evidence is "pair mismatch / continuity lost"; the cause is unknown.
- The two client proofs are combined as an OR, which is not extra safety — it is two independent ways to authorise "not sent", so each must be independently sound. Neither currently is.
- Validate response.requestId against the requested id; reject contradictory shapes (known=false with a terminal status) and degrade to Unconfirmed.
- The 28-check decision table lives in gitignored tmp/ and is enforced by nothing. That lets prose, TypeScript and Kotlin all agree on the wrong model. Commit shared protocol vectors and run them in BOTH languages in CI; assign stable invariant IDs (e.g. "a terminal negative implies a durable rejection fence") and reference the IDs from comments instead of copying paragraphs.
- Quiet bets now explicit: NTFS keeps its undocumented ordering; wall clocks are monotonic enough to authorise a destructive retry; timestamp equality is process identity; client cancellation means the server cannot later act; both paired files are never restored together; Android process memory lasts as long as the advertised 24h window.
- A whole-directory / volume-snapshot / backup rollback of both files is fundamentally undetectable by any two-file design. Detecting it needs an independent trust domain (TPM-backed state or a remote monotonic authority) — disproportionate here, but the limitation should be stated rather than implied.

content.subject: SQLite answer ledger with transactional CAS and coverage epoch
content.description:
DONE — schema, migration, ledger module, and proof. Not yet wired into the bridge (that is the next step) and not committed.

Schema (src/db/schema.ts, migration 0012 generated via `bun run generate`, never hand-written): `answer_attempts` keyed by requestId with the five statuses plus the new `closed_not_received` TOMBSTONE, and a dedicated single-row `answer_coverage_epoch`. Written by the first agent before it died mid-stream; I reviewed and kept it. Its reasoning was good — `createdAtMs` separate from `startedAtMs` so retention has one unambiguous clock across both row shapes, a dedicated epoch table rather than host_settings (that table is nullable user knobs any settings path can write; this is a notNull safety token the ledger must own), and `effect_indeterminate` deliberately NOT added because it is not distinct from `unconfirmed` here.

Module (src/companion/attempt-ledger.ts, written by me after the agent died): claimForAnswer / resolveStatus / recordOutcome / get / prune / rotateEpoch / currentEpoch. The CAS is `INSERT .. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` inside one transaction, so exactly one caller sees changes===1 — a decision procedure rather than a race. A SELECT-then-INSERT there would be the very bug being replaced.

Key implementation facts worth keeping:
- drizzle's better-sqlite3 transactions are SYNCHRONOUS callbacks, so the whole CAS is sync. Async wrappers would have broken atomicity.
- `tx as HostDb` does not typecheck and should not: a transaction has no $client. Helpers take a structural `Queryable = Pick<HostDb, "select"|"insert"|"update"|"delete">` that both satisfy.
- PRAGMA synchronous is ASSERTED to be FULL and fails loud. createDb does not set it, and in WAL mode NORMAL means a commit survives a process crash but NOT power loss — losing a committed in_flight claim is exactly the rollback the fence prevents. It fails rather than silently setting it because the connection is shared with the rest of the host service.
- recordOutcome updates WHERE status = 'in_flight'. That predicate is a safety property: without it an outcome could overwrite a tombstone and erase the fence, or revive a row a concurrent prune dropped. An orphaned outcome logs loudly and never throws (keystrokes may already have landed).
- Rows are validated individually at the read boundary, so one corrupt row costs ONE requestId its status — the JSON file quarantined all 24h of everyone's records for one bad one.

Proof tmp/verify-answer-ledger.ts, 20/20 against a real database:
- the overtaking race in BOTH orders (status-first plants the fence and the admitted answer is then refused permanently; answer-first claims and status reports in_flight)
- 32 concurrent claims -> exactly 1 winner, 31 idempotent replays
- a tombstone is never written over a real row
- a stale or absent coverage epoch degrades and plants NO fence
- pruning rotates in the same transaction, so a pruned request is never reported never-received
- an outcome cannot erase a tombstone, and the orphan is reported
- an incoherent row is refused and its neighbour is unaffected

UNLOCK that made this testable: better-sqlite3 has no win-arm64 binding here and the old tmp stub answered every query with nothing, so no database path had ever run locally. It is now a real shim over bun:sqlite (tmp/better-sqlite3-shim.js, in both gitignored node_modules). Real migrations, WAL, synchronous=FULL, real `changes` counts. The shim THROWS on anything unimplemented rather than returning a wrong answer.

content.subject: Pre-existing: pairing probe fails to open the step-4 sealed response
content.description:
RESOLVED — the bridge was right, the probe was four revisions stale. tmp/companion-pairing-check.ts now reports ALL PASS.

This mattered because that probe is the only genuine INTEROP test of the pairing key schedule: it implements the phone side from PROTOCOL.md §3.1/§4.4 rather than reusing the bridge's own helpers. It had been failing, and a red harness gets ignored — so "does pairing actually work" was unanswered while nothing had ever paired on hardware.

Four retired contracts it was asserting, each one the probe lagging a hardening:

1. K_dev derived as hkdfExpandLabel(prk, LABEL + pid + deviceId) — the ids as base64url TEXT. crypto.ts's INTEROP NOTE records that §3.1 was ambiguous, that the two sides once declared OPPOSITE conventions so pairing could never succeed, and that it was resolved in favour of RAW BYTES to match the Android client's KeyDerivation. Fixed with hkdfExpandInfo + hkdfInfoWithSuffix over decoded id bytes. This was the cause of the unknown_device failure.
2. The step-4 AAD in RESPONSE form (inventing a twelve-zero-byte nonce and a literal 200). §4.4 step 4 enumerates the REQUEST form — there is no client request nonce on that hop (the LAN messages are cleartext JSON, not envelopes) and no status code the client can bind before reading the body. pairing.ts records that an earlier revision did exactly what the probe was still doing, the AADs differed by 16 bytes, and every pairing failed the GCM tag as pair_bad_mac — indistinguishable from a real MITM.
3. createDeviceStore(dir) — it now requires the state anchor and key store, and (ONE-STORE-PER-ANCHOR) forbids two stores owning one anchor, so a simulated restart must close the previous anchor first.
4. Opaque keyRef strings ("k1", "k2"). keyRef must now be a canonical 22-char base64url id, because a keyRef named after anything guessable let a replayed deviceId overwrite a live device's K_dev before create() could refuse.

Evidence obtained, which is the point: K_dev derives IDENTICALLY on both sides, the step-4 sealed response opens, macDesktop verifies, and every negative path holds — bad MAC burns the window after three, wrong pid gives pair_wrong_peer, v=2 gives pair_version_unsupported, attempts are rate limited, and nothing is stored on any failure.

From opus-rev-client on f25e438, all verified independently, all PRE-EXISTING rather than regressions. Apply only after every reviewer has reported, to avoid editing files they are reading.

F1 (severe) BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:405-406 — read-back FetchResult.Failure maps to terminal AnswerOutcome.Failed, violating §11.6. Blast radius: :453 overwrites a stored Confirmed with Failed; QuestionSheet.kt:542-570 renders Failed as terminal and removes the resolve affordance; WatchBridge.kt:514-520 relays FAILED while app-watch's own failed-read path correctly keeps unconfirmed. Fix: map read failure to Unconfirmed; reserve Failed for status=="failed".

F2 BridgeCompanionRepository.kt:417-421 and :365-369 — confirmed/absent resolvedAtMs yields Failed(INTERNAL). Should be Unconfirmed.

F3 Answer.kt:430-433 — questionId/resolvedAtMs/failureCode are nullable without `= null` defaults, so an omitted key throws ProtocolException and lands in F1's path. The three new proof fields do have defaults; the asymmetry is the defect.

F4 Answer.kt:506-511 — provesNeverSent ignores status, so known:false + in_flight still licenses "not sent". Guard: require status in {UNKNOWN, UNCONFIRMED}.

F5 Answer.kt:473-480 — no plausibility bound on the claimed window; bounded to 24h only incidentally by the retention gate. Cap coverageAgeMs at ATTEMPT_RECORD_RETENTION_MS to make it structural.

F6 (mine, contract review) PROTOCOL.md §11.5 degrade-case list omits "no install generation supplied", though it reads as exhaustive. Production cannot reach it (openStateAnchor throws unless the generation is canonical) but the list should be complete.

VERIFIED CLEAN, do not re-investigate: field names/casing/types/units match exactly both sides; comparison strictness is `>` in client, PROTOCOL.md:1670 and types.ts:986; retention 86_400_000 both sides with an independent server clamp; no surviving trace in either repo of the corrected false claim about `confirmed` surviving restarts; elapsedRealtime cannot yield a too-small submitAgeMs (writeLifetimes is process-scoped, a reboot kills the holder); partial proof-field sets decline correctly; app-watch has no duplicate decision.
